Forza Horizon 5 isn’t just a racing game for me — it’s my “drop in and breathe” game. It’s the closest thing we have to a driving‑Minecraft: a beautiful open world where I can put on my own music, cruise, and unwind.  But after years of playing it this way, I can see exactly where the next Horizon game needs to evolve to support players who use the game as a driving sandbox, not just a race checklist.  This review isn’t about negativity — it’s about wanting the series to embrace the peaceful, immersive side of driving that FH5 already hints at.  1. FH5 is at its best when you’re just… driving The map is gorgeous. The lighting is incredible. The cars feel great.  But the game isn’t fully built for the people who want to:  cruise  explore  vibe  listen to their own playlists  enjoy sunsets and weather  treat the world like a meditative space  FH5 accidentally supports this playstyle. FH6 should support it intentionally.  2. We need a true Zen Mode A mode where:  all race UI disappears  no pop‑ups  no notifications  no skill score spam  no minimap  no “event nearby” interruptions  no festival chatter  Just the car, the world, and the road.  3. Let us control the world more FH6 needs:  time‑of‑day sliders  weather frequency controls  longer sunsets  longer nights  season duration options  Let players shape their own vibe.  4. Bigger maps or connected regions FH6 should explore:  longer highways  multi‑region maps  seamless travel between DLC areas  no immersion‑breaking loading screens  Even if it’s technically challenging, the dream is simple:  Let me drive from the base map into the DLC without teleporting.  5. Use Bing Maps to build something massive Playground Games already has access to real‑world terrain data. FH6 could finally give us:  real‑scale highways  long uninterrupted roads  natural terrain variety  a world that feels big, not just pretty  6. FH5 is great, but FH6 could be transcendent FH5 nails:  visuals  car feel  freedom  vibes  But FH6 could become the ultimate driving sandbox if it embraces:  zen mode  world controls  bigger maps  seamless DLC travel  longer roads  immersion‑first design  ⭐ 7. The interior camera needs to be dynamic Cockpit view is one of the most immersive ways to play, but FH5’s interior camera is:  stiff  poorly positioned in some cars  blocked by roll cages  inconsistent across vehicles  FH6 needs:  dynamic camera movement  seat height/distance sliders  FOV options  automatic adjustment around roll cages  optional head sway for realism  ⭐ 8. Traffic density and AI behavior need improvement FH5’s traffic is:  inconsistent  unnatural  sometimes empty  sometimes chaotic  prone to teleporting  FH6 needs:  adjustable traffic density  smarter AI  smoother lane changes  better spacing  less despawning  This would massively improve immersion for cruising players.  ⭐ 9. Let us play our own music through the car’s simulated sound system FH6 could simulate:  real‑world car audio tuning  cabin acoustics  speaker placement  bass response  EQ profiles per manufacturer  Letting players use their own music with in‑car audio simulation would be a game‑changer for immersion.  ⭐ Summary Forza Horizon 5 is one of the best “just drive and chill” games ever made. But the next Horizon title needs to fully embrace that side of the player base — the ones who treat the game like a peaceful open‑world driving simulator.  Give us the tools to shape our own experience, and FH6 could become something truly special.

After 103 hours in the driver's seat, you’ve clearly moved past the "honeymoon phase" and into the "lifestyle" phase of Forza Horizon 5. At this point, the game isn't just a racer; it’s a digital automotive playground that remains one of the best-looking and most satisfying experiences in gaming, even as we head into 2026.  Here is a short review tailored to your 100+ hour perspective:  Forza Horizon 5: The Ultimate Automotive Sandbox The "Feel" of the Road After 100 hours, you know that FH5’s greatest strength isn't just the car list—it's the physics. It strikes the perfect "sim-cade" balance: accessible enough to drift a supercar with a controller, but deep enough to reward a steering wheel setup. Every surface, from the scorched sands of the Dunas Blancas to the slippery jungle floors, feels distinct under your tires.  Why 103 Hours is Just the Beginning The Content Loop: Between the Festival Playlists that rotate weekly and the Accolades system, there is always a "carrot" on a stick. You're never just driving; you're unlocking a rare 2024 Lamborghini Revuelto or hunting down that last elusive Bonus Board.  Visual Splendor: Even years after launch, the lighting engine is a masterclass. Whether it's a tropical storm rolling over the coast or the sun setting over the Gran Caldera volcano, the game remains a benchmark for "photo mode" addicts.  Endless Variety: With 11 unique biomes and over 800 cars, the game wards off burnout by letting you switch gears—literally. One hour you're doing 200mph street races in Guanajuato, the next you're building a rock-crawling Jeep for the Baja tracks.  The Community & Creative Edge The EventLab has evolved into a powerhouse, with the community creating everything from technical drift circuits to "Hot Wheels" style gravity-defying tracks. It’s this endless stream of user-generated content that makes 100 hours feel like a warm-up.  Verdict: Forza Horizon 5 is the rare game that respects your time while constantly demanding more of it. It’s a vibrant, loud, and beautiful celebration of car culture that somehow never runs out of gas.

Horizon 5 is such a strange game to talk about, because while I'd say it's the best game in the series it has loads of flaws many of which have been carried forward from previous entries, sometimes over a decade old.  Mexico (and Sierra Nueva in the dlc) is an absolutely beautiful map, from the desert to the jungles to the volcano, to the mountain and the valley, to Guanajuato the extremely vibrant city. But a large portion of the map is just fields, and these fields make up the central area of the map where players are most likely to pass through. All of the amazing features of Mexico are concentrated around the outer edges of the map, and Guanajuato itself is also terribly small.   The story is bad. Awful, even. Previous entries didn't have a good story either but (aside from 4 which this is a direct sequel to) they were bad in the normal racing game way, that is to say you could just ignore it and nobody cares because we're here to race cars. Here it's just, so so so so terribly grating. Endless empty corporate positivity everywhere, the speaking of what I think was an attempt at spanglish? in a way that absolutely nobody has ever spoken. It didn't even seem out of place when I got to the hot wheels dlc and Haley just spoke advertisements for toys at me the entire time because really that's just the next logical step when your characters sit somewhere between middle management, HR personnel, and that one pepsi commercial with the riot police.  Cars are good, there's a lot of them. For the first time in the series the mods you put on can effect your engine's sound so you can audibly hear the difference between things like the exhaust options. The new handling model is rather great, though it does feel like it leads to annoying levels of oversteer on RWD cars at times. An annoying amount of cars are stuck behind wheelspins or whatever live service thing they wanted to shove in for no reason, though. Seriously you could just buy the Trueno immediately in 1-3 why have 4 and 5 decided to banish it to live service purgatory.  Unlike in 4 you can't set back the date on your computer to get old series rewards, if you're not connected to the internet it just pays out wheelspins as rewards instead. This is stupid and bad, why are you locking cars behind the auction house? There's not even a profit motive for it which makes it even stranger.  The PI system is still bad and extremely easy to game, because of the way it's calculated you can do things like have an AWD swap that costs almost nothing or cram an absurd amount of power into a given class cap because the AI driver used to calculate scores by driving it around a simulated test track always uses the default tune, so you can do things like adjust sway bars to fix understeer or adjust the gearing ratio to actually be able to use all of that power and it won't have any sort of impact on your car's class despite it clearly being much better than what the simulation suggests. This also makes online racing much less satisfying, because even without relying on these quirks to make a better build than what should be possible you can still end up with major performance discrepancies between the two PI numbers, and it can start to feel less like you're winning/losing due to skill differences and more like it's just a simple gap between the cars. Winning because I can corner better and at higher speeds is fun, winning because my car can corner better and go faster isn't.  Progression is basically nonexistent, you do races and then pick whatever story thing you wanna do next whether it's a showcase race where the rigging to be a photo finish has never been more obvious or an expedition where you drive around a closed off area of the map smashing stuff (these are still fun though). It's all entirely disconnected from me actually playing the game. There's no car class or type limitations on anything. If you wanna go through the entire game in nothing but the 2020 supra they give you at the start you can. Actually there is one limitation and that's with the midnight battles, which were added in a post-launch update and there's only 4.  Speaking of disconnected from me actually playing the game, wheelspins. Introduced in 2 (4 added junk item like horns and clothes to the pool) they're just lootboxes (you can't pay money for them though). You get either a random car, a random amount of money from 5-300k, a random piece of clothing, or a new car horn sound. Get unlucky on a wheelspin, you get basically nothing. Get lucky and suddenly you've gained either a car that sells for a substantial amount on the auction house or a bunch of credits, about 20 race's worth. At any given time I tend to be sitting on 1-3m in credits and an insignificant amount of these are actually earned via skilled racing. There's no accomplishment felt when buying one of the more expensive cars because I didn't actually *do* anything to earn it, I just got lucky on a lottery.  The livery editor and the vinyl maker are largely the same as they've been since 2. Gran Turismo has had SVG importing options since Sport which released in 2017, before Horizon 4 came out.  The AI cheats massively, if first and second can get away by the fourth corner you just restart the race because they're going to continue getting faster and faster to the point you can't catch up. Conversely if you get out in front the race is a time attack as the AI will make no attempts to overtake and will instead slowly fall further and further behind until half the pack DNFs. They have much better grip than the player and also follow the racing line extremely closely even when it's wrong, so the player can easily overtake in corners where they brake entirely too much (most noticeable on dirt or the hot wheels races)   Road, Street, and Dirt races all have mostly good layouts, and 5's new physics model makes dirt super fun to race on as well, so my only major critique here is dear god why are there so many walls. It's hard to take the McRae approach to rally when sliding slightly off the road actually means slamming in to the solid concrete wall set up right at the edge of every single corner. Also gives rise to wall riding, remove the walls and suddenly people who can't brake just go flying off the course instead of launching out of the corner in the right direction.  The anti-wall riding penalty in online is stupid. Someone slams into your rear instead of braking and you hit the wall? Five second slowdown penalty. Misjudge your braking zone and slam into the wall, stopping in the process and losing more time than taking it properly would've taken? Five second slowdown penalty. Intentionally go into a corner too fast but pull the handbrake to bounce the rear corner of your car off the wall? No penalty at all. Great system.  Cross Country races are bad. They have been bad since they were introduced in 2. I don't know who thought sweeping right into sweeping left into blind jump was good race design but it isn't. Full throttle for most of the race, and then rewind 15 times because you took the jump at a slightly wrong angle and either didn't land close enough to the checkpoint or you landed in such a way that you will go slamming into a building instead of through the narrow alley the next checkpoint is in. These are bad and they suck, please either stop making them in favor of more proper rally events or at least design them in a way that can be done without rewind.  Half the difficulty options don't even give you more credits anymore. Normal > Sim steering, Manual > M/C, Cosmetic > Full damage, and rewind off don't give more rewards despite taking more skillful play.  I really, really like the horizon series and it's a lot of fun but god does it have flaws some of which are over a decade old. Horizon 5 is still fun and it's absolutely worth the money, but it's not perfect. I really hope 6 brings major improvements to the franchise. Overall 8~9/10

This has been the first modern Forza game I've played since Forza motorsport 3 / 4 and honestly, if I could rate this as a maybe, rather than yes or no I would.   The game shoves are lot in your face from the start, and takes you out of what you're doing to show you something you probably wont care about nor want to do at that time, a notification would suffice rather than an abduction.  The map is diverse and the tracks are relatively entertaining, but dreadfully short other than for a couple specific examples that rarely come up. This is made worse by the tiny selection of them that are available to you when you go for PVP in each category, you will get to know the tracks available very quickly.  The number of manufacturers in the game is surprisingly wide, but for most the selection isn't that deep, for example the game includes a huge number of Porsche models that you will just stockpile before something interesting comes along.  Player base itself is probably one of the more ego fuelled cesspits I've come across in racing games, does not matter whether its cooperative modes or PVP, someone is out there every session to make your time miserable.  The system in place to penalise mistakes is very open to abuse, you can be rammed / T-boned / ridden into a wall and then be penalised with a speed reduction to top it off; the number of times I have been stopped dead and then suffocated by a 10 second crawl is maddening.  Rarely have I seen this trigger if you actually benefit from the contact.  This comes back to the tracks being too short, as any mistake often results in very little opportunity to catch up; you can be side by side with another player approaching a checkpoint and get pushed off the track at the last moment to miss said checkpoint, and that's it, race pretty much over for you.  With all that said, and I'm leaving things out, I probably will end up playing this with my group still, but the jury is out on whether I'll consider FH6.

Forza Horizon 5 feels like a vacation you actually keep going back to.  Most open-world games are theme parks: loud, impressive, and exhausting after a few hours. FH5 is different. It’s more like landing in a country where every road accidentally leads to something fun. You don’t log in with a plan—you just drive, and the game quietly rearranges your mood.  What surprised me most isn’t the cars (they’re flawless) or the map (huge, varied, beautiful), but how low-stress everything is. You can win without sweating, explore without a checklist, and switch from a hypercar to a rusty old truck without the game judging you. It respects your time and your vibe.  The sound design deserves its own trophy. Engines don’t just rev—they argue, purr, scream, and occasionally sound slightly unhinged, which somehow makes even casual drives feel intentional. Add dynamic weather that actually changes how you drive (sandstorms are humbling), and Mexico starts feeling less like a map and more like a place.  Is it perfect? No. Progression can feel a bit too generous, and the UI sometimes throws rewards at you like it’s afraid you’ll leave. But honestly? That generosity is part of the charm. FH5 doesn’t want to challenge your patience—it wants to be the game you boot up when you just want to feel good.  If you want a racing game that feels competitive, buy something else. If you want a racing game that feels alive, this is it.

Great game. It is arcade-style racing in an invented city and race tracks, as opposed to the more sim-like Assetto Corsa. It has fantastic cars that feel great, from classics to modern, from asphalt to dirt. I play it with a controller. Premium Edition is the one to get as it includes the expansions and most of the car packs. It's not without faults, but I can easily recommend this fun racing game. More details below.  [h2]+Respects your time[/h2]  One of the reasons I really like this game is because it gets the basics right. The cars, how they look/drive/sound. But most especially, it doesn't waste my time. I'll credit two hallmark features of the franchise for that: driving line and rewind.  Forza provides a driving line, which not only helps get positioned for turn-ins but also shows braking zones. Forza additionally has rewind. So if I blow a corner I can try it again immediately until I get it right. That means I can win most races "first try", depending on the difficulty settings and how well I know the car. I don't have to spend hours getting to know tracks. Instead I can focus on experiencing all the different races and challenges. And even doing that, the game has an immense amount of content. At 70 hrs in, I've done all of the base and hotwheels races, and have just started on the rally expansion.  [h2]-Gameplay Gripes[/h2]  There are some issues that hurt enjoyment of the game that are worth mentioning, but aren't deal-breakers.  [h3]Dumb Drift Events[/h3]  I quite like drifting. I'm constantly sliding into corners as I make my way to events. However drift events/zones are horrible. First, their scoring sucks. For example, you must counter steer during the drift to get points, but counter steering will take you out of the drift. Whereas long beautiful throttle drifts thru sweepers don't count for much. So getting the best score devolves into fishtailing back and forth. Which is more tedious than fun.  Second, drift zones/events are temperamental. Zones will cancel themselves sometimes if you spin out or go too far off the road. If it gets canceled, you can't rewind back to before that happened -- you have to completely start it over. Also rewinding cancels your skill combos. So if you accidentally or instinctively hit rewind during that 50k x5 skill combo you've been building... poof. Completely wasted your time. Might as well start the whole thing over. It's infuriating.  [h3]GPS Takeovers[/h3]  I've learned to absolutely hate speed zones, drift zones, and community events. Because most of the time I go thru them incidentally on my way to some other event. I'm in a car that I'm having fun driving. Not in one I would use to set records in those zones. Nevertheless, as I go thru them, they take over my GPS.  There are quite a few events that are in the middle of speed/drift zones. So after I make it to the end of the zone and the GPS goes back to the original destination, I realize I have to turn around and go back to my actual destination. This time, going around the zone entrance so it doesn't take over my GPS again. Grr.  Community events might be worse. Twice during my last play session, I happened to pass thru a community event as it started. It completely took over not only the GPS but the UI with warnings and messages to get back to the community zone. I have to manually quit out of the event to make it go away.  [h3]Greedy Car Packs[/h3]  I understand why some car packs exist. Some very desirable cars came out subsequent to the game launch. Such as the Porsche 718 Cayman GT4 RS or the C8 Corvette Z06. And I'm sure the mfgs want a licensing fee to include them. So things like that make some sense, but most of the non-included packs feel like greedy cash grabs. The pricing is laughable.  [h3]Cannot Replay Intro[/h3]  I wanted to try to get someone else into the game. A great way to do that would have been to let them play the amazing intro race. But I already played thru it and there is no option to replay it. Apparently the only way is to create a new Xbox profile. This is completely asinine, especially considering they spent 6 months building the intro.  [h3]Bugs[/h3]  I encountered a serious bug which has not been fixed. It occurs when you start the Hotwheels expansion. It makes the Hotwheels park your "home". Which apparently also kicks you offline permanently. The game acts like you can join until the last couple of seconds, then the timer disappears. This can be fixed by setting one of your houses on the Mexico map as your home. But it's very hard to discover the problem. I missed some seasonal stuff because of this.  A slightly less serious bug occurs with one of the major events (with a large map icon). I don't remember the name, but it's a race against monster trucks. If your computer has a high frame rate, due to how vehicle animation is coded, it becomes impossible to win because your competitors are too fast. The workaround is to use rewind right before the finish line, then cancel the rewind. This will reset the position of the other trucks and allow you to win.

This game is a mixed bag of good, community focused upgrades, quality of life features, but also some drawbacks that (in my opinion) make this game a flawed misstep in how to present this franchise. No matter if this review is marked as recommended or not, it really could be both, so don't interpret too much into that.   [h3]The good:[/h3] [list] [*]Graphics: To no ones surprise, this game is graphically gorgeous and very detailed, just like it's expected by Playground Games. Together with those great graphics, this game also runs very well and still looks pretty good on lower settings.  [*]Voicelines: The main character we play finally has voicelines, which makes quiet a difference for story missions, which are far more tolerable now that the conversations flows both ways.  [*]Breakable objects: Breakable objects are now easier to differentiate from solid unbreakable objects, especially on Trees and fences.  [*]Sound Physics: The Sound Physics have been significantly improved compared to Forza Horizon 4 to the point where I prefer not swapping motors on cars for performance improvements, just to keep the sound.  [*]Steam Deck and Linux Compatibility: This game and it's full feature set works flawlessly on Linux and runs (in my experience) better on Linux than on Windows. Online works and playing with friends too.  [*]Accessibility: This game is very accessible to disabled people. Before you buy, check if the required accessibility settings for your disability is included in this game. The Dialogues are even ASL interpreted.  [*]Custom Map Editor: The Super7 Map Editor together with a bunch of improvements has been added to Horizon 5s Event Lab editor, meaning you can create a whole new world inside the world of Forza Horizon 5 or Event Lab Island, which is a completely flat surface that you can build anything on. The Community has done incredible things with it and it takes my breath every time I see it. [/list]  [h3]The bad:[/h3] [list] [*]Radio: The radio went on my nerves pretty quickly in comparison to Forza Horizon 4, mainly because I don't feel like it fits the Festival setting. The music looping can make longer races (especially the Goliath race) very stale. I would like to have an option to enable and disable loops in game. You can already do so with mods, but I'd like to have confirmation from Playground Games that these kinds of mods are specifically allowed. What could also help with variety would be a fisher yates shuffle and more than 20 songs per radio.  [*]Flat World: The world feels very flat and doesn't have a lot of verticality. The mountain in the middle of the map does not help with that. It is very apparent that this map is optimized for "The Eliminator" gamemode, which is Forza Horizons equivalent for a battle royale gamemode. This optimization doesn't do the mode well either because it shifts away from skill and tactical driving like in Forza Horizon 4s map to just plain "better car = better chance". In Horizon 4 you were able to win a lot of Head to Head races, just by knowing the map and where to drive in order to not get stuck somewhere or get significant slowdowns. I don't like the mode itself either, which makes it sad that the map is optimized for this and nothing else.  [/list]  [h3]The ugly:[/h3] [list] [*]Realism: This game is trying to be as realistic as possible and usually sacrifices some realistic features for fun, but there's one outlier. It's the traffic, or the lack thereof. It is realistic that there are almost no cars on the road, but it also makes the game boring long term and I did go back to playing Forza Horizon 4 just to have something to dodge around. Something I'd like to see is an option for realistic and increased traffic. This would make me come back to this game more often just to drive around the map for fun.  What annoy me as well though is that the streets are unreasonably wide. I get that it makes sense to make streets wider for gameplay, but this is just too much. Something I'd like to see again would be denser roads,like they were in Forza Horizon 3. I would love to see that again. Maybe something like Rushhour times would be cool as well.  [*]Terrain Physics: In this game even if you have only 1 or 2 tires on Asphalt, you have full grip as if you were right on the road. You don't get penalized for getting off the road at all really. We need to go a few steps back, because this is just not the way.  [*]Story and Progression: This is the biggest flaw of them all. This whole game is built upon the Story of Horizon 4, meaning this is just a big expansion of that game. This means we play the same character that fought themselves up the ladder in the last Horizon Festival, which in turn means that we're already at out all time high when we even reach Mexico for the first time. From that point on the progression is already dead from the get go. You get cars, money and xp thrown at you like you've earned it and you don't even have to start doing races before you've unlocked the Goliath race. This is a huge misstep and shouldn't be done again. The Story missions are uninteresting as well (aside from the Anniversary Story, which finally brought my wish to life to be able to play the intro of the game again) and are only more tolerable now that the main character can speak now, but that doesn't exactly make them fun or good.  [/list]  At the end, it's an okay game and I had fun, but I'd seriously consider either playing Forza Horizon 4 if you haven't done that before or waiting for Forza Horizon 6 and see if it got any better there. On the other hand, they have done a lot of things right in this game, but they've done decisions that I just can't understand.

Set in a massive, ridiculously good-looking version of Mexico, FH5 nails that “just one more race” feeling like nothing else. The map is insane—deserts, jungles, beaches, volcanoes—and somehow it all blends without feeling copy-pasted. Every drive feels cinematic, even when you’re just free-roaming and absolutely not following the GPS.  The car list is stacked. Like, stacked stacked. Supercars, hypercars, classics, off-road beasts—if you’ve ever liked a car even a little, it’s probably here. Customization is deep but not overwhelming, and tuning lets sweats cook while casuals can just vibe using other people setups but i wish they can let me change the flame color of all the cars.  Gameplay-wise, FH5 is smooth as hell. Driving feels arcadey enough to be fun but realistic enough to reward skill. Events never get stale because the game constantly throws different challenges at you—races, stunts, festivals, seasonal stuff. Plus, Horizon Open and co-op actually work (most of the time), which is rare in modern gaming.  Sound design? Chef’s kiss. Engines sound mean, music slaps, and switching radio stations mid-drift feels illegal in the best way. And visually? Yeah… this game flexes. It’s one of those “pause and stare” games, especially on a good display.  Forza Horizon 5 isn’t just a racing game—it’s a comfort game, a flex game, and a “I’ll play for 10 minutes” lie. If you like cars even a little, this is a must-play. 9/10 — fast, beautiful, and dangerously addictive.

EDIT: It's only on NVIDIA GPUs, and most likely only on the Steam version. If you have the same issue, I have a guide: 1) Download NVIDIA Profile Inspector from GitHub. 2) Extract it and launch it. 3) Enable Unknown Settings ( there is a magnifying glass with gears on the top right, click it once and you'll notice some additional settings popping up ) 4) Select Forza Horizon 5 Profile from the drop-down on the top left. 5) Search for PS_CONST_FOLDING_GPU ( this pops up under a section called Extras ) and change it's value to 0xA2B53761. This setting disables shader optimization and prevents the crash because the shader optimization for some reason conflicts with the game's resource handling. Oh, and as a quick note... Verdict: A technically impressive open-world racer that balances accessibility with depth better than almost any driving game.  Forza Horizon 5 succeeds by letting players engage at their own pace. Casual players can enjoy spectacle and exploration, while experienced drivers can fine-tune builds and chase lap perfection. The handling model strikes a strong balance between realism and fun, making cars feel distinct without becoming punishing.  The world design is one of the game’s highlights. Mexico’s varied biomes create meaningful changes in terrain and driving feel, preventing the map from becoming visually or mechanically repetitive. Events are plentiful, and the game does a good job of constantly rewarding experimentation.  That said, progression can feel overly generous. While this keeps the experience welcoming, it sometimes undermines the sense of long-term achievement.  What Works Well  Outstanding visuals and performance  Wide variety of cars and events  Excellent accessibility options  Strong online integration  What Needs Improvement  Progression can feel too fast  Some events lack distinct identity  Final Thoughts: Forza Horizon 5 is a polished, content-rich racing experience that excels as both a casual and competitive game.

Forza Horizon 5 is an easy game to love — especially if you're a racing game fan like me. The Mexican setting is excellent: exploring the map is genuinely enjoyable, with a huge variety of roads, terrains and landscapes. The driving feels great, the graphics are impressive, the circuits work well and the cars, as is tradition in the series, are beautifully modeled. Overall, it delivers everything the previous Forza Horizon games already did well, with some solid improvements along the way.  The big problem is the progression — or the lack of it. Within minutes you're already handed an S-class supercar, credits quickly become meaningless and buying cars stops feeling rewarding unless you're after something very specific. This is a recurring complaint in the community: the game gives too much, too fast, and that classic sense of earning your way up — which used to be one of the strongest parts of racing games, including older Forza Horizon titles — just isn't there.  On top of that, the separately sold car packs leave a bad taste. If you just wanted to drive one specific iconic car, having to pay extra for it is pretty discouraging.  In the end, Forza Horizon 5 is technically excellent and genuinely fun to play, but it stumbles exactly where racing games usually shine: the feeling of progression and conquest. It's an incredible game to drive — just a little empty when it comes to long-term purpose.

It functions like any other Horizon game. You’re thrown into an open world with a lot of options for what to do. You can choose to only do street racing or go rallying. Maybe you don’t want any stress and just wind down by driving through some scenery or some speed traps. The map is pretty big, and there is a lot to do.  For some reason, the “story,” if you want to call it that, seems less enthralling than FH4. In FH4, I actually had the feeling that I was in a huge event and had to prove myself to some sort of audience. In FH5, it feels more or less empty. The one-liners come waaay too often, and most of the dialogue seems shallow. Your character also speaks in this iteration of Horizon. I find it more confusing rather than engaging that my character is speaking.  I also don’t like the setting in Mexico that much, but it’s fine. The graphics are quite pretty, and the scenery also gets nice at times, especially in the “swampy” regions with a lot of water. You can also inspect your cars in way more detail than in previous iterations. The car selection is fine; it’s just a little questionable that you don’t get all car passes even though you pay around $100 for a premium edition.  Regarding the DLC you can buy: The Hot Wheels DLC is horrendous. I don’t really know what to say here. I played it a while ago — the idea is good, but it plays like ♥♥♥♥. You drive around on empty set tracks like real-life Hot Wheels, which is obviously a very boring concept if you drive the car yourself. I remember a Hot Wheels game for the 3DS from my childhood; I think it was called Hot Wheels: Beat That! or something like that. You would drive races through an apartment, like a child’s room with toys lying around. That ♥♥♥♥ was reaaaaally fun. You also had power-ups, so it felt sort of like a Mario Kart × Hot Wheels game. Why didn’t they just do something like that here? Well, whatever — it’s just ♥♥♥♥.  The Rally DLC is alright. Some sort of “actual” rally driving. You get the corners called like you should in rally. Even though I don’t like the way the pace notes are called (light, medium, hard for the corners), that’s just personal preference — I like 1–5 better because it’s more precise. The real issue for me was that the pace notes came way too late. I was already in the “square right” my co-driver just shouted. I couldn’t find a setting for that, but it’s not the end of the world — it’s Forza after all. You can always rewind or just crash; doesn’t matter. The extra map for the Rally DLC is filled with quite a bit of content as well. Overall, pretty nice.  Regarding achievements: I don’t really know what the devs ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up in FH5, but achievements are really buggy. Sometimes I unlock an achievement which I was nowhere near completing, like the “Smash all Bonus Boards” one. I smashed about 60 when I randomly got it. Now I have 260/250 smashed, which makes no sense. Same for the Midnight Rider achievement and a lot of other ones. Right now, I don’t have any that I cannot get even though I did them, so it’s not a big deal — but still weird to have in a triple-A title.  Overall, solid game, but I would recommend you go play FH4 instead if you haven’t yet. The DLC for FH4 was just amazing and basically full games in themselves. FH4 GOAT.  3.9 really bad DLC out of 5

Forza Horizon 5 is definitely the pinnacle of open-world racing games, maxing out the joy of free driving. Set in Mexico, it relies on a massive map and stunning visuals—even if you don’t race, just cruising around can keep you entertained for hours, a must-play masterpiece for racing fans. Its most amazing feature is the open world. 50% larger than its predecessor, the map boasts 11 diverse landscapes full of surprises—dive down from an active volcano, splash through dense rainforests, then race along golden beaches, with unique scenery every step of the way. The dynamic weather and season system enhance immersion further: one moment it’s sunny, the next you’re engulfed in a sandstorm, drastically changing track grip, making every drive fresh and exciting.  Over 500 licensed vehicles are a dream for car enthusiasts, covering supercars, classic cars, off-roaders and more. The in-depth customization system lets you tweak everything from engines to paint jobs, offering great fun in building your exclusive ride. The driving feel balances realism and excitement—newbies can easily get started with assists, while hardcore players can turn them off for precise drifting fun, catering to all skill levels.  Its flaws lie in the somewhat "cheatingly" strong AI, which can set absurd lap times even in rain and occasionally block you maliciously. The Festival Playlist is also quite grindy, and some DLCs offer poor value for money. But these shortcomings are overshadowed by its strengths. Whether racing online with friends or exploring hidden relics alone, it delivers an unparalleled driving experience and remains a benchmark for racing games.

Forza Horizon 5 is the (soon not to be) latest open world arcade driving game in the Forza series. It follows the same formula as previous entries of using a Festival theme with various motoring events along with online play, this time in a Mexico themed setting.   Positives:  +++ Graphics. Yes, it has plenty of them and they look very good. +++ Car variety. It has those too. There’s something for everyone here. ++ Provides the same easy to learn, hard to master, Forza arcade driving experience as the rest of the series. ++ Options. Good stuff throughout. ++ Accessibility options. Even more good stuff, more than you’d expect in a driving game. ++ Music. Better than FH4 IMO ++ Car customization. It’s also good. ++ Tuning. Probably requires a degree to make anything good, but it’s there. ++ Liveries and editor. Probably requires godlike patience to make anything good, but it can get the job done and some people have really pushed it to the limits. +++ Track editor. Or as they call it now, “Event Lab”. It’s far more robust than the FH4 option with the creation of entirely unique tracks and settings possible. More advanced stuff takes a bit of programming understanding, but it’s there. +++ There’s always something to do. From races, stunts, drifting, car collecting, casual driving and the seasonal events, there’s always something going on. ++ Cars can be gifted to other players easily through the barn finds. ++ The Donut Media missions are probably some of the most fun ones in the game + Drifting is easier to do now than it was in FH4 ++ As before, going the Premium route gets you lots of nice extras, perks and cars dumped on you. ++ Online stuff. It has that and while I only dabbled in it lightly, there are various multiplayer events going on and matchmaking is fairly easy and timely. ++ Rally Adventures expansion. Provides a new area with point to point, timed races and the rally like co-pilot (even though it from a helicopter) system.  ++ Hot Wheels expansion. Provides another new area that is more about speed/track racing and adding some unique elements as hazard tracks. It may not jive with everyone but I thought it an interesting change of pace from the rest of the game.  Negatives:  --- AI/Drivatars. This is a cumulative negative that was a bit of a problem back in FH4, and I feel like it’s even worse in FH5. Put simply, the AI controlled vehicles operate with a different set of rules than the player (in other words, they cheat). It becomes quite obvious at higher difficulties and with cross country races, speaking of... -- Cross Country races. These just suck for many reasons. Again, these were bad in FH4, but they feel even worse now. The track paths are hard to make out, landing from jumps can stall your vehicle (but not the AI and boy do they love to have ridiculously high impact jumps in these) and combined with the AI issue above and you'll feel forced to lower the difficulty to just to get through with a fair chance. - Another negative for masking several events and races as being road or dirt, but in actuality are just more cross country races and should be approached as such. It’s a notable issue in the expansions. -- Scripted race events. This is more specific to certain events where no matter how skilled you are, the event is scripted to provide a fraction of a second win or loss at the finish. The margin of error for the these events is borderline insane and winning these are literally impossible for most players. There’s no way to adjust the difficulty for these. Notable examples are the Catch me in the Canyon (Train race), Buggy and the Beast and some of the Icons of Speed missions. -- The NPC hosts. These are some of the cringiest hosts/characters yet. I don’t recall the ones in FH4 being this obnoxious, but it’s notably worse here. These aren’t real car people, they’re caricatures of what someone thinks car people are. You want proper car people? The Donut Media people fill that role way better and with better voice over. -- Despite paying the extra for the Premium version of the game, there are still additional car packs not included. These will still show up in game, taunting you spend more money on the game.  -- Seasonal Championship events with forced Highly Skilled Drivatars. This is already bad due to the worse and cheaty AI in FH5 but having the difficulty locked is of benefit to no one. Easy fix, just let players change the difficulty, lower or higher. -- Cockpit view suffers from an annoying auto-exposure bug that can either darken things so much that you can’t see, or blind you with brightness (notable in tunnels). -- Leaderboard hackers. Is it really too much to ask that the devs remove the obvious 0 time records or script some automate process to remove/ban them? - The UI isn’t the best. I’ve seen worse, but this has a few issues. - Hot Wheels expansion. The tracks feel slippery no matter what car you use and the specific steering assist is on by default and that can mess with your handling - Bugs. There aren’t that many, but I’ve come across a few. I’ve run into laggy menus, especially in the expansion content, Hot Wheels has a weird bug that can disable online mode if you spawn in there and I had one crash (game crash).  So is this game any good? Well… yes. I enjoyed it quite a bit. More than being frustrated which is a plus I suppose.  However, as a game, I don’t think it’s quite as good as it’s predecessor, FH4. It does some things better than FH4 (easier drifting, music, track editor, accessibility options) while taking a step backwards in others (Drivatars, Festival hosts, Cross Country races, scripted events, Premium not including everything).  In general, I think if you enjoyed the previous Horizon games, you’ll find plenty of the same here, give or take a few things here and there.  I give it a 7/10 and a recommend. But maybe grab it on sale. Preferably before it gets desisted after FH6 comes out.

An Unrivaled Open World Playground Games’ recreation of Mexico is arguably the series' greatest achievement. The map is 50% larger than its predecessor and features 11 distinct biomes:  Visual Fidelity: From the arid deserts and lush jungles to the active Gran Caldera volcano, the level of detail is photorealistic.  Dynamic Seasons: Weather isn't just cosmetic. Dust storms and tropical hurricanes physically affect driving conditions and visibility, making the world feel alive and ever-changing.  Cultural Heart: The game weaves Mexican culture into its "Horizon Stories," giving players a reason to explore beyond just winning races.  Gameplay: The Perfect Hybrid FH5 strikes a rare balance between "arcade fun" and "sim-lite precision."  The Cars: With a roster that has grown to over 800 licensed vehicles by 2025, the variety is staggering. Every car—from vintage Volkswagens to the Mercedes-AMG One—has a distinct weight, sound, and handling profile.  Accessibility: Whether you are a hardcore racer using a steering wheel or a casual player on a controller, the game is highly customizable. You can toggle assists to make it as easy or as punishingly realistic as you like.  Progression: The "Accolades" system ensures that everything you do—drifting, jumping, or simply exploring—earns you experience and rewards.  Innovation & Community The game has evolved significantly since its 2021 launch through consistent updates:  EventLab: This powerful toolset allows players to create their own tracks and game modes, resulting in a nearly infinite stream of community-generated content.  Expansions: The Hot Wheels and Rally Adventure DLCs provide massive, unique playgrounds that contrast perfectly with the main Mexican map.  Cross-Platform Growth: In 2025, the game expanded to PlayStation 5, bringing a massive new wave of players into the Horizon Festival and proving its lasting appeal.  Technical Excellence Graphics: Supporting 4K and Ray Tracing (in specific modes), FH5 is a showcase for modern hardware.  Audio: The "granular synthesis" approach to engine sounds makes every exhaust note feel raw and authentic.  Performance: Even on mid-range PCs or older consoles, the game is impressively optimized, maintaining smooth frame rates during high-speed action.  The Verdict: 9.5/10 Forza Horizon 5 is more than a game; it’s a digital vacation. It celebrates the joy of driving without the stress of rigid simulation, making it an essential title for anyone who loves cars or beautiful environments.

# Forza Horizon 5: Racing Paradise with Minor Speedbumps  After cruising through Mexico's diverse landscapes for over 70 hours, Forza Horizon 5 delivers an exhilarating racing experience that shines particularly bright on the Steam Deck. This latest entry in the Horizon series continues to perfect the open-world racing formula, though not without a few minor detours from greatness.  ## Summary Forza Horizon 5 stands as one of the premier racing games available on Steam, offering exceptional value especially when purchased during sale events. With its massive collection of meticulously detailed vehicles and responsive controls that translate surprisingly well to the Steam Deck, it's a racing enthusiast's dream. While the Mexican setting doesn't quite reach the heights of its predecessor's British landscapes, the overall package remains impressive and worthy of your gaming library.  ## Gameplay Mechanics The core racing experience in Forza Horizon 5 is nothing short of spectacular. The handling model strikes that perfect balance between arcade accessibility and simulation depth, allowing both casual players and racing aficionados to find their comfort zone. The progression system keeps you constantly engaged with a steady stream of new events, challenges, and of course, cars to collect.  The vehicle roster is truly the star of the show here. With hundreds of cars spanning decades of automotive history, from humble hatchbacks to exotic hypercars, the variety is staggering. Each vehicle feels distinct, with handling characteristics that reflect their real-world counterparts. The customization options further extend the gameplay, allowing you to transform virtually any car into your personal racing machine.  Where the game slightly disappoints is in its map design. While Mexico offers diverse biomes including deserts, jungles, and coastal regions, the overall layout and memorable landmarks don't quite match the charm and variety found in Forza Horizon 4's Britain. The roads feel somewhat less distinctive, making exploration slightly less rewarding than in previous entries.  ## Technical Performance One of the most pleasant surprises is how well Forza Horizon 5 performs on the Steam Deck. Despite being a visually demanding title, the game maintains a stable framerate with appropriately scaled graphics settings. Load times are reasonable, and I experienced minimal crashes or technical hiccups during my extensive playtime. The developers clearly put effort into ensuring the game runs smoothly across various hardware configurations.  On standard PC setups, the game is equally impressive, with scalable graphics options that cater to both high-end rigs and more modest systems. The optimization is commendable, allowing the game to look gorgeous without demanding cutting-edge hardware.  ## Value Assessment At a value rating of 7/10, Forza Horizon 5 offers substantial content for its price point, especially when purchased during Steam sales. The sheer number of vehicles, events, and customization options ensures you'll be playing for dozens of hours before seeing everything the game has to offer. The seasonal content updates further extend the game's lifespan, providing fresh challenges and rewards on a regular basis.  ## Pros and Cons  ### Pros: - Exceptional performance on Steam Deck - Massive, diverse car collection with hundreds of vehicles - Accessible yet deep driving mechanics - Visually stunning environments and weather effects - Regular content updates keep the experience fresh  ### Cons: - Map layout feels less inspired than Forza Horizon 4's Britain - Some event types become repetitive after extended play - Online features can occasionally suffer from connectivity issues  ## Recommendation Forza Horizon 5 is an easy recommendation for racing game enthusiasts, particularly those looking for a premium racing experience on the Steam Deck. It's also an excellent entry point for newcomers to the genre, thanks to its adjustable difficulty and driving assists. While it doesn't completely surpass its predecessor in every aspect, it remains one of the most polished and content-rich racing games available on Steam.  If you're looking to pick up just one racing game during the next Steam sale, Forza Horizon 5 should be at the top of your list. The combination of portable play on Steam Deck and the sheer volume of content make it a racing package that's hard to beat, despite its few shortcomings.

Overall, this game delivers an amazing open world racing experience with top tier visuals, smooth performance, great sound design, and tons of content.  Highly recommended, especially if you have a capable PC to experience it at max settings.

So, first things first: All things considered, I barely recommend the game.  Don't get me wrong, it's a fun game! The racing is really good. BUT. I bought Forza 4 after this and it is better while all the things good in this game are basically there, too. Forza 4 may miss some raytracing and recent GPU features, but then again it runs smoother on recent hardware and did not crash for me yet (while still looking great). I had 3 CtDs on Forza 5 in comparison.  Forza Horizon 5 is basically an open world racing game with a big map to ride around in and pick various things to do from - get more cars, unlock more chapters in the game, do drift challenges, street races, dirt rallies, dangerous jumps, speed through speed zones... it works.  If you get this on sale, get premium. Else you won't have the expansions. (Though I don't really need the hot wheels thing.) Ridiculously enough, even a hundred bucks (regular price) "premium" still wants another fifty for a bundle to get all the cars possible. See why I rate it "barely recommend?" Compared to the previous game's Ultimate Edition, now Premium doesn't get you everything. AAA ripoff at its finest. You can even spend a few bucks to reveal the collectibles on the map...  To be fair: It's not pay-to-play. And with the exception of the actual game content DLC the rest is just fluff you don't need to enjoy the game.   Another little sticky point is that they kept the seasonal weather changes, but they barely do anything - weather is localized to parts of the map - which may be accurate to the various climate zones in the game, but it means the map is very static. In Forza 4 the seasons changed the look of the whole map, something I found stunning and rewarding.   Same goes for some of the game events. In Forza 4 I raced a hovercraft ferry to the finish line. That was as fun as it comes! In Forza 5 I drove a... parade float?? And I jump it into a canyon and don't see the landing? That had lame written all over it.  I dig the expeditions into remote places and ruins, and the bits about Mexican car history and lore. Not a huge fan of the jungle, myself, YMMV.   I really look forward to the release of Forza 6, because Japan promises the return of real seasons (I mean, the country is proud of its four distinct seasons) and a varied landscape. I bet it will be as much a DLC hog as this one, sadly.

Forza Horizon 5 surprised me — in a very good way. Coming from a long Need for Speed background, I didn’t expect this game to click as hard as it did. FH5 isn’t about instant chaos or brute force speed — it’s about control, balance, and understanding your car. And once that sinks in, it becomes incredibly rewarding. The engine optimization is outstanding. The game auto-tuned itself to my system and has been running rock-solid at ~70 FPS with almost no fluctuation. No constant tweaking, no anxiety chasing numbers — just smooth, stable gameplay. That alone deserves praise. The tuning depth is on another level. Power upgrades actually matter in context — you can’t just slap on turbos and expect magic. Suspension, gearing, drivetrain, weight… everything has consequences. Community tunes exist, but I quickly learned that building your own setups is far more satisfying (and often far more drivable). The world design is excellent: dynamic weather and storms rivers you can drive through varied terrain and elevation a sense of scale that encourages exploration Features like Barn Finds, Wheelspins, and even the ability to leave gift cars for other players add a quiet, thoughtful layer of progression that feels earned rather than rushed. It’s not perfect — if you’re looking for heavy visual damage, cops, or pure arcade chaos, this isn’t Need for Speed. Cities aren’t the main focus here, and the game leans more toward festival racing than street culture. But that’s a design choice, not a flaw. Bottom line: Forza Horizon 5 rewards patience, skill, and curiosity. It’s a game to savor, not rush — and once it clicks, it’s hard to put down. Worth every cent.

Forza Horizon 5 is a solid open-world racing game with plenty of content for people looking to kick back and relax, as well as those who enjoy a more competitive form of racing. As for what this game does well: racing is fluid, tuning is satisfying, and customization is solid. If that ain't your cup of tea, then there are plenty of community customizations/tuning's that you can choose from. The different systems such as arcade, campgain, and various multiplayer objectives, give players quite a bit of modes to choose from. Forza 5's racing events are also broken down into road racing, dirt racing, cross country, street racing, or drag racing which is dope when you inevitably get tired of one form of racing like I did. If you just feel like crusing around then there are plenty of non-racing objectives such as xp/fast travel boards,speed traps, speed zones, etc. The game also runs very smoothly on the steam deck. Only had a single crash in 10 or so hours that I played on the deck.  What I disliked about Forza 5 was the climate based seasons compared to the dynamic seasons of Forza 4. Albeit expansive, the Mexico setting didn't really pull me in to the same extent as Forza 4. Don't get me wrong, Forza 5 has plenty of cool looking areas and plenty of interesting tracks, but overall the games setting felt sorta bland. The campaign didn't really land for me either. The annoucers talk non-stop and I just didn't get a sense of emotion or purpose out of what they were saying. I honestly glossed over most of the campaign and dialogue. I get it's a racing game, and I'm not expecting some Hollywood level vocie acting or writing, but I would rather have no dialogue than whatever this soulless writing was. It's definitly somthing you can look past, but it was irritating nonetheless. When it came to racing, the AI could be wack on high difficulty. It could always be a skill issue on my part, that I won't deny, however, AI catches up and overtakes me with no issue whereas if you were playing against real players, moves like the ones they pulled off would be borderline impossible. I also experienced some connection issues during multiplayer. There was some rubberbanding here and there, but I didn't put in enough hours into multiplayer to know if this was a one time thing on my end, or a persisting issue for everyone.  Like the previous Forza title, this one will probably be delisted once the whatever licenses expire, however, it will still be playable. Pick it up on discount! Decent 8.24/10 for me.   Tl;dr Great racing game with plenty of content for casuals and competitive players alike. Satisfying customization/tuning. Annoying writing/voice acting. Some connection issues in multiplayer, but overall tolerable.

• Excellent graphics, performance, and optimisation. The game looks fantastic and runs extremely smooth. Performance is rock solid, load times are quick, and overall optimisation is excellent, making it easy to jump in and play without technical issues.  • Strong driving feel and overall balance. The driving feels great and is immediately enjoyable, with a huge selection of cars to choose from across many classes and styles. While meta cars do exist, the balance is strong enough that they don’t dominate online play in the way they do in Forza Motorsport 2023. Skilled players regularly use a wide variety of cars rather than being funnelled into a narrow meta, which allows experimentation and variety to remain viable and fun.   • Mixed skill racing creates a fun, welcoming experience. Online racing benefits from mixed skill lobbies, which keeps races varied and enjoyable rather than overly competitive. It works well whether you’re playing casually or investing longer sessions.  • Fun game modes and strong ongoing engagement. There is a good range of enjoyable modes, and the weekly challenges are a great addition that provide regular reasons to keep playing without feeling like a grind.  • Progression feels too generous and lacks a sense of earning cars. While the game is generous, being given large numbers of cars almost immediately, often through wheelspins, reduces the sense of progression.  It would feel more rewarding if cars were earned through completing races or challenges, without locking them behind heavy per car grind systems.  • Race lengths are too short across all event types. Races often feel over too quickly, including sprints and circuit races. Longer race options or extended championships would improve pacing and make events feel more substantial.  • The Mexico map lacks density compared to past Horizon titles. While visually impressive, the Mexico map often feels too open and empty compared to maps like Horizon 4’s Scotland, which felt more varied and engaging to drive through.  • The Eliminator mode doesn’t suit the map design. The Eliminator feels overly luck based and is not particularly enjoyable on such a wide, open map. It would work far better on tighter, twistier road layouts rather than open terrain. Additionally, when a challenge is initiated, both players should start from a fixed starting line; allowing one player to engage while already moving gives a significant and unfair advantage and further shifts the mode toward luck rather than skill.  • Audio and presentation are strong overall. While not analysing individual engine sounds in detail, the overall audio quality and presentation are excellent and add to the immersion.  • A genuinely fun game with strong longevity. Despite some flaws, Forza Horizon 5 remains highly enjoyable and easy to return to. The strong foundations, variety, and ongoing challenges make it one of the most engaging entries in the series and leave a positive impression for the future of Horizon.  Overall, Forza Horizon 5 gets far more right than wrong, and I’m genuinely looking forward to seeing how these strengths carry forward and improve in the next Horizon game.

TLDR: great game but definitely fits the "Forza Horizon 4.5" nickname  I've played every forza horizon game, most of which I have over 200 hours on and I think this one's just ok. Its definitely a covid game. Out of every game in the series, this one is the smallest jump in terms of what this game adds to the series.   FH1 was the first and has the best progression in the series. FH2 added more cars, a new handling model, and cross country races. FH3 added bodykits, event blueprints, and had the best expansions imo. FH4 added seasons, a festival playlist, and a basic level editor via "Super 7". FH5 adds... not much more tbh. The most significant addition is fleshing out the level editor, and allowing you to add items to races instead of just the Super 7 stuff. The handlings improved. This game has the most *stuff* in the series. Most cars, most tracks/events, most bodykits, most pr stunts.   Although, because this game is set in mexico, the seasons are actually downgraded compared to fh4. Instead of having 4 distinct season, each with there own interesting changes. In fh5 they just kinda mesh together. The most it changes is some parts of the map have a bit more water now and the top of the mountain has some snow. Thats about it.  Speaking of snow, I do find it odd that this is the only game with snow tires that are separate from rally tires, yet there almost entirely useless. They had the chance to make a Blizzard Mountain expansion 2 but never did. And more generally, the class system is the most unbalanced in this game. horsepower doesnt effect PI much at higher classes. So having 900hp cars in S1 is common, meanwhile tires spike PI way to much. To make things worse, most tracks favor speed over handling, so trying for a handling setup puts you at a heavy disadvantage.  Rally cars don't fair much better. Most cars can get mud tires. Not a problem by itself but they usually cost less PI than rally tires, while also handling better than rally tires offroad.  The idea behind this is that rally tires handle better on road, hence why it costs more PI. In reality, because most rally tracks are mostly or entirely offroad, mud tires just gives you free PI and better handling. To make things worse, because mud tires are cheaper, many famous rally cars can't hit the top of S1. So you can get a fully upgraded rally car with 900+hp and be stuck at like 862 PI.  But, while I made a long rant about the problems with the game, said problems are relatively small. The seasons problem doesnt take to much away from the game, and the cars being unbalanced only effects online races and rivals mode. Outside of those 2 problems, its fh4, but more. and considering you cant buy that game anymore (rip but not playground games's fault), this game is an easy recommendation.

Still a really good, solid game to consider, even at this time.   For [b] casual [/b] players, the map is always beautiful and very spacious - each time you drive, even often on the same roads, but at variable scenery (whether it's at the beach, atop of mountains, through the rainforest, or simply over the stretching desert roads) - these driving experiences will never ever feel the same each time, it's always different.   Relaxed, cruising at controlled, enjoyable speeds, and simply appreciating the splendid views - that's the perfect recipe for a nice, 'spirited driving' experience.   From a [b] competitive [/b] standpoint, it's very easy, even for beginners, to obtain top tier cars and as well to apply free, community-made tunes shared by other players - to build a whole, challenge-worthy but widely varied garage, for relatively non-expensive in-game currencies, also easy to earn and not so timely.  Sometimes however, a few online race tracks might feel 'unforgiving', or the race itself might feel 'unfair' - mainly because of the tricky nature of challenging routes (no room for error or 'skill issues'), and/or also due to other players as well (too good/bad or 'lucky').  Regardless, as in other games, trying to complete the race is always a must for learning, and so is having good sportsmanship, as I very often noticed, is also present in this game (for instance, racers often using 'Link' (in-game, quick chat feature), to simply say 'sorry' when they make mistakes affecting/impacting other racers).   The game never lacks [b] content [/b], as quite regularly, new challenges/events are added to unlock exclusive and amazing cars (voted by players - very cool), which all players can then get for free (for points earned), and players can even claim any previous ones which they missed (requires a 'backstage pass' which costs higher points, but still free to unlock one previously missed, exclusive car per 'season' - from any earlier season - also very cool). This is yet another reason why many players, including myself often come back to the game.   I'd say that the [b] price [/b] is also very fair and reasonable - for the amount of content and gameplay, so it's very much worth its value, and even more so - at the 50% off discounted price, especially during certain Steam sales events.  I'd recommend playing this game using a controller, and of course, on a decent, average gaming rig (this game is also already optimized for your device after each update - very convenient)   [b] Overall [/b], I'd highly recommend this game, especially if you are fond of driving, racing or such simulation games. Even I still find it to be the most visually immersive driving game - with good, engaging and some random gameplay as well. Online competition and completing challenges are quite fun sometimes, but, I think it's much better to appreciate the drive along the relaxing views, one place at a time, y'know, and I'd suggest giving this a try too, from time to time.  At this point of time, if you are considering getting the game, it'd be much more worthwhile if you'd continue playing - because 150 GB is quite demanding. Another way is you could also use the Steam storage management feature (in settings) to transfer the game to another storage drive and play again later.   Forza Horizon 6 is also right around the corner (next year), so you could also consider skipping straight to that, however, expect full price for quite some while after release, before eventually the getting lower prices from much later sales events.  However, as seen from several recent games, the graphical recreation and maps of Japan have already been really impressive, and now it's only imaginable what FH6 is going to be like. Only time will tell, but it probably won't disappoint, that's for sure.  So, if you don't have FH5 already, I'd still recommend getting it as of right now, and I don't think that it would not be worth it. But again, certain things considered, it's always your choice.   Well, that's a pretty long review... I guess I might as well become a game critic now :3  Nah but anyways, thanks for reading, I hope that in some way, you have gotten something out of this :> I wish you a very happy gaming holiday!

Two years ago I started playing the series with Forza Horizon 4. I was six years late, but when I finally played it I fell in love.  I never had the money for an Xbox or a good PC, so for years I just watched other people play. I built a PC and started FH4 on integrated graphics. I saved up, bought a GPU, and later picked up Forza Horizon 5 on sale.  I played FH5 three years after its release, and it became my most-played game.  Even now I haven’t completed everything, there are too many challenges, too many boards, too many cars. FH4 has about 700 cars; FH5 has around 900. It never ends.  The story writing is basic and the voice acting is bad, they’re there but you will not care about them because the fun is completing the challenges.  The Hot Wheels DLC, Rally DLC and the free DLCs (like the donut media one) are great: lots of content, lots of fun.  What is annoying is the Premium Edition situation. Years later they still release small car packs with only 4–5 cars each. After 900 hours of playing if you want to have everything you have to buy the Ultimate Car Pack Collection.  The map is huge but often feels empty. Too much desert, too much jungle, and too many long, empty roads. If the Rally DLC map were part of the main map, the world would feel better it has better, more fun curves.  The seasons doesn't make sense. It’s Mexico, so it basically like “hot” or “raining,” and that loses a lot of the seasonal atmosphere that FH4 had.  I definitely recommend it, the game is fun if you play alone and its fun if you play with friends, it is just like previous titles but with some better mechanics and more content.

After spending around 177 hours in Forza Horizon 5, I can confidently say that it is one of the most engaging open-world racing games I have played. The map set in Mexico is vibrant, diverse, and full of life, offering deserts, jungles, beaches, and mountains that make every drive feel fresh. The graphics are impressive, with detailed environments and cars that look almost real, especially when weather effects or lighting change the atmosphere.  The gameplay is accessible but still rewarding. Whether you enjoy drifting, racing on asphalt, going off-road, or simply exploring the world, the game gives you complete freedom. The large collection of cars and the tuning system add depth, letting players experiment with different builds and driving styles. This makes the experience fun even after many hours of play.  However, the game also has a few weaknesses. After long sessions, some activities start to feel repetitive, and certain story missions lack impact. The formula does not innovate much compared to previous titles, so experienced players may notice familiar patterns.  Even so, Forza Horizon 5 remains an excellent racing game. Its beautiful world, huge variety of cars, and relaxed but exciting gameplay make it worth playing for many hours. For me, it has been a memorable experience, and it still has plenty to offer even after 177 hours on the road.

### Review of Forza Horizon 5  **Rating: ★★★★★ (5/5)**  Forza Horizon 5 is nothing short of an absolute joyride! The level of detail is incredible, from the sun-soaked beaches to the lush jungles and bustling cities. It feels like a vibrant, living world that invites exploration at every turn. The customization options allow you to truly make your vehicle your own, which adds a personal touch to the racing experience. One of my favorite features is the dynamic weather system and seasonal changes. Each season brings a new flavor to gameplay, whether I’m racing through a rainstorm or enjoying a sunny day. The variety keeps the experience fresh and exciting.  Multiplayer is also a blast! Racing against friends or participating in community events feels competitive yet laid-back, allowing for fun, social interactions while doing what we love—driving.  Overall, Forza Horizon 5 is a masterpiece that captures the spirit of racing while providing endless opportunities for exploration and creativity. Whether you’re a die-hard car enthusiast or just looking for an engaging game to unwind with, I can't recommend it enough!

Steering wheel support and overall handling and driving is better in FH5, but not THAT much better when compared to FH4. This is one of those moments when it's tough to rate a game due to Steam forcing you to go for black or white, when in reality this game cannot be polarized in such a manner due to it having many shades of gray.   Yes, I do have nearly 500 hours for this game at the time of the review, which probably means that I sort of like it, but like I've said, that's only partly true.  Don't get me wrong, it's very fun if you are a casual petrolhead, and if you like collecting stuff in general. It helps a lot that the game is very easy on the eyes, especially on low-end of the specification spectrum. I'm getting almost consistent 60fps on my device with an integrated GPU, more specifically AMD Radeon 680M, and the game still looks extremelly pretty.  Additionally, you can adjust the difficulty according to your needs. If you want a challenge, you can have a challenge, but if you want to sit back and relax, and easily do (most of) the weekly challenges, you can do that as well.  On the negative side of things, the most annoying one is predatory behavior of the developer, releasing a bunch of rather expensive (for what you get) car packs, that cost money to get even though you've splurged on the Premium edition. You will probably want to grab them if you are a completionist, but at the same time you'll probably think three times before spending what you've paid on the full game for less than 10% of the cars in the game in total (extra car packs are about 100 cars in total, and the entire game has almost 1000 cars).  Also, when the game got released for PS5 in April of 2025, PC version on sale costed more than what it was back in 2023 when I got the game. The situation got a bit better during the sales in late 2025, but it's still not at the point where it was two years ago or even one year ago.  Yes, you can do most of the stuff while playing as a single player, but there is a challenge here and there where you need to hop into multiplayer games, and that's where another big problem in the game becomes apparent. You'll encounter lots (and I mean LOTS) of people who want to ruin your fun just for ♥♥♥♥ and giggles, and there's no easy way to report them. You would need to upload a video on developer's website as proof, and that requires a lot of hassle for something that should be fairly straightforward.  Other issues would be inability to control the weather and day/night cycles in offline mode. Yes, you can do it through blueprints, but I would prefer it during free roam. Then there's a huge problem of short lifespan of Forza games, you can probably expect that the servers for FH5 will be live until the end of 2027 or something like that. The game's plot is also extremelly silly and way overcomplicated. NPCs talk way too much.  If you can look past these issues, and if you prefer arcade racing games as opposed to realistic simulations, this game might be for you. If you always wanted to fit offroad wheels to your average Ferrari or Lambo and go bonkers in an off-road race, then this game is definitely for you. Hey, you cannot crack your oil casket if the entire undercarriage of the car is not even modelled, right?  Definitelly scratching that itch, but I still miss TDU and TDU 2.

When people ask who is dumb enough to buy the premium edition, think of this review. I play with a racing wheel, and I feel it helps with immersion, but onto the review.  Going from Brittan to Mexico was a let down in my opinion, going from the dynamic season changes in the countryside to the mostly brown and bland map of mexico was one of the biggest let downs for this edition. Now they do keep the seasons, but I feel that there are certain parts of the map that just dont get effected no matter what.   Hot Wheels is something they really need to do with the horizon series at this point, as I see this as the only good DLC content in the bundle. The map for it is huge, and the new physics system brings a whole new depth to going through the loops and climbing to the highest points of the orange track.   Car selection is always really great in the Forza series, giving a good mix of luxury, local brands, classics, and every day cars with performance packages. I had the car pass so I had even more of a selection right off the bat and I will say a lot of those cars I did end up using, but certain gimmicky ones like the fast saga were not my cup of tea.  Overall, Forza is Forza, and if you like Forza, you'll like this one, I hope that they continue to push the boundaries like they did with the first three games, because it might end up growing stale.   (6's trailer was released, they better not screw up Japan.)  Tech wise, you need a beefy system to run  this at higher res and frame rates. Following just the requirements would not get you a very good experience. I get around 180 frames at 2k with a 4070ti super, max settings, and 5th gen Ryzen. HDR and ray tracing look really good in this game too, but will effect your performance significantly.   If you are wondering, my order for the series (starting on PC) is 4,3,5.

Forza Horizon 5 is an incredible racing game, with perhaps the most jam-packed open-world from Playground Games to date and a massive collection of cars available. Playground Games continues to strike a perfect balance between simulation and arcade-like car handling and physics, which is in the same spirit as FH3 and FH4. That being said, FH5 brings very little new to the table in comparison with FH3 and FH4.  For example, seasons were introduced in FH4 which was an amazing feature since it transformed the map from week-to-week and made the world feel alive. In FH5, seasons are also present, but since the game takes place in Mexico there is very very little difference from season to season. The only difference is amount of rain and humidity, and it gets repetitive quickly.  The Horizon Festival is drastically smaller or at least less relevant than in the previous Horizon games, which makes the world feel more empty in many areas. In other words, FH5 is on paper larger, prettier and better than any past Horizon title, but it doesn't always feel that way. In a sense,  FH5 lacks any real character in comparison with past Horizon titles.  That being said, there are many things that FH5 does better than its predecessors. Car sounds for example are better than ever before, and although the car sounds aren't always unique across different cars, they are significantly better than they were in FH4 and change depending on the upgrades you apply to a car. There are more upgrade options than ever before which is another welcome addition, and lastly, the game looks stunning.  Even if you have the smallest enthusiasm for cars and racing, Forza Horizon 5 will likely prove extremely enjoyable for you. For returning players like myself, it's another solid Forza Horizon, although with not that many new additions as one might want. All in all however, Forza Horizon 5 is an incredible game that I can't recommend enough.  8.9 / 10
