⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ Forza Horizon 5 — Still the King of Open-World Racing  Forza Horizon 5 nails what a racing game should feel like fast, fun, and loaded with things to do. The game throws you into a massive open world based on Mexico, and there’s always something happening: street races, off-road events, drift zones, drag strips, Horizon Stories, seasonal challenges, collectibles, and a huge amount of community-made events. You never run out of things to race or unlock.  Car handling strikes a great balance between arcade and semi-sim, the car list is huge, and the visuals are top-tier. The weather effects, lighting, and overall vibe make the world feel alive, and the soundtrack fits perfectly with the Horizon festival atmosphere.  ✔️ Likes  Tons of events, races, challenges, and content to keep you busy for hundreds of hours.  Huge car list with fun tuning and customization options.  Beautiful graphics and one of the best open worlds in any racing game.  Solid balance between casual and more realistic driving.  Seasonal updates and community creations keep the game fresh.  ❌ Dislikes — Mexico Map  Some regions feel too open or repetitive, especially the desert areas.  Heavier focus on off-road/dirt compared to FH4 may not satisfy asphalt-focused players.  City areas like Guanajuato are great but too small, not enough dense street-racing zones.  Several biomes feel underused with big empty spaces unless tied to seasonal events.  Jungle and sandstorm areas can hurt visibility and make some races feel messy.  Overall, the map is huge but not as tightly designed or balanced as FH4’s.

Forza Horizon 5 — Review  Forza Horizon 5 is an open-world racing masterpiece that blends eye-popping visuals, a massive and varied world, and an incredibly deep car-collecting and tuning system. It’s one of the best entries in the Horizon series, striking a near-perfect balance between arcade fun and realistic driving feeling.  What Makes It Great  Stunning World & Setting The game is set in a beautifully rendered version of Mexico. The map is diverse, with deserts, jungles, volcanoes, coastal highways, and more. The attention to detail in the landscapes makes every drive feel fresh and visually rewarding.                            Spectacular Graphics & Sound Forza Horizon 5 takes full advantage of modern hardware to deliver high-fidelity graphics, realistic textures, and vibrant lighting.    On top of that, the audio design is excellent — engine roars, environmental ambience, and tire sounds feel rich and immersive.   Huge and Varied Car Roster There are hundreds of cars — from classic muscle to hypercars — and you can really customize them. The tuning options are deep, letting you tweak performance parts to match your driving style.   Accessible but Skillful Driving Whether you’re new to racing games or a veteran, Forza Horizon 5 welcomes you. You can play with driving assists, or go more hardcore by turning them off. The driving feels smooth and responsive, making it fun to explore or race.   Variety of Activities There’s always something to do: races, challenges, seasonal events, drift zones, and more. The Horizon Adventure system gives structure, but you’re also free to just drive around and enjoy the world.   Long-Term Engagement With seasonal updates, a constantly changing open world, and live events, the game has a lot of replay value. Players keep coming back, especially if they like collecting cars or competing in different modes.   Accessibility Features The game does a great job with accessibility: many players appreciate how inclusive its options are.   Minor Drawbacks (But Not Dealbreakers)  While the map is huge and varied, some players feel that parts of it can be a bit repetitive.   The story and mission design are not very deep — it’s not really a narrative-driven game; the focus is more on driving, exploring, and having fun.   For some, the in-game economy and reward system (like wheel spins) might feel a little grindy.   Verdict  If you love racing games, Forza Horizon 5 is a dream come true. It’s visually stunning, loaded with content, and offers a driving experience that’s both accessible and rewarding. Whether you want to race hard, drift around just for the fun of it, or explore the open world at your own pace — this game delivers.  Highly recommended for:  Players who love car variety and tuning  Fans of open-world games  Those who enjoy long-term multiplayer and seasonal content  Anyone who just wants to hop in a car and drive through beautiful landscapes  Less ideal for:  Gamers looking for a strong, character-driven narrative  Players who dislike long grinds or “gambling-like” reward mechanics

Forza Horizon 5 hit me way harder than I expected. The whole vibe is just electric - Mexico feels like one massive sun-soaked festival where something’s popping off every 100 meters. Events, races, wheelspins, new cars, seasonal stuff… the game floods you with content to the point where 100 hours barely scratch the surface. And yeah, I’m already 80+ hours in, still glued to it like it’s day one.  Gameplay? Super fun. The handling felt a bit sticky at first, especially on a controller, but that actually made it more addictive. Those cursed corners made me want to bump the difficulty, retry events, and actually learn how to take turns on a high-end car like a human being. The soundtrack slaps too - different stations, different moods, never gets dull.  I’m not a racing game person at all, I just love cars so the physics threw me off at first. But as soon as I got used to it, it turned into a whole advantage. Especially once you dive into the tuning and customization. It’s ridiculous how deep it goes. You can tweak weight, build parameters, tire pressure, engine setups - it all genuinely changes how each car feels.  The game both looks and sounds insane. Wet roads at night? Peak visuals. Absolute perfection. The sound design/engines/weather, everything just elevates it even more.  Favorite activities? I’m basic in the best way. Give me road races, closed-circuit races, anything on asphalt. Off-road? Miss me with that. But jumping into a new car and discovering how it behaves is pure dopamine. The more I unlock, the more I want to play - it’s that kind of loop.  Now, the one thing that actually tilts me sometimes is the Drivatars. These bots straight up break the laws of physics, break my confidence and sometimes break my will to live. They get traction in places where your car just slides into the shadow realm. The fix? Either race real people online or mentally tune out the bots entirely and focus on your own run. If you stare at their behavior too long, it gets frustrating fast on high difficulty levels.  I’d recommend Forza Horizon 5 to anyone who loves cars, tuning, or arcadey racing vibes. No matter skill level, it just grabs you and doesn’t let go.

Like in my prior review of Forza Horizon 4, I have A LOT more hours in this game than my Steam hours suggest due to having owned the Xbox version of this game since it first came out 4 years ago. After seeing the Ultimate edition of the Steam version on sale for a surprisingly low price, I had to snatch it up purely for the benefit of having a copy of this game that's not completely tied to Microsoft's operating systems due to it being confirmed playable on Steam Deck/Linux via Proton.  Now that my reasons for having bought this game twice are out of the way, here's my actual review. I've been a fan of the Forza Horizon games since the 3rd entry. While Gran Turismo and Forza's parent series, Forza Motorsport, have been increasingly losing me due to shifting their focus towards E-Sports over the main appeal they've always had for me, which is just simply getting to live out the escapist fantasy of collecting and driving rare and exotic cars that you're not even likely to see on the road, let alone drive, with beautiful graphics and solid, realistic physics, Forza Horizon has not only been filling the niche that those two series have been leaving for me but doing a damn fine job at it.   For people who don't really care about accurately simulating real world motorsports, this series has proven to be a true automotive playground and Forza Horizon 5 is no exception. The amount of stuff there is to do in just the base game alone is more than worth the price of entry IMHO. Not just because of the sheer size of the game's open world and the amount of cars to collect but because of all the different race routes, stunt spots, story missions and other activities. You can very EASILY get lost in this game for hours at a time!  The only real complaints I have about this game have really just been that some of the DLC's that are not included in the Ultimate bundle are questionably priced (looking at you, Universal car pack) and the story characters are admittedly pretty bland to the point of being annoying at times. Still though, this is still a Forza Horizon game at its core so I wholeheartedly recommend it both to existing fans and people looking to try the series out!

[h3]Just another racing game ? well, not really[/h3] I was kinda hesitant for a long time, wondering if I should even buy it. The story is nice, it keeps you excited, even if some story races are insanely hard to get 3 stars. Icons of Speed Past Midnight is the only time in my life I hated a Supra, but it is what it is.  Different environments across the map, like jungle, mountains, desert, not sure if Mexico is like this, but it looks amazing. Side challenges around the map, treasure chests or barn‑finds where you get legendary cars, are also nice, a cool way to reward players in story mode.  [h3]Hot Wheels DLC? Absolutely worth it. [/h3] The DLC takes you to some floating islands up in the sky, each with its own environment: a forest‑canopy island, a snowy/volcano‑tundra island, and a canyon‑desert island. There are insane loops, jumps, magnet‑tracks, water‑slide tracks and wild gravity‑defying stuff.  The challenges and races are amazing, and I actually completed them, it was really short, but fun. It took me about 30h to hit 100 % completion. I started playing this instead of the story mode, because why not 😂  Overall, cool DLC, worth it. ...though I’ll be honest, the sharp turns on this map were a pain in the a** sometimes 😂  [h3] Conclusion. Online play is smoother than ever, and joining Horizon Arcade or seasonal events with friends feels effortless and rewarding.  Visually, Forza Horizon 5 is absolutely stunning—arguably one of the best-looking racing games ever made. Forza Horizon 5 is an open-world racing game developed by Playground Games and published by Xbox Game Studios. Set in a vast, fictionalized version of Mexico, it expands on the formula of its predecessors with improved visuals, refined physics, and a seamless blend of arcade accessibility and simulation detail.  The core gameplay revolves around freedom of exploration. Players can race on-road, off-road, or through city streets, jungles, deserts, and mountain terrain. The map is massive and diverse, offering dynamic weather systems and seasonal variations that significantly alter driving conditions.  Car handling strikes a balance between realism and fun. Every vehicle feels distinct, yet controllable across multiple surfaces. Tuning options, upgrades, and customization systems allow players to fine-tune performance and appearance to match their driving style. The feedback loop of earning, modifying, and mastering cars remains deeply satisfying.  Visually, Forza Horizon 5 sets a benchmark for open-world graphics. The lighting, skyboxes, and environmental detail are exceptional, from volcanic peaks to coastal highways. On modern hardware, the game maintains high frame rates and resolution with minimal loading, making exploration fluid and uninterrupted.  The soundtrack and audio design are equally polished. Ambient sounds, engine roars, and radio stations create atmosphere and variety. The adaptive music system reinforces pacing—quiet between races, energetic during events. Voice acting and festival chatter maintain the game’s upbeat tone.  Multiplayer integration is seamless through the “Horizon Life” system. Players can join events, convoys, and races instantly without interrupting single-player flow. The community-driven seasonal challenges, creative modes, and online leaderboards extend longevity far beyond the main campaign.  Overall, Forza Horizon 5 is one of the most complete open-world racing experiences ever made. It combines technical excellence with freedom, accessibility, and an infectious sense of discovery. For both casual drivers and car enthusiasts, it represents the high point of the Horizon series—a world built for speed, creativity, and constant motion.

Perfect realistic art style (people may disagree with me on this, but i prefer realistic graphics art styles compared to more cartoony ones, much like how it was in Forza Horizon 4), the graphics in my opinion are one of the best graphics ever made for a video game. The only games that look better or are on par with Forza Horizon 5 is something like Ready or Not (one of the only good UE5 titles where the devs actually cared for its artstyle and AMAZING performance, which is unbelievable to be said about UE5 titles), the upcoming GTA 6 and RDR2. FH5 is a tough title for me. I love racing games, but because I've never owned an Xbox console I've never played any of the Horizon games. It feels like a 9/10 game but is hindered by an overwhelming career/story mode and cluttered UI. I still recommend it, but it's not for me.  On one hand, the visuals, location, soundtrack, and car roster are all top tier. You'll pretty much be able to find a little of everything in this game, as you'd expect.   The things I don't like are minimal, and maybe down to personal preferences, but they still ruled my experience. First, I just don't vibe with Horizon's physics in this title. The cars seem to just skate over any surface, and while cars can seem like they have weight when throwing them into corners, they also just bounce off walls, cars, or other immovable parts of the environment. If I think about all my favorite racing titles, they all make you feel like what you're driving is centered in the world. I rarely felt that way in this game. Most importantly of my criticisms comes down the gameplay: there is simply TOO MUCH to do. You are constantly being pulled in different directions, which seems like the ultimate game experience because you'll never run out of things to do. For me I was looking for more of a linear story, with side quests thrown in, but there's seemingly no "continue" point. This isn't helped by the fact that, from the start, you have a huge budget and are given one of every class of vehicle. Not to mention you get a new car after every other race, you're soon flooded with too much choice.

🏆 "The Ultimate Open-World Racing Experience" ⏱️ ~20+ hours played 👍 Helpful Review  I’ve played a lot of racing games over the years — arcade, sim, open world — but Forza Horizon 5 hits a level of polish and freedom that very few games ever reach.  From the very first drive, it feels incredible. The controls are buttery smooth, every car has its own personality, and the sense of speed is addictive. But what truly makes this game special is how it manages to be both relaxing and thrilling at the same time. One moment you’re drifting through mountain roads with a sunset in the background; the next, you’re blasting through a sandstorm in a million-dollar hypercar. It’s pure joy.  The map — a stunning recreation of Mexico — is honestly one of the most beautiful open worlds I’ve ever seen in any game, racing or otherwise. The diversity is insane: jungles, volcanoes, cities, deserts, beaches… all seamlessly connected. You can drive for hours and still find new places, new routes, and new surprises.  Customization is another huge win here. You can tune, paint, and modify your cars in countless ways, down to the smallest detail. The community paints and liveries are basically art. Combine that with a massive car list — classics, supercars, off-road beasts — and it’s impossible to get bored.  Online play is smooth, fun, and totally integrated into the experience. No endless menus or waiting lobbies — just hop in, and you’re racing with friends or randoms in seconds. The Horizon Festival feels alive, and that feeling of being part of something bigger makes the world feel dynamic and social.  The music is top-notch, the atmosphere is unmatched, and the performance (especially on PC) is fantastic. Even after hundreds of hours, I still find myself launching the game just to cruise around, take photos, and enjoy the scenery.  If you love cars, freedom, or just beautiful worlds to get lost in, Forza Horizon 5 is the best it gets. It’s not just a racing game — it’s an experience you feel.  ⭐ 10/10 — “Just one more drive.”

After spending about 120 hours in Forza Horizon 5 and unlocking almost all of the achievements, I feel like I have experienced nearly everything the game has to offer. First of all, the game is visually stunning. The map based on Mexico is beautiful, the car selection is huge, and the driving physics are still some of the best in the arcade-racing genre. However, after a long time playing, the gameplay starts to feel repetitive. Many events begin to feel the same, and this is something that also reminds me of Forza Horizon 4. The core gameplay loop hasn’t changed much between the two games. The DLCs are a mixed experience. The Rally Adventure DLC is actually quite interesting. The rally mechanics, dirt roads, and more technical driving create a refreshing change of pace compared to the base game. It feels more focused and challenging, which I appreciated. On the other hand, the Hot Wheels DLC was less interesting for me. While the tracks look impressive and creative, the gameplay quickly becomes more about spectacle than driving skill, and the novelty wears off faster than expected. One mode that I personally didn’t enjoy is “The Eliminator”. While the idea of a battle-royale style racing mode is creative, in practice it often feels frustrating and somewhat random. Encounters can depend too much on luck, car drops, or map positioning rather than pure driving skill. Because of this, the mode never really felt satisfying or balanced to me, even though I appreciate the attempt to add something different. Another downside is the lack of a meaningful story. There are some narrative elements, but they are very light and mostly serve as short introductions to events. Compared to how big the game world is, the story content feels minimal. Overall, Forza Horizon 5 is still a very polished and enjoyable racing game, especially in the first dozens of hours. But after completing most of the achievements and spending over 120 hours in the game, the repetition and lack of deeper progression or story can make it feel a bit monotonous. Still, for fans of arcade racing and car collecting, it remains a solid experience.

I've already put in 200hrs, and I haven't even got to the DLC maps (not to mention the weekly festival playlists).   PROs + Great racing game with a large variety of races and cars. Truly overwhelming in terms of scale.  + Diverse biomes with alternating seasons.  + New challenges weekly (most of which are fun) + Great car handling and physics. a sweet spot between simulation and arcade. Makes you work hard to master each car. And you can truly feel the differences between tuned cars.  + Multiple difficulty levels for each player. Allows you fine grained control over the difficulty. Also allows you to grow as a racer. (games like NFS have very few modes, and the highest difficulty is either not hard enough, or rubber-banding physics-bending AI) --> this is not the case in this game.  + Events, Class Tiers and Tuning makes all the cars viable and usable. Also encourages us to use a variety of cars throughout our playthrough). Also encourages us to play at different Tier levels, all races are skilled and fun, and the skill levels are very balanced and controllable. + Not pay-walled or pay-to-win! + Lots of post game content, careers, jobs, events, adventures, makes the game worth every cent.    CONs + Poor map design, very sparsely populated. large open spaces, very very boring. I don't know how you managed to make Mexico (a place so full of life) sooooo boring. One convoluted city which is rarely visited in events or races, in a corner of the map. And the houses are repetitive and non-memorable. It is a nice city, but could have made it a little less repetitive, and also make a few more city like regions in the rest of the map. + AI is very good, but seems to lose its spirit when you take the lead. Needs some work for overtaking aggression. + Progression is kinda lame, no real sense of achievement or progress besides self-motivation. The story of the festival is getting kinda old too. None of the characters or NPCs are memorable.  + Maybe implement a slowdown (or time penalty) for folks who miss a checkpoint instead of a 5 second countdown, and then full reset. This sets you back 10-15 seconds in total, which is akin to losing the race. It does not encourage a catch-up but instead just forces you to restart the entire race. (at least for offline races) + Allow for keybinds for tuning while driving, without stopping and making the changes in menu. Like a tuner mode.   THINGS THAT NEED FIXING :  + Poorly optimized for PC controls. Mouse clicks don't work in half the menus.  + When we start a race, the default car option should be the current car (WTF, how is this still not a thing??!) + Please allows us to choose what is shown on the mini-map (just like the main map). Some icons are very large, permanent and block other visuals, and other important things. + Allow for tunes and paints to be changed without visiting the festival or home. *(this can maybe be unlocked or achieved like fast travel) + When we fast travel to any race on the map, the car teleports to a point ahead of the "race start marker" so we have to reverse or spin around every time, instead of just starting the race. Really weird! --> Maybe just make the race start bubbles a little larger, and allow for moving cars to start the race easily. + S2 and X cars with high initial acceleration need enhanced traction control (especially at launch) for KEYBOARD players (if controllers can have aim assist in other games, maybe you can help keyboard players for once). + Move all the on-screen notifications to the side during races (like car mastery points, skills, achievements).  + Allow us to choose the difficulty level for weekly playlist championships (like in FH4), you can set a minimum difficulty, but allow us to raise it. (Also note that : highly skilled (in championships) and unbeatable (in trials), might be very hard for new players, consider lowering that minimum ceiling, but allow for higher difficulty options for those who want it) + Allow the tires to be unlocked from the rest of the tuning setups so that we can still use the same tunes for different surfaces and weather conditions with a simple tire swap. + Allow us to zoom all the way out on the map, so we can sometimes see the whole map. (we don't mind black bars on the screen sides when in map mode) + Allow folks to opt into Forzathons (maybe a pop-up "ENTER" request like when matchmaking) (not just if they are present in the Forzathon bubble), as passing cars or disinterested parties accidentally join the event and don't contribute.  + Sometimes at dusk, the sky is brighter than the road and terrain, this looks very pretty, but makes it the most difficult race in terms of visibility, as the eye cannot adjust to the dark terrain while the sky is so illuminated). + Red-smoke shader is pixelated at all resolutions and quality settings. Needs to be fixed.

Forza Horizon 5 — Gorgeous Cars, Disgusting Online System  I genuinely want Forza Horizon to keep getting better — this series has been with me for years and given me countless moments of joy. That’s why it hurts to see how badly Forza Horizon 5 handles its online experience.  Let’s be fair: Forza Horizon 5 could’ve been the best open-world racing game ever made. The cars look amazing, the map is huge, the driving feels great — until you go online.  The moment you join a multiplayer race, it turns into a demolition derby. People ram you at full speed, shove you off the track, block you on purpose — and laugh while doing it. Want to report them? Good luck. You’ll have to record a video, take screenshots, manually type in their nickname, and then pray that someone at Playground Games actually bothers to look. Spoiler: they don’t.  In the end, the system punishes fair players with frustration and rewards griefers with total freedom.  What’s worse is that other racing games already solved this years ago. iRacing uses a Safety Rating system that automatically penalizes dangerous driving and off-track behavior; Gran Turismo 7 tracks contact frequency and “sportsmanship scores.” And Forza Horizon 5? Still living in the 2010s, pretending that “manual reports” are enough to keep races fair.  If Playground Games actually cares about online racing, here’s what they should do:  Add an in-game instant report tool that automatically saves the last five minutes of gameplay;  Use diverse, data-driven calculation methods (relative speed, collision angle, impact frequency, trajectory changes after contact, etc.) to detect intentional ramming;  Toughen penalties for high-speed or deliberate collisions — ghost offenders, kick them from lobbies, or restrict ranked play;  Or just remove player-to-player collisions entirely in public lobbies if you can’t manage them properly.  It’s 2025. Other games already use advanced algorithms and unique detection methods to maintain fair, clean racing — yet Horizon 5 still relies on player “self-discipline.”  If you can’t even guarantee basic online fairness, stop pretending to be an MMO. Focus on what Forza Horizon used to be — a pure, joyful single-player racing experience.  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------  总的来说地平线算是这十几二十年历程里综合最优秀的赛车游戏，陪伴了我近十年的时光，但是不得不说，如果线上游戏维持当前的监管水平那playground还是别做把地平线网游化，增强社交属性的春秋大梦了（乐  玩家在比赛里乱撞、恶意挡路成，举报流程又繁琐得一匹——录视频、截图、输入昵称，还要填写违规行为，甚至还要专门的术语，处理速度短则几天长则半年，大概率是最后没人理。 我就纳了闷了，是别的赛车游戏没有安全评分或算法识别恶意驾驶的例子吗，这么大家公司不会学习吗？《地平线5》多少年了却还停留在不知道多久的过去？？？ 解决方法说白了，要么加入游戏内即时举报和自动录像，完善监管 ; 要么彻底取消玩家碰撞体积 又想要车辆碰撞的趣味性又不维护在线环境，世上没这种好事 2025年了，靠玩家“自觉”维护公平多少有点贻笑大方了

There's a lot with this game so I'm just gonna to a pros and cons list:  Pros: - As of 2025 standards, the game is visually stunning. - Weekly/Monthly challenges so there's reason to come back in check in. - Some of these cars are FUN to drive. Controller or wheel some of these cars are just a blast to use. - Again as of 2025 standards, the system requirements are pretty broad so you can kind of play this game on anything. - Online is a blast! I love this! let me pull off some insane stunts! It's much more friendly for a casual audience that just wants a good time with no headaches.  Cons: - It's nice that there's a butt ton of cars... But like 40% of them feel like hot garbage to control, and most people don't wanna spend hours to make their car feel good to drive in. - Car availability is HORRIFIC!!! You want a certain car that's not in the autoshow? Pray it's in the auction house and have an extra 20mil credits ready to hopefully buy it out before someone else does. You can literally game the system and earn credits faster by scalping and reselling cars in the auction house compared to actually playing the game. - (This is a Steam specific issue) If you buy Horizon off steam and want to play it on your Xbox you have to buy the game again on the Xbox storefront. It's an "Xbox play anywhere" title so it should support this, but this is a totally separate issue that's from my understanding on Steam's end and not Microsoft's. - DLC. I get the game has expansions, but some of the "car packs" offered are just a waste of money. - Bots have overran the leaderboards. Forza Horizon 5 is one of those games that never really gets old. From the moment you drop into Mexico, everything just feels alive — the lighting, the weather, the sound of engines bouncing off canyons and jungles. The map is massive but never empty; every corner has a race, a barn find, or just a reason to floor it.  The driving physics strike that perfect balance between realism and fun. Every car feels different — from rally monsters sliding through the desert to hypercars screaming down the highway. The tuning and customization go deep, but even if you’re not into that, the game’s accessible enough to just jump in and enjoy.  Online play is smooth, and the community events keep it fresh. The only real downside is the progression can feel a bit too generous — you earn cars so fast that collecting loses some meaning. Still, that’s a small complaint in a game this polished.  Forza Horizon 5 isn’t just a racing game — it’s a celebration of driving. Whether you’re cruising for the views or chasing leaderboard times, it’s easily one of the best open-world racers ever made.

🏎️ Forza Horizon 5 – Personal Review   I’ve played a lot of racing games over the years, but Forza Horizon 5 is easily one of the best I’ve ever experienced. From the moment you drop out of that plane into Mexico, the game grabs you and doesn’t let go. It’s not just a racing game — it’s an open-world celebration of cars, speed, and freedom.  🌎 World & Visuals  Let’s start with the obvious: this game is absolutely stunning. The Mexican map is huge, diverse, and alive. You can go from racing through a dusty desert to tearing through a rainforest, climbing a volcano, or speeding across the coast — all without a single loading screen. The lighting, weather effects, and car detail are next-level. Sometimes I just drive around with no destination because the world feels so alive.  🚗 Driving & Gameplay  The driving is near perfect. It finds that sweet spot between realism and fun — you feel the weight of the cars, the grip of the tires, but it’s never frustrating. Whether you’re drifting, off-roading, or street racing, the controls feel smooth and responsive. Every car has its own character, and tuning them adds even more depth.  The variety of events is huge — street races, off-road challenges, stunt jumps, drift zones, drag races, and even fun seasonal events. And the freedom to just do whatever you want is what makes Forza Horizon 5 stand out. You can spend hours just exploring, collecting cars, and customizing them to perfection.  💬 Online & Replayability  Online play is solid for the most part — though you’ll run into the occasional disconnect or lag spike. The Horizon Life system makes the world feel alive, with other players zooming by and sharing the same open world. Seasonal events, community challenges, and constant updates keep the game fresh even years later.  ⚙️ Minor Downsides  It’s hard to find serious flaws here. Some bugs and server issues can pop up occasionally, and the AI can feel too forgiving at times. The in-game economy also leans a bit toward grinding if you’re not using wheelspins or lucky draws. But honestly, none of that ruins the experience — it’s still pure fun almost every time I play.  💬 Final Thoughts  Forza Horizon 5 is everything a racing game should be — fast, gorgeous, accessible, and endlessly replayable. It’s one of those games you can lose hours in without even realizing it. Whether you’re a hardcore car fan or just want to relax and cruise through an open world, this game delivers in every way.  ⭐ Final Rating: 9.5/10  Breathtaking visuals, incredible driving feel, and endless freedom. Forza Horizon 5 is the gold standard for open-world racing — it’s pure joy on four wheels.

[h2]The epitome of modern open-world simcade... with flaws[/h2] [b]Purchased Premium Edition & played on Steam Deck LCD[/b]  There’s nothing that I can say about this game that hasn’t already been said. [i]Forza Horizon 5[/i] will be remembered less as the great open-world 2021 racing game of the year, and more as the placeholder until the next [i]Horizon[/i]; filled with empty deserts, FOMO seasonal playlists, and META cars locked behind either DLC paywalls, or long-since gone time-limited events that cease to return. It really leaves you feeling like it’s a “what could’ve been game," whilst paying little homage to the culture of the country it took place in, with there being only two Mexican cars in the entire roster. Additionally, the content gets very overwhelming at times, flooding you with tasks leaving you no room to breathe and enjoy the scenery until you’ve completed them all. [i]FH5[/i]’s biggest redeeming factor was its ability to make you miss its predecessor, when there was a simpler currency system pre-accolades, where there were proper seasons, and what felt like a much more colorful game in [i]Forza Horizon 4[/i] than its 5th rendition counterpart.  Conversely, there is no [i]Forza Horizon[/i] game that I wouldn’t buy, as there isn’t a close alternative- not even by the likes of [i]The Crew[/i] or the [i]Need for Speed[/i] franchise (which EA has shelved at the time of writing this): neither having the semblance of [i]Forza[/i]’s atmosphere. Despite this game leaving more to be desired, it really shines when it comes to rallying. The simcade physics with simulation steering turned on, is quite an enjoyable experience whilst offroading. Both expansion packs can be summed up as "nothing short of amazing." Not to mention the variety of traditional, or sometimes purely fun nonsensical, vehicle builds that you can race competitively against other players. Most of all, [i]FH5[/i] is a really easy title to pick up and run on low to mid range hardware such as the Steam Deck. It was and still is worth my time to play until the inevitable release of [i]Forza Horizon 6[/i]’s Japan, and I’m sure it will be worth yours as well.  [i]Forza Horizon 5[/i] is a fun experience in the dying genre of racing games in spite of its flaws, and you should definitely buy it when it’s on sale. I highly implore purchasing all the DLC given that Microsoft is very stingy with their licensing, because DLCs, along with the base game, do eventually get removed from all storefronts making them impossible to find keys for thereafter.

Before getting deeper into this review, I want to mention, that I've never even thought, I'd ever play and enjoy a car racing game, as I'm mostly into RPGs and MMOs.   With that being said though, Forza Horizon 5 is a very enjoyable racing game. To be completely honest, one of the most enjoyable games I've played in a long time. With only 18.5 hours in currently, I'm far from being an expert on this subject, but this game honestly feels like a RPG packaged as a racing game. You gain levels and currency through participating in races, which you unlock, as you gain more accolade points through various activities and unlock more parts of the Horizon Festival. And that honestly feels pretty much like doing quests and exploration in an RPG. I do like that approach very much.    The driving feels very good, the handling of the various cars do have weight to them, without feeling floaty or overly realistic, in my opinion, its the perfect middleground between realism and arcade, which I also appreciate very much, as I think I probably wouldn't enjoy realism as much as the more "arcadey" approach Forza Horizon 5 has. Racing rarely gets boring either, as the game keeps recommending me higher and higher difficulties, as I keep winning races, and thanks to me repeating races until I can reach 1st place, I currently play on the Expert difficulty level, which really makes it challenging, ngl. The learning curve from Highly Skilled to Expert was exceptionally steep, so that it was a bit frustrating at first, but I'm slowly getting the hang of it after some hours of practice! I will probably update this review, as I progress more and experience more parts and features of this game.

In a vacuum the game is great and would absolutely satisfy a great deal of players. It is even suitable for those that may not be that into cars or sim racing. I myself am in this camp, and it is why I bought Forza 5 to begin with.  However, my grievances with it, and why I have chosen to request a refund are purely grounded in the technicality of the game's "playable" status on Steam Deck. The warning reads "some functionality is not accessible when using the default controller configuration, requiring the use of the touch screen or virtual keyboard, or a community configuration." Fair enough, unless that 'some functionality' is the connection of your steam account to a Microsoft account, without which you cannot play this game at all.   Having spent approximately half of my playtime experiencing the various ways in which this warning is disingenuous for this particular game, I cannot in good faith recommend it.  During initial setup, Microsoft's authentication dialogue boxes scale incorrectly, rendering critical UI elements inaccessible on the Deck's native display. Text entry fields and confirmation buttons appear off-screen or unusable, and were highly unresponsive even when I did find them in the end. Indeed, I did manage to get this to work after roughly 6 attempts, using a USB dock, mouse, keyboard, and the time honoured tradition of button mashing. Even with these peripherals—which most Deck users won't have available portably— this initial start up was a massive pain in the bumper.   The playable badge promises that a game works on Deck with some warts and jank that one must account for. And again, fair enough. But I believe that Valve should revoke playable Steam Deck status for Forza 5 until Microsoft fixes their UI scaling for the authentication flow. Because for those unlucky enough not to get past this verification roadblock, the game isn't actually playable.   It's also kinda silly that the game with a €50 'Premium' edition which doesn't even get you the complete experience can get such intricate monetisation and hamster wheel mechanics right, yet no one seems to have thought 'yo, wouldn't it be useful if people could actually connect to this extraneous service of ours that no one actually likes?' Come on Microsoft. But I recognise that this is me being pedantic rather than pointing out objective technical failures.

Forza Horizon 5 feels like a [b]tech demo[/b].   [h2]the core and technical aspects[/h2]  the core of the game - driving and racing the cars - is incredibly well done and has clearly had a lot of effort and time invested towards it over the course of the franchise's lifespan. the simcade engine is the best of its kind and no other competitor comes close. driving remains immensely satisfying irrespective of the type of vehicle you're maneuvering, the terrain surface you're on, or weather conditions you're under.  the game consistently looks, sounds, and performs very well.   [hr][/hr]  but it ends there. it's as if the developers had invested a lot of time and care into creating an incredibly solid base for a racing game, but then skimped out on all the additional aspects that wouldn't have required nearly as much effort or resources, but that would've greatly contributed to the quality of the final product. that's where the tech demo analogy comes from.  first case in point:  [h2]the map[/h2]  the team was clearly capable of creating a large, varied, beautiful, and functional open world map. Mexico certainly ticks all of those boxes, and more: the volcano, the jungles, the many long, winding and twisting roads with great verticality, the beach town, the stadium and test track - i could go on. [b]on paper it's perfect[/b]. i much prefer it to the predecessor's Edinburgh. but holy sh*t is it [b]empty[/b]. the NPC vehicle traffic is so incredibly sparse. there are [i]zero[/i] pedestrians, like, at all. there's no people. there's no proper intersections, no parking garages, no gas stations, no traffic lights. there's no [i]things happening[/i]. no airplanes in the sky, boats on water, no service vehicles, no wildlife (outside of howler monkeys? and some birds), no events. the one urban area in the game feels like a complete ghost town. it's embarrassing. it looks and feels completely fake.  this has been the case throughout the entirety of the franchise's lifespan. The Crew perfected the open-world racing map in 2018. so why can't Forza Horizon?  [h2]story[/h2]  terrible and completely dispensable in every possible aspect. ninety five percent of the storylines revolve around you driving a vehicle from point A to point B on the map while some at best completely forgettable and at worst extremely annoying character yaps about some boring ♥♥♥♥ in an irritatingly fake and forced spanish accent with involuntary spansih lingo sprinkled in occasionally. it's all totally dry, inoffensive, and boring, with zero character, no emotion, and a total lack of any plot. just absolutely terrible.  the only slightly redeemable aspect are some of the scripted "Showcase" events, which seem more like technical presentations rather than parts of the story.  [h2]progression[/h2]  there is none. the currency model is optimized... - for the 10 year old playing the game on the living room Xbox whose parents bought it for him at $80, and who certainly wouldn't appreciate driving a beat-down Ford for the first 10 hours of the game. and that's fine. but there has to be a fine line, a compromise?   the game showers you with rewards at every possible step. you earn credits as a reward for completing races, showcases, and events - and cars (and their upgrades) [i]do[/i] cost credits - but that aspect very quickly becomes totally irrelevant as you're constantly rewarded with Wheelspins, which in turn give you credits and cars in extreme abundance.  the new "Accolades" system is a diamond in the rough -  a good idea in isolation, which ultimately suffers from being part of a larger, flawed system.  the one aspect of progression that's done right is what the game aptly calls [i]Hard To Find[/i] cars - ones that cannot be purchased outright using credits nor won in a wheelspin. instead, they appear for limited time in either the [i]Forzathon Shop[/i] or as a reward in a seasonal Festival Playlist. and it is this limited nature and the FOMO associated with it is what makes you want to play the game and acquire the car, and what ultimately makes it that much more satisfying once you do. -- but even so it's hard to make these cars appear special or unique next to their cheap, readily available 150,000 CR supercar counterparts.  so - if there's no story to follow or get invested into, and little feeling of progression as you play - what's left?  [hr][/hr]  well, it's not all bleak. again, the activities that benefit most from the game's great foundation are thankfully the ones you'll spend most of your time on - racing (whether against AI or online versus real opponents) and simply cruising around the map. and they're very polished, really enjoyable, and in my opinion enough to just barely overshadow all the negatives. at its core, Forza Horizon 5 is still very enjoyable. it just sucks that i can't help but keep wondering just how much better it would've been with a bit more effort.

I recommend this game, but it has some significant drawbacks.  Overall I give it a 7/10 and if you're looking for a casual, open world racing game with a TON of cars and lots of stuff to do, then it's pretty good.  Positives- 1.  There's a massive amount of cars of all types from many different car companies.  There's over 800 cars in the game which is almost an overwhelming amount.   They have every major brand and a lot of obscure ones too.  There's cars from almost every era including 1920s racers  but it mostly focuses on modern stuff. 2.  The open world is very well designed and there's TONs to do and explore.  There's desert dunes, jungle waterfalls, a snow topped volcano and everything in-between.   They did a great job on the level design and the whole place is filled with fun stuff to do. 3.  There's a wide variety of racing types and tracks.  There's rally, cross country, midnight run style street races, circuit races, drag racing and tons more.   There is also a track designer that is very flexible and you can make your own tracks and share them and race with friends.   You won't run out of tracks. 4.  Car customization is excellent.  You can paint your car how you like or use other peoples paint jobs and tuning setups.  Really nice to be able to paint your car how you like.  5.  You can tune the difficulty of AI racers to how you like.    Negatives-  1. The competitive multiplayer is ABSOLUTE TRASH.  Do not buy this game for the online racing aspect, unless you're going to play with friends.  Once you get to a certain point in the game, you will need to do a weekly "coop" race with other online players VS. the hardest AI drivers in a best of 3 battle.   Unfortunately, over half the time your idiot teammates will spend most of their time and effort ramming and wrecking you and other players instead of beating the AI team, causing the whole team to waste 20 minutes and get nothing.   In any type of online racing, you will be mercilessly rammed by online jerks and there is ZERO penalty for them to do so.  There's no damage model and no points penalty for ramming or forcing other players off the road to miss checkpoints or hit stuff.  The online racing is a complete dumpster fire full of jerks who WILL ram and wreck you constantly. 2.   The developer is incredibly greedy.  Despite launching a 100$ Premium edition, they still released a bunch of DLC cars (that you totally don't need) that were not included in the purchase.  To make things even worse, these extra car packs NEVER go on sale (at the time of this writing).   The greedy developers also stopped releasing any NEW content early in 2025, despite the fact that FH6 will not be out for years.  So everything you're buying will just be recycled events and there will never be any new cars.  Expect this game to get delisted from steam in a few years like they did with FH4 because they're literally too cheap to renew the car licensing rights.    3. The game has total Xbox-ification.  You will need to make an xbox live gaming account and will be forced to use this awful system to find your friends, etc. despite this being on Steam. 4. There is no real car damage in the game.  Your million dollar supercar can ram through metal guardrails, stone walls, fences or even small trees with absolute ease!  The worst damage your car will suffer is a cracked windshield, which is annoying if you play in first person.  Your car can look a bit scuffed up, lose a spoiler or side mirrors but the damage never affects performance, which is one reason people ram into each other so much.  This is NOT a realistic racer.  The only stuff that will really stop your car is a large tree, massive boulder or a building.  There's also no tire wear or refueling. 5.  You always start near the back of the field in ANY race.  There is no qualifying or practice options, you just go in cold with no warmup laps or anything to get to know the car.  There's so many cars that you're constantly changing so you don't really get used to racing with one car for long periods of time.   6.  The "plot" is just junk.  They try to make a plot around you being the best driver in the world and it's just paper thin.  They also try and fail horribly to incorporate Mexican culture and history into racing.   One example of this is there is an entire storyline about Mexican Wrestling and cars, and yes, this plot is absolutely as horrendous as you'd expect.   Forza Horizon 4 had Top Gear as the guests for one plot series and it was good and funny.  This game has the insufferable goons from Donut Media cleverly mispronouncing words like horsepower.   The plot is luckily skippable and you don't have to play much of it to unlock the whole game. 7.  This is not a SIM by any means.  Besides the aforementioned lack of damage, tire wear, or fueling, I would say the physics aren't 100% accurate.   Rain seems to affect traction very little and there is literally not a single pothole or manhole cover in the ENTIRE country of Mexico!  Amazing!  There's no bumps in the road or even a speedbump.   Don't expect extreme realism here, it's more a game you can play with a controller than requiring a wheel.  This is more of a casual, have some beers and race around type game. 8.  The hotwheels expansion isn't that great.  It turns out that racing around narrow plastic orange lanes at super high speeds gets old after a few hours.   9.  The game throws so many cars at you early in the game that you never really establish a bond or an affinity for many cars.  It certainly doesn't have a career mode or anything.  You'll just get a ton of fast cars right away.  10.  Every global leader board for fastest times are completely filled with hackers and totally impossible times and the developers refuse to fix them or delete them.  So with all these negatives, why do I give this game a 7/10?  Well, it's super fun for what it does.  It's a casual open world racing game where you can do what you want and collect and customize over 800 cars, which is pretty badass!   The open worlds are huge, full of different terrain, they did a fantastic job with the level design.   Just know that this is a more casual racer, that the developers are super greedy and that the online mode with random people is absolute trash due to ramming.   If you love cars and just messing around driving, you can easily have 200+ hours of enjoyment out of this game.  You can also really make the game your own with a custom dressed up character, totally custom paint and a full, powerful map editor to make your own tracks and share them.   Just don't expect sim level physics, any kind of damage or the plot to be any good!  If you've got friends to play with instead of randoms, the online component gets better as well.   Also, since this game is getting "old" now and will likely get some pretty good Steam discounts, I highly recommend the Complete Edition since you'll get double the VIP points (used for getting weekly rare cars) and comes with both expansion packs which add large areas to the game.    Hope this helps and watch out for those rammers!

how to make delicious Butter Chicken. ----------------------------------------------------------- Ingredients for 4 servings, 2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast (910 g), cubed salt, to taste pepper, to taste 2 teaspoons chili powder, divided ½ teaspoon turmeric 6 tablespoons butter, divided 1 ½ cups yellow onion (225 g), diced 3 teaspoons garam masala 1 teaspoon cumin 1 teaspoon cayenne pepper 1 tablespoon ginger, grated 3 cloves garlic, minced 1 cinnamon, 3 inch (8 cm) stick 14 oz tomato sauce (395 g) 1 cup water (240 mL) 1 cup heavy cream (240 mL) rice, for serving fresh cilantro, chopped for garnish.  Preparation In a large bowl, season the chicken breast with salt, pepper, 1 teaspoon of chili powder, and the teaspoon of turmeric. Let sit for 15 minutes to marinate. Melt 2 tablespoons of butter in a large pot over medium heat. Brown the chicken, then remove from the pot. Melt another 2 tablespoons of butter in the pot, then add the onion, garam masala, remaining teaspoon of chili powder, the cumin, ginger, garlic, cayenne, cinnamon, salt and pepper. Cook until fragrant. Add the tomato sauce and bring to a simmer. Add the water and cream and return to a simmer. Return the chicken to the pot, cover, and simmer for another 10-15 minutes. I can recommend this game ONLY if you seek something where you can drive cars around and nothing else. This aspect could give you a dozen or so hours after which you will get bored and put the game on a shelf (if you can endure everything else about the game).  Yes, it is extremely well optimized, has loads of cars and has great visuals.  However.  There is no progression. The second you launch the game, you are awarded with gazillion of hypercars, currency and dozens of gambling spins. Besides driving the cars the game will, basically, play itself. You do not start in some rusty hatchback that your dad left you and progress from the bottom. You do not need to strive to do races to get some shiny supercar you always wanted. You do not have an opponent you really want to beat as every other driver is a faceless shadow without personality, or a face and personality so horrible you wish they didnt have either. You do not feel like your reputation grows, like you overcome something. There is no stroy. There is no decision making. There is no ending because you already start with everything bending to your will. Every event you do is meaningless - you DO NOT need to adapt or overcome the challenges to progress. You cannot lose, often even if you finish 10th, because the game doesn't want you to feel sad. Yes, the game literally treats you like a social media addicted basement dweller that gets offended from a single word. Or a journalist. Don't know which is worse. A race? You can drive whatever the hell you want and upgrade your car however you like, your opponents will just adjust to whatever you roll to the starting grid. A time trial? Just drive through the flat desert in your koenigsegg without even thinking about using the road (because of course your hypercar can drive on sand and dirt like a rally car) and finish minutes ahead of the "best" score. High score challenge? Just do whatever, no need to try chaining drifts into jumps and precise traffic avoidane - I am serious - game rewards you with points for EVERY action you make, just dont crash too hard.  Map design is atrocious, as beside the edges of the map (20% of the whole thing) where there are actually some obstacles or problematic terrain you might need to cope with, the rest is a flat, boring, uninspired desert. And why is it there, you ask? Because devs thought that a car battle royale would be a good idea. It wasn't.   Like I said earlier, there is no story. But what about the dialogue? Yes there are plenty of voice acted lines. You would wish they weren't the second you hear a single one. Everyone is so over the top, cheesy, and cringy while doing their voice over for poorly written dialogue that the game actually becomes a better experience with voices turned off completely.   Music choice is bland and just barely above the atrocious taste of whoever picked music for recent NFS games. Yes they also mute words like "die" if they appear in lyrics.   AI will either be a grandma with asthma or a volkswagen beetle that would blitz past you with 30km/h speed advantage despite you driving a bugatti at its top speed.  If you played other FH games the "big events" the game throws at you do not have that "wow" factor you got after racing a plane for the first time, or trying to outplace some dirt bikers in a forest. It was all done before, and there is nothing in them besides the heavily scripted "tense" moments sprinkled here and there.  Overall, and I'm completely serious here, FH games have so much untapped potential to become best in genre, but the developers simply refuse it in favour of appealing to kiddies who are satisfied from just seeing shiny cars go fast.  I really, really hope (but have zero realistic expectations if we look at how they addressed these problems before - they didn't) that the next franchise entry would have a proper career mode with an actual engaging story and progression. That these stupid gambling wheelspins would be locked until you complete it. That the map and physics would be designed in a way so you can't cut a corner of a well-paved road through some mud while being in a lamborghini and gain time. That the dialogues would be written by an actual writer and not some blue haired middle aged woman from their HR department. That the purchases you make would have importance and require weighing pros and cons of different cars before you buy one. That the devs would actually take time and handcraft races with proper limitations to force players to interact with different car classes and mechanics - force them to buy some japanese sportscar to attend a championship, force them to upgrade their car to gain an advantage, force them to save money to get that hypercar for the final part of the game. Maybe also make purchase of housing mandatory if palyers want a bigger garage? At least up until the story is over and they can do whatever? Please?   It's such a shame that's this franchise is [i]still[/i] somehow the best option racing genre has to offer. Forza Horizon 2, 3, and 4, were all way better in my opinion. This game suffers from extremely generous progression (e.g. allowing you to get multiple supercars and hypercars within the first few hours of playing) which feels nice at first but quickly discards the necessity of ever using the majority of your cars. The roads feel very easy to drive on; there's very few hairpins or chicanes/esses and the roads being wide and generous exacerbate the design philosophy of cars going fast rather than drivers. It makes the sense of speed in this game feel slow, with high centre-of-gravity cars remaining extremely planted and having a large margin for error in terms of steering angle even at 300-350km/h. The AI also feels very strange with lower difficulty AI being easily overtaken with trail braking and switchbacks and then suddenly jumping in difficulty to where AI drivatar trucks can take hard turns better than track-focused cars like Porsches. I understand the game is arcade-y but weight transfer isn't really a worry in that regard for cornering, and cars with the best specs seem to dominate rather than having cars play into specific strengths (i.e. Porsches best at cornering and Corvettes for off-the-line power). Lastly, many of the iconic cars (NSX-R, SVJ, GT3RS, 720s, F90 CS)  are either only acquired through time-limited events (FOMO) or have incredibly high auction prices, and there's nothing to differentiate them spec-wise other than their demand as there's no reason to purchase one considering you're essentially guaranteed to have an S2 or X level car within the first 10ish hours anyway.   This game is serviceable in my opinion as an arcade open-world driving game but if you're looking for something more focused in terms of the actual driving experience, I'd recommend Assetto Corsa instead.

[b]Overall, a good Forza Horizon game. Not without flaws, though.[/b]  My second Forza Horizon game that I played. Overall, I enjoyed this game, mainly from the gameplay aspect. It's better than FH4, gameplay-wise. Starting from the improved physics, better server connection (much faster), great car sounds (compared to FH4's, which are horrendous), and more things to do (EventLab is a great addition to the franchise).  Of course, despite these improvements, this game is not without flaws. First, the most obvious one: story. Man, the story feels like it's catered towards three-year-olds. Even then three-year-olds would most likely hate it. Second, the soundtrack. Don't get me wrong, they're nice to listen to. But it's obviously not curated. The songs sometimes feel like they're chosen because they're popular, not because they fit the festival vibe/theme. Also, the censorship is actually even worse than in FH4, and I hate that. Third, the map. Stupid decision to cater it to The Eliminator. A mode that has been abandoned since release. The result? Boring map. Yes, there's a lot of stuff here and there, but the middle of the map is just too empty. You obviously can still put stuff there. Major miss since Mexico still has more to offer.  The rest are minor issues, like the quirky server (convoy missing randomly, not all players visible), some accolades not working (bugged), and the lack of progression (can make the game feels boring faster).  I hope FH6 doesn't have the flaws that FH5 has. Better story (age rating shouldn't influence writing like in FH5), better server (FH4 server with FH5 connectivity speed), better map (catered towards car culture, preferably), better soundtrack (curate it and don't censor it to kingdom come (GT7 doesn't censor their soundtrack despite having the same age rating as FH5. Hell, even FH3 didn't censor its soundtrack with the same freaking age rating.), and some other improvements, minor or major. Also, improve the customization (improve or remove those garbage-looking Forza Aero).

Having never had an Xbox before the Series X (which I subsequently sold to finance my GPU on my first (and current) PC a couple years ago, The Forza Horizon series was always one I'd wanted to play. Fortunately I was able to track down the disks for the first 3 before I sold them and my console. I worked my way through all the games while on Xbox and all of them were fantastic. Knowing they discontinue entries after a time I immediately re-purchased FH4 and 5 on PC.   One of the most standout things about FH5 is its return to having something of a story! Although I loved every game, the first entry always held a special place because it had a little story to it. FH5 returned to form with that, and also featured some cameos that got me in the feelings. lol. It would not have hit me the same way if I'd missed out on the previous games. It's unfortunate many won't have that same experience.  I'm playing on an RTX 4080 Super/Ryzen 7800X3D. The game runs flawlessly at 4k maxed settings. Without DLSS my framerate is in the triple digits. With DLSS (no framegen) the game maxes out my OLED TV at 144fps. The raytracing is FANTASTIC, as is the sound. Racing across the landscape is as fun as ever, as are the street races. Learning a bit about the history of the Volkswagen Beetle was really cool, and the NPC friends in the game are fun to hear from and drive with.  The game handles as awesome as every other entry, with a large diversity of cars. If I'm ever in a poor mood I can  always fire this game up to pick me up. It's just good, bright, FUN! TL;DR Buy if you like sandbox games and a lot of stuff in a game overall, if you hate grinding, or if you want a more realistic racing game than other arcade ones. Better don't buy for competitive multiplayer racing.   Forza Horizon is not your typical arcade racing franchise. [b]It's more realistic[/b] with all its pros and cons. You'll find yourself countersteering to avoid unwanted drifting, managing the throttle, finding best parts combinations for your playstyle and the event etc. You will not drift every corner and once you mess one up, the consequences will be immediately noticeable (especially in multiplayer). However you can adjust the difficulty pretty thoroughly, as well as add several assists. With the right adjustment the game can be accessible even for pretty young and inexperienced players.  Possibly the biggest advantage of the Horizon franchise has always been the [b]enormous car list[/b] and this title is no exception. With all DLCs and rare cars it goes beyond 800 vehicles (there are a few semi trucks lol), all with unique handling and capabilities.  Speaking of cars, they are extremely easy to obtain. This is a part of another unique (and subjective) thing about the franchise - [b]extremely fast progression[/b]. You can easily get around 3 cars per hour (not even counting rewards from weekly events), as well as other rewards such as clothes and money (which you can use to buy even more cars). Btw money is usually not a problem at all (unless you're trying to buy all the most expensive cars) so you will never find yourself grinding for upgrades (which are all purchaseable with in game currency; no levels or microtransactions there), unlike in most of the other games.  The game [b]does not have a proper story[/b]. The "campaign" is basically just a long tutorial. After that you're free to do whatever you want. All features are unlocked.  That brings us to another major difference of Forza Horizon compared to other franchises - [b]the game is a sandbox[/b]. This means you need to know how to entertain yourself and use the game's features for it. There are weekly challenges with rare rewards but that's basically it in terms of what the game "wants" you to do. Everything else is up to you, whether you like it or not.  When it comes to competitive playstyle, the game offers quite a lot of options, and the leaderboards are extremely competitive. There are also less competitive gamemodes such as Playground Games (various arcade games), The Eliminator (battle royale) and Hide And Seek. However it's important to note that [b]the game is not built for competitive play. Factors such as FPS may affect the laptime and result in an unfair experience[/b]. There are also cheaters but you can just report and ignore those.  [b]Performance and optimization are great[/b], just like in FH4. The game works on any decently modern hardware. You don't need a high end PC even for ultra settings.  The game features some microtransactions but the only thing you can get from them is common cars which you can also get for in game currency. You can't even get rare cars for real money. That is really good. I won't even highlight this section.   When it comes to FH5 specifically, there are some differences from the previous games. Most noticeably, [b]car handling was simplified[/b] on keyboard and controller, offroading was simplified overall, and wheel support was greatly improved. So if you want a more hardcore experience on anything except for steering wheel, I'd suggest FH4 or FH3. Trust me, it can get very intense there, especially offroad. Also there are more arcade gamemodes in FH5 which have already been mentioned above.   In terms of [b]issues[/b], the most noticeable one is [b]meta gaming[/b]. It means that some cars have an unfair advantage in their respective use cases. This can make the experience repetitive if you're trying to be very competitive.  Similarly to that there is [b]ramming[/b] - unsportsmanlike behavior of others players who try to ram you off the road, resulting in you losing the race. The issue is really common and needs to be aknowledged at all times during multiplayer sessions (aka get ready to get rammed and use defensive manuevers in any suspicious situation). Also note that your teammates can ram too (very frustrating ik).   So in conclusion, the game features extremely fast progression and a lot of features but does not force the player to do anything specific. This can be good or bad depending on your preference. I personally love that. Also the game is far from the best in terms of competitive play so do not buy it just for that.

As a car guy, or a car enthusiast, Forza Horizon 5 provides a tonne of touches into the car details. From the stunning graphics that bring each vehicle to life to the intricate sound design that captures the roar of the engines, every aspect has been meticulously crafted. This attention to detail not only enhances the driving experience but also immerses players in a vibrant automotive world.  What makes this game feel different from any other racing series? Is its philosophy. Where Need for Speed thrives on underground street racing and title challenges, Forza Horizon embraces the celebration of car culture itself. It’s not only about racing; it’s about exploration, creativity, and community.  The open-world setting in Mexico is expansive and diverse, offering everything from deserts and rainforests to bustling towns and ancient ruins. Players are encouraged to drive not just to compete, but to discover, photograph, and enjoy the beauty of the world. Beyond traditional racing, the Horizon Festival format allows for casual cruising, stunt challenges, showcase events, and even player-created content, making the experience broader than a simple competition.  With an unmatched car roster, seamless multiplayer integration, and constant seasonal updates, Forza Horizon 5 stands as both a tribute to automotive passion and a playground for anyone who simply loves the joy of driving.  Verdict: More than a racing game, Forza Horizon 5 is a living celebration of car culture — blending authenticity, freedom, and spectacle in ways no other franchise does.

This is the best racing game out there. Just based on technical issues, I can safely not recommend you buy it though. This might seem odd, but hear me out: The game constantly crashes. But it saves everything up to the crash and it crashes either before the race begins or after it ends. Saving your progress along the way. So crashing isn't as frustrating, but you also cannot skip the intro cutscene, which is prerendered in 1080p. So that's not going to look all that great in the future (or until like the release of the game, where 4k displays already existed). You don't earn money. You gamble for it. Usual races average around 10.000 credits. The cheapest car costs around 40.000 credits. The most expensive thing you can buy in the game is a house for 5.000.000 credits. The credit reward of every single race combined won't give you enough money to buy that house. Even if you haven't spend anything of it. Even if you didn't upgrade/tune your vehicles. Anytime you level up, you get to play a slot machine. The average reward of a slot machine is around 40.000 credits. The game looks great. I feel indifferent for the car handling. The sound is good. The story is underwhelming. The races are generally fun and the open world also has a charm to it. But, I cannot stress enough, that this game has crashed about 20+ times in my 30 hours of playtime on the newest nVidia driver. There are collision bugs in the stadium as well. There's a drifting mission that has released broken for controller players since it's launch and I am quite certain, that it will not be patched out in this timeline. I was thinking of recommending it, because it is a truly good game. But I just can't recommend a game, that crashes this consistantly. It's like recommending a sportscar, that turns off every time you drive more than 2km. I really wanted to like this game, especially after FH 4 which was near perfection for an open world racing game with very few flaws.  Sadly after around 8 hours of trying I uninstalled and went back to FH4 as it still is the superior game in my opinion.  There are a few areas where this game does improve over 4 but it's not the parts which make the game compelling and give you reason enough to stick around.  [u]The Positives[/u]   It is graphically superior, performs well outside of a few minor issues and it does fix one glaring problem 4 had which was customisation.  FH4 only had 4 engines in upgrades, gearbox choices where limited and aero also had few choices.  5 did improve on this and the engines in 5 sounded a lot better.    Driving physics were also tweaked and improved which was a bonus, even if its not driving sim level its a nice touch and adds to the experience.  The weather storms are also a neat feature and some of the tracks and scenery is very well detailed and aesthetically pleasing.  This however is where the problems begin as the nicer tracks and scenery are very few and far between.    [u]The Negatives[/u]  Sadly the really fun tracks and beautiful scenery is sparse due to probably the biggest problem this game has, The map itself.  It's bigger which isn't the issue, it's what they did with the map which is.  In FH4 the map was smaller but the quality was there throughout.  It was visually appealing, the seasons were actually distinct and the it had variety be it driving in the north or through small cosy villages.  In 5 however due to the location and geography available the huge map just looks very bland, very brown and lacks any charm or distinguishing features for the most part.    The lush forests and small town tracks are nice, but due to the lack of enough of it as a whole it just comes across as soulless and uninteresting.  It was all too often that the lack of anything interesting on the map meant that instead of seeing places or roads that felt alive and worth exploring it just became tedious.  Exploring became dull, races not being helped by uninspired track design and nothing to make them pop visually trackside meant that the fun wasn't there as it was in previous incarnations.  When it's pretty it is really well done and the graphics shine but unfortunately there wasn't enough of it.  The second glaring issue is the car choice.  In FH4 and before there is a good mix of classic cars, current cars, performance cars and a few quirky oddball cars which have a lot of charm going for them.  In 5 they really started to swing towards electric cars and made other odd decisions when it came to car choice.  Some of the classic cars from previous incarnations are scrapped for a lot of Electric vehicles which visually and sound wise are nowhere near as fun and lack the soul of some of the cars which where dropped for this game.    There are a few gems hiding in there and some of the cars available that weren't before are pretty good.  The problem is a lot of the newer cars or dlc are either uninteresting, dull to drive or just not on the same level as the ones available on previous games.  Pretty much most of the dlc cars in 4 where very good outside of 1 or 2 dlc packs.  They all added something new and fitted in nicely with the car roster.  In FH 5 however most of the dlc cars are either mid at best or very uninspired.  The base roster itself is ok but a lot of the newer additions for 5 just lack the fun element while driving them. [u]Conclusion[/u]  As a product FH5 looks better, has more choice when it comes to customisation and has nice touches which show it could have had potential. The tracks feel like a step backward when it comes to design and very few of the new cars available make it worth hanging around for.  FH4 may be technically inferior but for the map, for the racing and for feeling vibrant and alive it is still the superior game. I’d describe my experience with Forza Horizon 5 as a love/hate relationship.  On the positive side, the game (and the series as a whole) feels like a spiritual successor to classics like Need for Speed: Underground. It offers a wide variety of cars, deep tuning options, and a massive open world to explore, along with a good mix of race types. That freedom and variety are what keep me coming back.  That said, I mostly stick to offline play. Online racing has lost a lot of appeal since cheating seems rampant, and just a glance at the leaderboards makes that obvious. Offline racing is decent enough, though the “drivatars” can be hit-or-miss. They usually get the job done, but at higher difficulties their behavior can feel erratic and frustrating.  One of my biggest frustrations is car availability. Too many vehicles are locked behind the “Horizon Backstage Pass,” and others are only obtainable through time-limited online events. It feels unnecessarily restrictive, especially for players who do not want to engage heavily with online features.  Cosmetics are another mixed bag. Earlier games gave us a nice range of gloves, suits, and hats. This entry instead leans on additions like prosthetics. They may be meant to feel inclusive, but they came at the cost of variety in the more traditional options people actually used and wanted.  Another ongoing issue is the unskippable NPC chatter. This problem carried over from previous titles, and unfortunately it is still here. The constant dialogue and forced map interruptions feel more grating than immersive, and I would much rather just get back to driving.  In the end, Forza Horizon 5 is still a fun game, but it carries its fair share of irritations. For better or worse, I enjoy it for what it is, though I cannot help wishing it were a little less flawed.

What Works Really Well  1. The Map is Drop-Dead Gorgeous The variety in biomes is incredible: from jungle ruins to coastal beaches to neon-lit cities and towering mountains. The lighting is stunning. The weather systems — especially the dust storms and tropical rain — really make you feel like you're driving through something dynamic.  2. Tons of Cars, and They Feel Great There are hundreds of vehicles, from hypercars to off-road buggies. Whether you're bombing down a highway in a Koenigsegg or drifting through a canyon in a JDM legend, the handling is tight, smooth, and satisfying. You can tweak a lot, but it's also super accessible — anyone can jump in.  3. Smooth Progression Without Pressure Unlike most racers, Forza Horizon 5 doesn’t really punish you for anything. You get rewarded constantly: XP, wheelspins, accolades, cars, credits. It’s less about “winning” and more about enjoying the ride — literally. The game’s tone is relentlessly positive and chill.  4. Online Works Better Than Ever Whether you want to explore solo, co-op races, competitive events, or just mess around in The Eliminator (battle royale mode), Horizon 5’s online is integrated well. Playing with friends is finally smooth, and online events don’t feel tacked on. 5. Accessibility & Customization The level of tuning and control options is insane. Assist settings make it easy for newcomers, while hardcore drivers can go deep with simulation options. There's even a full Event Lab that lets players create custom races and challenges — and it’s surprisingly robust.  What Doesn’t Work (Or Got Old)  1. The Festival Vibe Is… Corny The game leans hard into the “car festival” theme. The dialogue is painfully cheerful, the voiceovers can feel scripted to the point of cringe, and everyone acts like you’re some god-tier celebrity driver. It’s meant to be fun, but sometimes it's a little too over-the-top.  2. Repetition Creeps In Yes, there are tons of events… but after 10-20 hours, you start to notice a pattern. Street races blur together. Cross-country events feel similar. If you're not actively switching up how you play (online, tuning, photo challenges, etc.), the core loop can get stale.  3. Bugs & Online Glitches (Especially at Launch) At launch, the game had some rough online connectivity issues. Things are much better now, but every once in a while, you’ll hit a weird bug — like AI cars freezing, races not loading, or leader boards glitching out. Nothing game-breaking, but definitely annoying when it happens.  Score: 9/10 “A vibrant, high-octane sandbox that never stops giving — even if it gets a little too friendly sometimes.”
