Why the Game is not really worth the price Missed Potential Coupled with Jaw-Dropping Visuals Forza Horizon 5 offers an eye-wateringly beautiful open world packed with a massive car roster and well-realized environments. However, when it should be delivering the genuine car culture experience, especially social car meets and multiplayer sessions, it slips up in many critical areas.  Car Meet Experience The game is lacking in good, well-planned car meet spots. Most of the spots are small, uneven, or filled with random traffic that hurts normal meets.  The Horizon Cars & Coffee update added a more car meet-friendly spot, but it's small and doesn't address the overall demand for big, adaptive meet spots.  Spawn experience desecrates the mood with crass festival tunes and messy settings, clashing with the chill atmosphere car enthusiasts require when gathering.  There is no dedicated car meet mode, so there is a makeshift lobby that players must settle for which is often buggy and awkward to manage.  Progression and Racing There is a minimalist progression system where players are dropped right into hypercars like Bugattis, spoiling the grind to get through car classes vibe.  Tracks are mostly improvised road courses or loops with no real racing curbs, predetermined racing lines, or specific race courses, so racing is lifeless and unsatisfying.  Races are shorter and rubber-banded, decreasing challenge and replay value.  Car tuning is ancient and restricted, especially compared to modern standards.  Multiplayer and Crossplay Crossplay is only available on Xbox consoles and Microsoft Store computers, with Steam players essentially locked out, and social play is impossible.  Private meet hosting and car meet hosting are problematic with platform constraints and inconsistent matchmaking, usually capping meet sizes at a handful of players.  With a relatively small online community and technical issues, hosting dynamic large-scale car meets is quite a challenge.  Final Thoughts Forza Horizon 5 is an incredible idea for a social racing game, but technical limitations and design choices keep it from fostering a lively car enthusiast community. No meet spaces, linear progression, and cringe multiplayer severely restrict the game's allure among players looking for genuine car meet ambiances and meaningful racing experiences.  All that aside, the modding community and car enthusiast meet groups try their best to fill in the blanks, but the game itself can do with some actual improvement in these areas. If Playground Games pays attention to these issues in upcoming patches or sequels, then FH5 can truly be a must-have for automotive enthusiasts.

It’s the first racing game that truly hooked me since Need for Speed: Most Wanted (2005 — the GOAT). From the moment I launched FH5, I felt like I was 12 again: controller in hand, throwing cars sideways through traffic like a maniac.  FH5 doesn’t pretend to be a simulator. It’s big, loud, colorful, unapologetically arcade — and that’s exactly why it works. Cars feel great, the map is gorgeous, and everything flows: races, challenges, stunts, barn finds, dumb little stories… you’re never stuck, and you’re never out of things to do.  No need to tune gear ratios or worry about tire wear. Just floor it, drift through a jungle, fly off a cliff, land at 250 km/h into a checkpoint — and the game rewards you with fireworks.  Is it realistic? No. Is it fun? Hell yes.  That said, it’s clearly designed with consoles in mind. Menus feel clunky with a mouse, you’re constantly interrupted by scripted events and unskippable popups, and the game bombards you with unlocks, pings, and missions you never asked for. Forza Horizon 5 - A step in the wrong direction. I love Forza. I am a new player, saw a lot of FH3, played 100 hours of 4. I love this franchise, but Forza Horizon 5 sets trends that will kill this franchisw for me.   I will compare this game to FH4.  ■ The first, worst part of this game is the map design. The map itself is flat, with non-sensical roads without a lot of life in them. There are bearly any landmarks worth remembering, bearly any cities, houses, anything. The map is like the new skate game. The roads were built for racing, not for finding good tracks to race on normal roads.  The problem with that is that this game is missing a map that is alive, and even when they made roads purpose built for races, they are not that fun.  Sierra Nueva, the map of the rally dlc showed me that playground games is competent when it comes to making good tracks. We will need to see the same quality in FH6. ■ The progression just straight up sucks. I unlocked the final race of the road series in my first play session. FH4 had the progression down to science, and here we got this weird sticker progression that opens up the game way too fast, and honestly. The expedition required to open up each series were boring and irritating to do. I don't mind the game handing me cars left and right, but getting cars is straight up rng. I made more cash in wheel spins, than i did in races. I got better cars by gambling, than by unlocking. The drip feed or cars in playlists makes some online, and completionist features not worth doing. I joined the game right at the end of it's official update cycle. So car pictures are impossible for me to do, since i cannot get playlist exclusive or wheelspin exclusive cars easily. Also the way you get cars amplifies the issue, since you can get like 10 cars in an hour, which makes changing the cars, to take pictures irritating and not worth doing. ■ Online functionality is awful. I don't play with other players because first, there is no rating/penalty system which makes each lobby full of dirty rammers playing bumper cars. Searching for a race is randomized as well since you cannot pick a playlist for the race type/class you want.  ■ Drive avatars are a placebo. The A.I doesn't see you, is often confused and the front members are always way too fast. It's just a gimmick to put on a box. ■ Seasons make 0 difference. Weather types make zero difference. Again. Another Placebo, gimmick to put on a box. Horizon 4 changed the way the map worked, and it was fresh and exciting to drive on each season. Now it's just nothing. ■ Most radio stations are grating to listen to. The music doesn't flow, some songs are tied to a track, and some songs hurt my ears. I never got tired of Horizon XS in my 100 hours of FH4, but here i hop stations often. A lot of the time i have the radio turned off.   ■ Why did i spend over 100+ hours in this game then? The driving is simply amazing. The feel of the physics is superb, even better than FH4 and the wheel support is good, but not great. They need to improve it further.  If they don't fix most of this stuff, i reckon i will not stay with Forza much longer. I have a lot of small things i'm not going to point out, because that would make this a full blown essay. These are the core problems with Horizon right now.

Overall Score: 6/10 - The gameplay is engaging and fun, especially with friends. However the problem lies within its half-baked story, bland environment and locked content.  Gameplay: 4/5 -  The gameplay is quite fun! It feels very intuitive and easy to pick up. Allowing you to play on both controller and wheel.  Story: 0/5 - Unfortunately the story feels pretty uninspired, the characters lack much depth and the entire plot doesn't serve much purpose to the game as a whole. Obviously it's not a major part of the game, but it's still apart of it regardless. But easily the worst part about it, is a lack of skipable cutscenes. You have to watch every single one in full, which can get a bit annoying after some time. I'd rather just drive my cars and not be apart of the cutscenes entirely.  Difficulty: 2/5 - At first it may be difficult learning how the car reacts to the road, especially if your new to racing games. But fairly quickly you'll get the hang of it without much trouble.  Progression: 2/5 - You can get tons of cars for just playing. However some cars are locked behind either DLC, or weekly challenges. Forcing your players into weekly challenges just to unlock certain cars feels pretty bad. Not to mention if there is a specific car you want, you have to pray it comes back, without guarantee it ever will.  Replay Value: 3/5 - Single player gets a bit stale.  Community: 5/5  - Friendly and not toxic.  Graphics: 3/5 - It looks good, but the environment isn't very captivating.  Audio: 3/5 - Cars sound nice. The soundtrack isn't particularly astounding.   Price: 1/5 - Buy on sale.  Conclusion: Do I think FH5 is worth it? That depends on what you want in a racing game. If you want a fun and engaging community with solid gameplay to support it. Then this game is perfect! If you would like to collect every car and be a completionist, then please know it's not really possible in its current state. But that's okay! Because at its core it's a fun game. And that's enough for most people.

The map is stunning, the car handling feels smooth, and the game offers a great mix of arcade fun and realistic driving. Despite the good level of realism and focus on racing for gameplay, the Forza Horizon series has always been more of a car sandbox than a racing simulator, the races are only there to give a sense of direction and a basis for interacting with other players. While this leads to very fun gameplay, there is a distinct lack of story that comes with the car sandbox genre, Winning races feels meaningless as profit is the only incentive, upgrading vehicles feels pointless as the CPU opponents always scale their vehicles around yours, and I often open the game and have no idea what to do, despite having dozens of unplayed races and undriven cars. Forza Horizon has the same core issue that The Crew did (excluding the first The Crew game, may it rest in peace): there is a massive amount of stuff to do and almost no reason to do any of it. Forza Horizon can be a very fun game, but it's important to know if it's right for you. Horizon focuses on gameplay above all else, even at the expense of story, but the gameplay is enough for a positive review.

The first 50 or so hours are enjoyable, however after you collect most of the cars, the game slows down and the grind for backstage passes kills it for me. The passes are an interesting idea, but it just boils down to a "What can we make into a microtransaction in our $60 game?". Don't get me wrong, I think the idea of doing challenges for cars or items is cool, but the grind is too much and after doing it two or three times. The grind only seems to be there not to reward the player, but to incentivize the player to make another purchase.  The map, while visually impressive, is too spaced out and not dense enough to make it fun. The roads are too wide and do not convey a sense of speed very well (something Forza 4 was very strong in). This review is coming from someone who played All Forza Horizon games starting from FH 1.  [h1]PROS:[/h1]  1- i like it, it's very well optimized, it's really fun and packed with a lot of activities, The graphics are peak, The cars are very diverse and fun, Attention to detail is very well done too. The map is better than FH4's map.   2- Also i am not much of a DLC believer, and i genuinely think most are a waste of money, BUT For FH5's Hotwheels DLC this is a rare exception and a very very fun DLC and well put and very well executed.  [h1]CONS:[/h1]  1- The menu UI is although not bad and well got used to by most players since it follows the same design from previous titles. i think it should be worked since it can be a bit overwhelming for new players. and organised a bit more.  2- a other concern is that they need to add an option called something like "Manual+Clutch for Manual-Only Cars" or something along those lines. The reason is that when I drive cars that are auto-only and I fail to clutch and shift properly, I get a gear-up/down delay. I get it for manual cars that makes sense but for auto-only cars, there should be an option that removes that delay, since those cars in real life don't require clutch input in the first place and i hate to switch constantly from Manual+clutch to Manual. or maybe provide the ability to assign a hotkey to quickly switch between the two. It's a small thing, but it would make the experience smoother and more realistic for people who use Manual+Clutch across all cars. but i guess this is just a opinion of mine.  In the end i definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes cars. a solid 10/10.  Also next fh pls pls pls make it in japan.

So, I caved. I HAD to find out what the hype was about with Forza Horizon 5, and in true impulse-buy fashion, I spent way too much money on it. But to be honest? It was actually pleasantly surprising.  The driving mechanics are silky smooth, the cars feel weighty and responsive, and the open-world Mexico setting is stunning. The moment I got behind the wheel and started shredding through sandstorms and street races, I understood why people were obsessed.  But here’s the thing no one tells you: driving games eventually start to feel like déjà vu on wheels. No matter how many different cars or race types you try, it slowly becomes the same loop — drive fast, win money, buy car, repeat.  Then there’s the auction house. Oh, the sweet, soul-crushing auction house. I spent hours scrolling, watching, waiting… only for that dream car — listed at a decent price — to be instantly snatched up within milliseconds. I’m convinced there’s a secret underground cabal of players using some sort of turbo-click software because by the time my finger touches the button, the car’s gone. Every. Single. Time.  That said, I’m no hardcore car fanatic, but even with my casual knowledge, I found the game near-perfect. I'm sure proper car nuts could point out areas that need improvement (tuning, realism, maybe car sounds), but for someone like me? It was just right.  In short: If you love cars, racing, or just want to zoom around a digital paradise with vibes and horsepower, Forza Horizon 5 delivers. Just don’t expect the auction house to ever show you mercy.

The Good and the Bad of Forza Horizon 5 – Is It the Ultimate Racing Game?  Forza Horizon 5 is one of the most visually stunning and expansive racing games ever made—but is it perfect? The Bad 👎 ❌ AI Still Feels Unfair (Sometimes) – The "Drivatars" can feel rubberband-y, especially on higher difficulties. ❌ Online Issues at Launch – Server problems and connectivity bugs were frustrating (though mostly fixed now). ❌ Repetitive After a While – If you’re not into collecting cars or doing similar events, it can get grindy. ❌ Microtransactions Exist – While not pay-to-win, some car packs and cosmetics are locked behind extra payments.  Verdict? Forza Horizon 5 is one of the best open-world racing games ever, offering insane visuals, tons of cars, and endless fun—but it’s not without flaws. Forza Horizon 5: The Participation Trophy of Racing Games  I booted up Forza Horizon 5 thinking, “This might finally be it, the racing game I’ve been waiting years for.” Instead, I got what can only be described as Fast & the Frivolous.  Let’s start with the positives. The game is stunning. It’s so pretty it makes real life look like it’s still rendering. The controls? Tight. Soundtrack? Fire, if your Spotify playlist is curated by a hyper-caffeinated intern trying to appeal to twelve demographics at once.  But here's where the tire marks start to skid. The moment I finished the tutorial, the game tossed me the keys to not one, but several million-dollar cars. I didn’t earn them. I didn’t buy them. I basically blinked and suddenly I owned more Lamborghinis than common sense. At one point I thought, “Did I accidentally buy the DLC where Jeff Bezos plays the role of your race team manager?” Nope. Just standard gameplay.  The whole experience feels like showing up to your first day of work and being made CEO for spelling your name right on the application. Where’s the grind? Where’s the thrill of clawing your way up from a beat-up PT Cruiser with mismatched panels and three working spark plugs? Where’s the part where you duct tape a spoiler on and feel proud about it?  Instead, Forza seems to have been designed by the same committee responsible for modern school award ceremonies. “You showed up! Here’s a Bugatti!”  And don’t even get me started on the in-game commercials. You’re mid-drift and suddenly you’re getting bombarded with adverts for DLC and other in game events you likely want no part in. I wanted to race, not attend a digital flee market.  Also, if you dare to have WeMod installed, not running, just installed, Forza will throw a tantrum like a toddler who’s been told they can’t lick the dog. I had to perform a full digital exorcism just to get the game to stop auto-closing itself. I’m playing offline, Forza. Calm down. I’m not trying to hack into NASA.  Look, maybe I’m bitter. Maybe it’s because my kids expect trophies for showing up, too. Maybe I’m just nostalgic for the days of Gran Turismo and Need for Speed, where you actually worked for your success. And when you finally got your dream car, it meant something.  In summary, if you want a game that throws exotic cars at you like Halloween candy and congratulates you for breathing, Forza Horizon 5 is your jam. But if you're looking for a meaningful climb from rags to RPMs, this one feels more like riding shotgun in someone else’s power fantasy.

This game has only one purpose: Pick a car, and drive around. Once you've completed all the races, there's literally nothing to do. The map somehow feels lifeless and dull, and I kept constantly asking myself, "What now?" I did all the races, I have all the cars I want, I own all the houses. I'm bored.  "Play online!" And what, get crashed into every 5 seconds? Wait 5 years to get into a session? Be forced to use meta-builds if I ever want to actually have a chance at winning a race? Be forced to literally cheat (going off road while racing between races) if I want to get a chance for first place? Play The Eliminator (a.k.a Fortnite with cars)?  Yes, cars sound better. Yes, there's more customization. I simply don't care. There's no real career mode I can reset and play again like in old NFS games. Rivals is a waste of time, thanks to hackers. Playing on harder difficulties just makes one Drivitar extremely fast and basically unable to catch. Getting anything less than first place means you didn't actually complete the race. The auction house is simply horrific. I could go on, and on.  But sadly, there's nothing quite like Forza Horizon out right now. No other racing game does what Forza can. An open world and an insanely long list of cars is actually pretty hard to come by. And that's why you'll buy this game, anyways. That's why you'll sink over 100 hours into it, even though you're bored after just an hour. It's tragic.  On a final note: God, the characters are so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ annoying. Is it just me, or does anyone else find the egregious "Spanglish" irritating? None of my Hispanic, Latino, or Mexican friends talk like that. One of my Latina friends who used to watch me play would literally scream, "Shut the ♥♥♥♥ up!" whenever one of the characters just randomly swaps between languages. There's also absolutely no life to these characters. I was never once interested in any of them, and would audibly groan whenever I had to listen to them drone on and on about Hot Wheels, Aztec cities, or a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Volkswagen. I've seen ASMR YouTube channels write better characters than Playground Games. My friend's Dungeons and Dragons characters have more compelling backstories and arcs than Forza, and he's not even close to being a writer! How are they so bad?  I don't recommend buying Forza, but there's nothing else like it. So, you'll buy it anyways, and that is truly sad.

Is the game fun? Yes. Is it rewarding? Well...   Forza Horizon 5 is fun at first glance the driving feels good, the car list is massive, and visually it's stunning. But it quickly becomes clear that the game lacks any meaningful progression. Within the first hour, you're given dozens of cars, including supercars, with no reason to even use most of them. The constant flow of free vehicles kills any sense of reward or accomplishment.  The "festival" theme feels hollow. There's no sense of rising through ranks, no rivals, no endgame – you arrive as the best and stay there. Maybe I’m biased because I just replayed Need for Speed: ProStreet, which I consider to have one of the best progression systems and festival atmospheres ever made. In comparison, the "festival" in Horizon 5 feels pointless.   Now let’s talk about the map. What is this? Horizon 3 (Australia) and Horizon 4 (UK) had fantastic, memorable worlds. I loved how seasons in FH4 changed the vibe and even your driving strategy. Here, you're just driving across a giant flat plate. Nothing feels iconic or immersive. The city is painfully bland. I started Forza Horizon 5 on its release day, November 5, 2021. It was my first ever Forza Horizon game, and I dove into it casually—no rush, just enjoying the ride. Fast forward 287.4 hours later, I’ve completed the game with 100% of achievements on Steam, and what a journey it’s been.  From the start, what really hooked me were the stunning visuals, tight driving mechanics, and the massive open world. The game’s version of Mexico is vast, vibrant, and full of life, easily one of the most beautiful and enjoyable maps I’ve explored in a racing game. I’ve played other similar titles like The Crew 2, but Forza Horizon 5 quickly became my favorite.  One of the best aspects is how player-friendly the progression feels. I spent most of my time driving the Lamborghini Sesto Elemento Forza Edition—an absolute beast—and never felt rushed or pressured. You can go at your own pace, whether you're chasing seasonal goals or just cruising for fun.  That said, some achievements are time-gated, particularly those tied to the Festival Playlist, which updates weekly every Thursday. To complete these, you’ll need consistency and patience, especially for challenges like the smashables, which only appear once per series (a month-long rotation). If you stay on top of them, they’re manageable, but missing one can set you back quite a bit.  PvP and online-related achievements require dedication and strategy, but they’re far from impossible with some persistence and good matchmaking.  In the end, I’d give Forza Horizon 5 a 9/10. It’s a phenomenal game with endless content and polish, but interestingly enough, before this game I tried Forza Horizon 4 and ended up liking it even more—perhaps for its setting or its slightly different vibe.  Still, if you’re into open-world racing and want a game that respects your time while delivering top-tier fun, Forza Horizon 5 is hard to beat.

Forza Horizon 5 doesn’t just build on the success of its predecessor—it roars past it. Set in a vibrant, hyper-detailed version of Mexico, this is the most visually stunning, content-packed, and downright fun open-world racer yet. Playground Games has taken everything that made Horizon 4 a classic and turned the volume all the way up.  If you’ve played Forza Horizon before, you’ll feel right at home—but better. The core arcade-sim hybrid handling is still here and still top-notch. Cars feel weighty, responsive, and grounded, whether you’re tearing across sand dunes in a trophy truck or hugging corners in a McLaren.  Racing in Horizon 5 is endlessly satisfying. Whether it’s a street race at sunset, a cross-country rally through the jungle, or an impromptu drag race on a deserted airstrip, every drive feels exhilarating. The map is huge and diverse, and there's always something to do just around the next corner.  Let’s not beat around the cactus—Horizon 5’s version of Mexico is breathtaking. The map is Playground Games’ biggest and most varied yet. Lush rainforests, sprawling cities, ancient ruins, dry deserts, active volcanoes, and tropical beaches all blend into a seamless playground of speed.  Dynamic weather (including sandstorms and tropical storms), time of day, and lighting make every area feel alive. Simply driving around feels rewarding.  With over 500 cars at launch, from exotics and muscle cars to off-road monsters and classic tuners, the car list is stacked. Each vehicle is faithfully modeled, and the tuning and upgrade system gives gearheads plenty to obsess over. Paint jobs, widebody kits, engine swaps, and even horns and sound systems can be customized. Want to turn a Beetle into a dragster? Go for it.  The campaign is much more player-directed this time. You build your Horizon Festival by unlocking new outposts across Mexico, and each expansion adds different types of races and events (street, dirt, cross-country, etc.). It gives the game a sense of purpose without being restrictive.  Expeditions are a standout—story-driven adventures that mix exploration with racing and give the world context.  EventLab allows players to create their own races, mini-games, and even stunt challenges. Some user creations are wild, like Hot Wheels-style tracks or demolition derbies.  Multiplayer is packed with content: Horizon Open, Eliminator (a battle royale with cars), co-op races, and community events.  Online integration is smooth. You’ll see real players seamlessly driving around your world. Quick matchmaking and tons of seasonal content keep things fresh. Weekly playlists and challenges encourage you to come back regularly for rewards—but thankfully, they feel optional rather than obligatory.  However, there’s some bloat and UI clutter when it comes to menus and notifications. The game can be overwhelming at first with how much it throws at you.  Forza Horizon 5 isn’t just a racing game—it’s a celebration of cars, culture, and creativity. From its stunning Mexican backdrop to its overflowing content, it’s hard to find a game more joyful and well-crafted. While it builds heavily on the foundation of Horizon 4, it does so with enough new ideas, polish, and sheer scale that it firmly earns its place at the front of the pack.  If you love cars or just love having fun behind a digital wheel, Forza Horizon 5 is the best it’s ever been.  Rating: 8/10

It’s a game focused on multiplayer, tuning your cars, and just enjoying massive variety. While the cosmetic tuning options aren’t as deep as what you get in something like NFS Unbound, there’s still plenty of performance and visual customization to mess with. There’s a huge car list and lots of fun racing. The Rally Adventure and Hot Wheels DLCs are nice additions too - they bring more content and variety to the game, and feel like worthwhile expansions. If you enjoy open-world racing games with a big community and tons of cars, Forza Horizon 5 is definitely worth checking out.

[h3]⚠️ If you have an NVIDIA graphics card, you'll probably want to read this.[/h3]  After more than 100 hours of gameplay, I can state that Forza Horizon 5 is without a doubt one of the most complete and entertaining racing games I have ever played. One of the aspects I appreciate most is the amount of content available: there is always something to do, such as races, challenges, seasonal events or even just driving around the map enjoying the scenery, which can often be therapeutic.  Also, the visuals are a show: the map, inspired by Mexico, is rich in detail and has an atmosphere that makes you want to explore. The graphics are amazing, and Photo Mode stands out as a powerful tool to capture all this beauty, offering advanced options for camera control, focus and exposure.  The gameplay maintains that arcade feel the series does so well, easy to learn and pick up, but with enough depth for those who like to tweak every little detail of the controls or the car. Driving feels smooth and responsive, making the game accessible to newcomers and still rewarding for experienced players.  But unfortunately not everything is perfect. If you, like me, use an NVIDIA graphics card, it is worth knowing that the game still suffers from random and unpredictable crashes. I have lost several online races and even stopped playing for a few days out of pure frustration and despite trying dozens of fixes found on the internet nothing worked. It is frustrating to see this kind of issue persist in a title released in 2021.  In the end I partially recommend Forza Horizon 5, especially if it is on sale. It is a great game with many strengths but one that still suffers from technical problems that should no longer exist. [h1]"Would you recommend this game to other players?"[/h1] Steam asks. My answer: [b]Yes, but with caveats[/b].  I bought the game at launch on Xbox One X and sank about 300 hours into it. The issues it had back then are still present today.  [h2]1) No challenge[/h2] [i]Forza Horizon[/i] has always been too easy. The AI is predictable, making races trivial even on the highest difficulty setting. Challenges reward the wrong things—why is finishing a new race worth more than winning one? Smells like a participation trophy.  [h2]2) The menu[/h2] I've hated the menu system since [i]Forza Horizon 2[/i]. The tile layout is clunky and unintuitive, and the structure often makes no logical sense.  [h2]3) The "story"[/h2] Sure, no one expects meaningful storytelling in a racing game. But when it’s this badly written, it deserves mention. Every character is hollow and overly cheerful. You're the superstar—everyone loves you. It’s painfully bland. Even worse, you can’t skip the cutscenes.  [h2]3) Pandering to fringe groups[/h2] Accessibility options are a good thing and should be standard. But Playground Games takes it too far, pandering while forgetting the core player base. You can equip prosthetics and hearing aids—but not create an overweight character. What’s the message here? [i]Virtue signalling[/i].  [h2]3) Paint jobs[/h2] The livery editor hasn’t changed much since 2007. It’s practically the same as in [i]Forza Motorsport 2[/i]. Meanwhile, recent [i]Gran Turismo[/i] titles run circles around it.  And why the hell do I need to travel to the festival site just to repaint my car—while tuning can be done anywhere?  [h2]4) Developer laziness[/h2] It’s clear the devs are out of ideas. The “Hot Wheels” DLC is recycled, and the rally DLC feels unnecessary. And now, they rely on the community to generate content. Let’s be honest—most user content is garbage.  [hr][/hr] I’ve deliberately focused on the negatives. If you’re looking for praise, look elsewhere. I’ve invested thousands of hours into the Horizon series, which shows how much I care. But at this point, [i]Forza[/i] has become generic fluff no one needs if they’ve played the previous games.  [h2]Recommendation?[/h2] [b]Yes[/b] – if you’ve never played a Horizon game before.   [b]Yes[/b] – if you’re a casual player.   [b]No[/b] – if you’re looking for an actual challenge.

So it's ass, because the game has an assload of content and zero initiative to do anyhting with it. This is the gen alpha "six seven" kid of racing games.  The positive? It's still a good game if you just need something mindless. This is that game you pick up when "idk what to play" sets in. If you don't take it serious and just treat it as a sandbox game, there is plenty of fun to be had. It's not a "bad game," it is a bad Forza Horizon. Do I think you should buy it? Not at all, FH6 is coming soon, and is shaping up to be a return to form, with an actual progression system, and some cheeky inspirations from Test Drive Unlimited and Need for Speed. This game is going to be obsolete and dead in 4 months. IF you have the extra money, or the game is on sale, you could buy it, but you're better off waiting, because this game is going to be a laughing stock when FH6 drops in May 2026.

Right from the start, you’re dropped into the gorgeous, sprawling landscapes of Mexico, and the game wastes no time in showing off. Volcanos, deserts, jungles, ancient ruins, neon-lit cities, and tropical beaches — every biome looks breathtaking and plays differently. It’s the kind of map where you can actually get lost in the best way possible. One second you’re flying down the highway in a Bugatti, the next you’re drifting through mountain switchbacks, or crashing through a cactus field in a monster truck.  Gameplay-wise, FH5 is everything you want it to be. Tight, responsive controls that feel great with a controller or a racing wheel. A massive garage of meticulously modeled cars — from beloved classics to cutting-edge hypercars — each one handling with its own personality. Whether you’re a gearhead who tunes every gear ratio or just someone who wants to slap anime decals on a Lamborghini and go nuts, the game meets you where you are.  Then there's the event variety. Races, story missions, stunt challenges, barn finds, seasonal championships, drifting zones, drag races, street scenes, and the absolutely chaotic Eliminator battle royale mode. You can set records, compete with your friends, or just vibe alone in the beautiful world. Want to create your own custom tracks or play ridiculous user-made events where you jump over planes in a Peel P50? You can. And you should.  The Horizon Festival theme adds charm and personality that never gets old. NPCs actually talk to you like you're a legendary racer (even if you just wiped out in front of them at 200mph), and the upbeat tone of the game keeps everything light and fun. Combine that with real-time seasons, weather changes, and live online events, and it always feels like there’s something new happening.  Graphics & Sound? Incredible. One of the best-looking racing games out there. HDR sunsets, detailed interiors, ray-traced reflections — it’s pure eye candy. And don’t even get me started on the sound design. From the roar of a V12 to the sharp squeal of tires around a tight bend, every audio detail is crisp and immersive. The radio stations are loaded with bangers across genres, and they even throw in some fun commentary to make it feel like a real festival.  Oh, and the accessibility options? Top-tier. From driving assists and difficulty sliders to visual customization and input remapping — Playground Games clearly put a lot of thought into making FH5 playable for everyone.  TL;DR:  🔥 Insanely fun driving and racing  🌎 Massive, varied, and jaw-droppingly beautiful open world  🚗 Huge car roster — from beaters to beasts  🎮 Great for both casual players and racing sim fans  🎉 Constant events, seasons, and live updates keep it fresh  🛠️ Excellent car customization and community content  If you’ve ever dreamed of owning a garage full of dream cars, drifting through a rainforest in a Porsche, or launching off sand dunes at 150mph while a mariachi remix plays on the radio — this game makes it happen.  Final Verdict: Forza Horizon 5 is pure joy on four wheels. Buy it. Download it. Fire it up. And prepare to lose track of time. 🏁

Reluctantly, this is my "I don't know what else to play so I might just spend 20 minutes on this before I figure out what else to do" kind of game  Engagement and entertainment value is provided by a weekly slop of objectives and events to do to accumulate points to redeem for cars you will never drive and passes to redeem cars you will absolutely never drive. Because why would you - all cars feel the same, all cars sound the same. What's the point anyway  Driving aspect briefly - Cars are either gripping or sliding. RWD and AWD cars always oversteer, FWD always understeer. There is no nuance whatsoever, so it's either driving on rails or driving on ice. Change of surface essentially modifies rolling resistance and allows for more slip angle (that's quite the stretch) before you go into slide mode  You just know that the tyre model doesn't exist, that suspension model doesn't exist, that the physics are as detailed as Need For Speed Carbon, except that the cars seemingly weigh 10 times more  Racing aspect is infuriating. AI does what AI does best - block, brake, rubberband and drive in a line like a bunch of ducks. Special shoutout to Showcase events that are designed to always end in a photofinish, with rubberbanding galore. If only the physics were a bit more sophisticated, especially in regards to crashes  Crash physics don't exist. There is zero elasticity in crashes. You hit a tree? Complete stop, not even a bounce. You scrape a wall of a building? Complete stop, not even a spin. You land on the ground? Infinite damping and a random speed factor to slow you down, nothing more. You hit another car? Again, no elasticity, just glue. You hit an event wall? Just hope you haven't breached a critical dead stop angle, otherwise you can in some instances freely wallride around, game doesn't care. And if you hit debris, you slow down by a determined factor, your car doesn't get unsettled by anything.  Narrative and story, or whatever that drivel is, is barely filler, and for your own sanity you shouldn't engage with it for even a nanosecond longer than absolutely necessary. It's insultingly bad. Written for simpletons, toxic in its approach to everything really, stripped of any emotion or ambition  So what are you actually paying for in this game?  A weekly serving of automotive slop in a forgettable environment that you can turn on every week, or even every day if you have a child, and just waste your time away. It's a little bit better than giving your kid an iPad just because you can actually see what's happening on screen  Forza Horizon. Forza Horizon 5 – The Best Car Game I’ve Ever Played  In my opinion, Forza Horizon 5 is the best game about cars I’ve ever played. From the moment I started it, I was blown away by the stunning visuals, the incredibly detailed cars, and the vibrant, diverse world set in Mexico. The map is massive and full of life, with deserts, jungles, cities, and even volcanoes to explore.  What makes it stand out for me is how perfectly it blends realism with fun. The driving mechanics feel great whether you're racing on the streets or off-roading through the jungle. You can feel the difference between each car, and there are hundreds to choose from. Customization is deep but accessible, and the upgrades actually make a noticeable impact on performance.  The game also gives you a lot of freedom. You don’t have to follow a strict racing career — you can drive wherever you want, do stunts, compete in events, or just cruise. It’s that open-world freedom that makes it so enjoyable.  Overall, Forza Horizon 5 isn’t just a racing game — it’s an experience. If you love cars or even just open-world games with great graphics and gameplay, I highly recommend it.

I put a "yes" here because I do have a lot of fun in this game.  However, you should definitely think carefully before purchasing.  Pros: -There are a lot of cars available, and most cars can be tuned to very different capabilities than stock.  You can have a rally McLaren P1 or a drag racing Mini.  -The graphics look really good at higher settings.  Sure, it definitely leans more into vibrancy than realism, but it matches the tone of the game.  -The game (at time of writing) is still actively developed, so there are new cars, events, courses, etc. that get added to the game.  -The game has pretty decent social aspects, so it's easy to have fun with your friends.  Neutral: -Like all Forza Horizon titles, it forgoes realism in favor of casual fun in a lighthearted open world atmosphere.  The game is best enjoyed exploring the open world in whatever car you want and jumping into races as you please.  -There isn't really progression, in the traditional sense.  You make money quickly and there isn't a storyline as much as there is a collection of side storylines for you to do at your own discretion.  As an arcade racing game, it's fun because you can jump into all of the action almost as soon as you pick up the controller.  However, this is not a strong choice for those who want a real career mode.  Cons: -It's not an old game, but it has been around long enough that FH6 is on the horizon (no pun intended).  While that won't kill FH5's events immediately, it will have an effect on player count and the devs will definitely focus more on the new game.  -It has a lot of random bugs.  Some wall collisions are incorrect, the character animations are messed up, and I've even had a mission that just... couldn't end.  The finish line literally didn't work.  Some of the menus also run really slowly and seem to be more demanding on the system than the actual game.  -This game relies heavily on the fear of missing out.  It offers so many limited time exclusives that it's impossible to do everything if you have a job.

The last racing game I played was NFS:MW 2005, which I think is a masterpiece for its time. I wanted a modern racing game, so I went for this. Even though the racing mechanics and driving experience are pretty good and the game features a great variety of cars, I would not recommend this game (I do not think it is worth it for the price) for the following reasons: [list]     [*] The presentation of the game is watered-down and [b] too [/b] family-friendly. I feel like the "story", the dialogues etc. appeal only to kids. It is really painful after some point. Also, the UI seems Fortnite-like; that should tell you everything you need to know.      [*] The online is not as fun as it should be. Depending on the racing category, you have to wait at least 2-3 minutes to enter a tournament, and even then, there is a minute or so waiting time between races. That is, almost half the time you spend on waiting. Apart from that, most online players seem to use the same couple of (exclusive) cars to achieve high ranks. Of course there is skill involved, but seeing the same cars over and over again is not a coincidence. This makes the online experience a lot less fun.     [*] There are too many paywalls for my liking. I probably wouldn't go as far as to call the game "pay-to-win", but still.     [*] Even though the map is pretty big, there don't seem to be a lot of races. Most (if not all) online races are the same you would play in singleplayer, which, again, are not that many.     [*] There exist some annoying BS such as: you cannot easily change a car when entering a singleplayer race (you have to exit, get into another car and enter the race again), the UI isn't designed for PC at all, so good luck scrolling around to find the one car you want to buy in an auction (no search bar or anything like that, just a single field with the selected car), the game spams your garage with junk cars you win from spinning wheels, unskippable and cringe cutscenes etc. [/list]  Overall, I feel you should be able to buy a better and more enjoyable racing game for this price.

Forza Horizon 5 is an open-world racing gem that is as much about style as it is substance. Set in Mexico in a breathtaking remastered and vibrant world, the game boasts a humongous map with diverse biomes, real-life weather patterns of the world, and stunning vistas so that every ride is an experience.  The vehicle list is breathtaking, tailoring is more pronounced than ever, and the driving is nicely balanced between simulation and arcade enjoyment. Whether you careen through a desert sandstorm, blast through jungles, or cruise along the coast, the game continues to astound you with its variety and liberty.  Multiplayer is enjoyable and silky-smooth (discounting some hopefully well-behaved servers), and the seasonal content adds a pleasant shakeup. There remain the occasional intermittent bugs and connectivity issues, however, and the UI has the occasional clunky moment.  Overall, though, Forza Horizon 5 is an absolute must-play for anyone who enjoys racing and open-world exploration with a high-octane spin.

Bought this game on sale a few years ago. Had played it before through PC Gamepass, and loved it then. Played it for just over 2 hours, then my game stopped connecting to Xbox servers. Issue would not fix itself, there was no in-game ability to connect to servers, and I could not find any methods to fix it on Steam.  I applied for a refund through Steam, but Valve refused it, saying I'd played more than 2 hours (to be fair, the refund was a long shot anyways). I played maybe 3 more hours, then uninstalled.  Came back to it less than a week ago, and my game could connect to servers again. Put another 2 hours in, and today it can't connect to servers again.  My guess is that it stops connecting to servers after 2 hours of playtime, or after so many days of playing. The only solutions I've found are uninstalling and reinstalling (on a 100+ Gb game, no thank you), or to reset the Xbox app in your pc's settings (which apparently deletes ALL XBOX DATA on the pc). The latter solution, I've yet to try (for the aforementioned reason of losing my Xbox app data), and doubt it works for me anyway (why would the Xbox app affect my game, if it's owned an run through Steam?).  Why does this matter? 1) Many crucial features, such as the auction house, community livery, and community car tunings, all require internet to access. These features allow you to buy cars for cheap, download high-quality car wraps, and make it easy to use pro players' auto tunings. Most importantly, all these features make the game more beginner-friendly. 2) Car vouchers (basically have no idea how to get those) require connection to the servers to redeem (no idea why). 3) I mentioned the auction house requires a connection to the servers, and that means cars for cheap. Some cars are also only available through the auction house, so a whole catalogue of collectibles becomes inaccessible. It can also be used to sell cars (which pays much better than racing, in my experience), so the economy is ruined by this issue.  This has been a problem for years. Xbox QA has known about it for years. Valve has known about it for years. Nobody is doing anything to prevent the issue, only suggesting temporary fixes that need doing 2-3 times a week.  I love Forza Horizon 5. It's the standard I hold every other driving game to. This issue, this inability to use so many core features, ruins the whole experience. Every menu I enter, the game reminds me I cannot play online. Every time I log on, the game makes a point of rubbing it in.  If Microsoft ever pushes any meaningful fix, I would change this review. Until then, heed my warning, and play Need for Speed or Burnout.

Forza Horizon 5 has truly become my "Session Game" meaning it is one of those games where you can play anytime, for 30 mins or 4 hours, everyday or even once a week, and can never get tired of it. Just load up the game, pick a race either solo or online and you'll have a great time driving your favorite cars.  The Good: [list] [*]A very fun simcade racing game where you can pretty much do all the racing you want and can from street races to off-road, solo or online [*]You can collect many cars without much grind or stress [*]Upgrading and tuning cars is really good, and you can make the best tunes possible or ones that defy physics (it's a simcade racing game so I don't mind) [*]Cars and Graphics still look incredible even after many years [*]The amount of beautiful liveries, cracked tunes and different race layouts made by the Forza community is abundant [*]Hours of content to play (especially if you buy the Premium Edition) [*]The DLCs: Hot Wheels and Rally Adventure IMO have decently sized maps and racing on them is also pretty good (The FH4 LEGO DLC is still better tho) [*]You can own 8 Koenigsegg cars cause you can't in real life [/list]  The Bad: [list] [*]Map is dull when compared to FH4 (but that doesn't mean that it is downright horrible, it is still enjoyable IMO) [*]Seasons are not that noticeable (I sometimes forget what season it is and I have to check the Playlist just to know) [*]The only fun online gamemode is Horizon Open, the others are just meh (especially The Eliminator) [*]Horizon Open ain't perfect tho, you WILL still get rammed by players who can't drive (a stricter penalty system should really be in place for online racing) [*]I am pretty sure that about 50 hours of my playtime is because of loading screens where it has to "Fast Travel Other Players" for at least 1 minute after EVERY online race (I have a decent PC and run the game on a SSD so I know it really is server side) [*]There are DLC car packs that are not included in the premium edition (it costs 50$ if you want to get them all through the Ultimate Car Pack) [*]There are over 100 cars that you can't get unless you snipe them at the auction house or get lucky in the Festival Playlist rotation (You're luckier if those cars get added to the Backstage) [*]Dialogue is pure cringe and you are forced to listen to them [/list]  If you enjoy just driving around and enjoying the sceneries, racing with bots or other decent players (if you're lucky), collecting cars, designing them and finding the best builds then this is most definitely the game for you.

I’d like to preface this by saying that 90% of my time in Forza Horizon 5 is spent aimlessly exploring the expansive open world in whatever car strikes my fancy that day. Rarely do I tear around a track or follow a defined route, and I’ve barely scratched the surface of dirt or drag racing.   Man, Forza. What can be said that hasn’t already been said? I still can’t believe the sheer beauty this game delivers from the moment you start. What’s more impressive is how it sustains that magic and adrenaline throughout every session.   Let’s begin with the environment. FH5’s open world diverges from previous titles by fully embracing Mexican culture and what I assume are semi-accurate landscapes. From desert highways to lush jungles and treacherous swamps, the terrain blends naturally and, more importantly, feels real. The way the world is crafted is genuinely astounding.  And the graphics—man. There’s a reason Playground Games sits at the top of THEIR game. The visuals speak for themselves, plastered all over the store page. But what those screenshots can’t convey is the scale. No matter how close the camera is to the car, I always feel small roaming this world. Whether I’m in the cockpit or observing reflections, the landscape feels vast, often desolate, occasionally lonely. Then, off in the distance, enormous mountains loom. FH5 plays with scale masterfully—empty plains suddenly broken by distant peaks, overcrowded forests contrasted by massive terrain just meters away. It’s a brilliant manipulation of perspective, and I absolutely love it.   Now, onto the handling. Using a G29 with a gear stick attachment, the car’s response to the wheel and pedals feels deeply immersive—about as immersive as fake wheels and sticks can get. But hey, who’s judging?  The car’s response to the wheel and pedals feels incredibly tactile—like the difference between flipping a switch and pulling a lever. There’s a physicality to it that caught me off guard. Every bump in the road, every shift in terrain—whether it’s coarse gravel crunching beneath off-road tires or a slick, rain-slicked motorway—feeds back through the wheel with unexpected precision.   The force feedback is punchy but never overwhelming. Turning requires intent and conscious, controlled effort. Taking tight corners at high speeds demands real technique, but without ever veering into full-on simulation. That’s the magic of FH5: it nails the sweet spot between realism and arcade. It’s immersive without being intimidating. You don’t need a motorsport degree to slide sideways through a turn, just do your best and we’re all sweet!   Furthermore, each car handles with its own distinct personality. A nimble front-wheel-drive hatchback jitters under pressure, nervous in its movements. A burly muscle car, on the other hand, practically begs you to wrestle it through corners, brute force over finesse. Switch to an all-wheel-drive machine on a mountain trail, and it’s like you’ve grown four extra limbs (haha that’s hilarious). And that’s just with the default tuning. Even without diving into advanced settings, the baseline handling is more than satisfying for someone like me who just wants to feel the road.   That said, I did make a few small adjustments. I dialed back the centering spring and fine-tuned the steering sensitivity to eliminate that slightly floaty feel the wheel had out of the box. It only took about ten minutes in the settings menu, and suddenly everything clicked. From that moment on, it was smooth sailing—or, more accurately, smooth sliding, depending on the vehicle.  Ultimately, the handling is a huge part of why I keep coming back. I don’t need to chase wins or climb leaderboards to enjoy myself. Sometimes, just shifting through gears manually while the sun pierces the mist above the jungle canopy is all I need. It makes the act of driving feel meaningful, even when there’s no destination in sight.   As for variety—oh, there’s plenty I’m missing. I mentioned it earlier, but the range of vehicles is staggering. Sleek sports cars, hefty jeeps, everyday civilian rides, there’s something here for everyone. If you like A CAR, you’ll find A CAR you’ll love.  Customization is excellent. From decals to glossy materials, you can truly make a vehicle your own. The community-created designs are especially cool—thousands of players have shared their work for you to use, saving you time and dropping you right into the action. Car tuning works the same way: plenty of user-made presets available if tweaking settings isn’t your thing.   On a more personal note, Forza has even reshaped how I view music. I’ve never been a big music guy, but cruising in this game encouraged me to pull up playlists that match the vibe of my car—‘80s tunes for an ‘80s ride, for example. Music still might not be “my jam,” but I’ve gained an appreciation for different styles and artistry. And all thanks to this game. It never told me to “put on music,” but somehow, it kind of did.   Lastly, I appreciate that FH5 doesn’t force you into anything. Sure, you need to complete a few story missions, but I’ve done maybe five. The rest of my time has been pure, unstructured exploration. There’s a wealth of content, but with a few HUD tweaks and filters, you can create the exact experience you want. Competitive players can chase leaderboards. Meanwhile, I’ll be cruising through vibrant towns and mountain roads in the jungle, fully relaxed.   So, do I recommend it?  C’mon... have you been here this whole time? AB-SO-LUTELY!

Forza Horizon 5® has a very light, playful story with tons of side-stories to experience.  There are a seemingly endless number of street and off-road vehicles to choose from, and with the wheel spins, challenge and story rewards, purchase options, and even gifts from other players, it's easy to build up your garage to a massive collection.  The ability to upgrade your vehicles and tune them in specific ways provides a wide range of driving experiences.  The environment is beautiful with very detailed flora and fauna and a truly immersive weather system.  The addition of small rally racing world and, especially, the Hot Wheels® track (Imagine a life-sized Hot Wheels® track built on some kind of quasi-futuristic, floating, multi-biome, sky-island) brings a ton of replay value to the game.  Having played Forza Horizon 4® and this, I'd be hard-pressed to say which is better, but I think this one has a slight edge.  Mainly, I feel like the story in this one is a little more coherent and has a lighter feel to it, it has a slightly larger selection of cars, and the Hot Wheels® partnership was a little more streamlined than the Lego® partnership in the previous iteration of the game.  Overall, I'd give this 4.7 out of 5 stars, with just a small irritation (which I had for the previous game, as well), in that I felt that all the cars available in the game should be available to purchase instead of making some only available as prizes for wheel spins or racing challenges.  But that's truly only a very minor gripe.  If you like racing, but you'd like to drive your race car around an open world and not be restricted to just a race track, I don't think you'll be disappointed by spending your hard-earned money on this gem!

Game has some very amesome Angels, but also some very frustrating Demons.  Angels:  The game feels very arcady and it's main goal is have fun rather than being a racing similator. And I must say they succeeded in that. They have created something more fun than reality.  Graphics 5/5 Racing fun 5/5 Car choice 5/5 Tuning options (racing as well as visual) 5/5 Music (that intro when you enter the game is just perfect!) 5/5 Car responsiveness 5/5  Demons: (FYI, some of these issues have been addressed, especially the community shared tuning saves a lot of time and make cars amazing)  As you progress in the game you start to encounter some Demons. Mainly the amount of Admin you have to do and how they could easily mitigate the time waste  but don't have the options for it.   1. Finding car filters never have the ones I want.  -If you get a new car, there is no filter to find new cars and when you a lot of cars the can take up to a frustrating minute per new car you aquired. -When you pick a car to start the race, you see all cars from that class(which is a great auto filter). But there is no filter on 'equipped tires' which is the main qualification for a car to be picked. Which causes the selection screen to be filled with a lot of useless options. -Car stats are relative to the weight of the car, most usefull stats are displayed but not the weight. So a car with seemingly terrible stats might be you best just because it very light. So it would be great to actual have meaningfull stats for the cars.  2. Tuning -Once you have played for a while, or instantly, you might wanna start tuning cars to make them better. But this can only be done via you garage. A strong suggestion would be that when you start a game you always get 40 seconds to pick a car, and then you have to wait 30s up to 3 minutes to actually join the race. This waiting time (wasted time) could be put to use by allowing you to tune your car and start the 40 second timer once the first car crosses the finish line.  You have a lot of different car types, which all have their strengths and weaknesses. f.ex. a racing cars might work well on non bouncy offroad tracks, but very bad on bouncy tracks. Same with highspeed race cars work well on non sloping cornering and tracks with fewer 90 degree plus turns, but very bad on city tracks. with tight and sloping cornering. I love this game people. It's got everything that I want wrapped in a great package---a fulfilling tactile experience of racing with responsive tuning integration and super customizable difficulty and feel to deliver exactly the kind of race you're looking for. If you want an open-world, sandbox type racing experience than this is it. The amount of choice that you're given can feel overwhelming for newcomers to the series (I would point them to earlier titles like FH3 if they feel this might be an issue), and the game's recommended cars for each race can do only so much to direct your progression. With lots of different race types and an unapologetically generous approach to giving the player free cars, you'll be thrown into high action racing as soon as you can download it. It's got MUSIC INTEGRATION like crazy... people I know have brought up previous horizon titles as introducing them to great songs and Horizon 5 certainly carries that torch. Picture this: bumping to the radio while street racing in a souped up 911. As the music crescendos by a festival location and massive banging speakers fade in with the cheers of the onlooking crowd over your car radio. It's an unforgettable feeling when it hits in the right moment, especially if you bring along a friend and you're pulling 1st and 2nd place. To quote a friend, "the radio goes hard." I'm not the one to give a detailed rundown of the mechanical side of things, though the user-end side of things makes it very easy to search for exactly what you want from a player-made tune with predetermined keywords like "best for speed" or "grip" or search for your own keywords. Smarter folk than me make great tunes and I have loved to take advantage of these, but if you fancy yourself a mechanic then trying your hand with the tuning system will feel greatly rewarding. I can imagine that feeling when you overtake on a tight corner will be even better when you've tuned the car yourself, but that's all I can say on that. Customization elements feel pretty freeing with lots of options to create personal car designs with a vinyl shapes that you can position creatively for your own use in however many layers you desire, or simply opt to search for user-created designs similarly to the tuning system. Great great, moving on. Seasons are great! Every week you'll have new activities and new racing conditions based on the weather. You'll still have options to opt for the weather conditions you want to play around with if you'd prefer, but the game thrives in this variance with the basis already being in its sandbox approach (it's Mexico what did you expect. but its not all sand there are jungles too). Lots of different racing types to offer, with Road, Street, Dirt, Cross-country... whatever you're looking for, you should build up a car and try it out in FH5. I especially appreciate that the developers seemed to know that the longest races in the previous games were my favorite. There are something like 5 before the expansions and they're all great in their own way. It has its flaws though. As mentioned before, it can be overwhelming for newcomers to the series or racing games as a whole. I did not have this experience, coming from previous FH titles. Without this context, I suspect I would have felt a little left out of what makes a car particularly good for the different race types. When choosing your car, you'll be directed with recommended cars but it doesn't do much more unless you pay close attention to the offshoot events that give you more direction. But if you're willing to give it a little time, then it will make it worth your while. anyway I'm done for today thanks for reading

Forza Horizon 5 - Racing Through the Beauty of Mexico  [Introduction]  Forza Horizon 5 is an open-world racing game developed by Playground Games and published by Microsoft. Released in 2021 for Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, and PC, Forza Horizon 5 is the fifth installment in the Forza Horizon series, offering players a breathtaking open-world experience. This time, the game is set in the vibrant and diverse landscapes of Mexico. With stunning graphics, a free-roaming driving experience, and impressive environmental interactions, Forza Horizon 5 perfectly blends automotive simulation and arcade racing.  [Gameplay]  Forza Horizon 5 offers players the freedom to roam across a massive and varied map of Mexico. From deserts to forests, tropical beaches to mountainous regions, the world is filled with diverse climates and breathtaking views. This expansive map invites players to explore while offering a variety of racing modes and events. As part of the Horizon Festival, players can take part in different races, participate in events, and customize their cars.  The races are arcade-style — fast-paced and fun, yet incorporating some simulation elements. Whether driving various types of cars or engaging in different activities, there’s something for every type of player. The dynamic weather and time-of-day cycles further enhance the racing experience, making every event feel unique. Additionally, the "Horizon Life" mode allows players to create their own journeys and racing series, personalizing each moment within the game.  [Graphics and Sounds]  One of the standout features of Forza Horizon 5 is its stunning visual design. The natural beauty of Mexico is brought to life with exceptional detail. Sunlight filtering through mountains, rain hitting the ground, colorful flowers, and rich vegetation are beautifully rendered. Car models and interior details are also meticulously crafted, with each vehicle’s texture and movement realistically portrayed.  The sound design is equally impressive. Car engines, changes in terrain, and weather effects all contribute to an immersive experience. The soundtrack adapts to the gameplay, changing dynamically depending on the pace of the race. Fast races feature energetic tunes, while slower moments might include more relaxed tracks.  [Conclusion]  Forza Horizon 5 goes beyond being just a racing game. With its expansive open world, impressive graphics, and detailed gameplay, it offers an unforgettable experience for players. The vibrant and culturally rich map of Mexico invites discovery and adventure, while dynamic weather and changing racing conditions make each event unique. With modes that cater to both casual players and racing enthusiasts, Forza Horizon 5 has firmly established itself in the world of racing games.  For racing fans, this is definitely a game you won’t want to miss. It’s enjoyable to play, visually stunning, and offers something for players of all ages. Whether you’re a beginner or an experienced racer, Forza Horizon 5 is a fantastic choice.  Rating: 8/10

I do recommend this game, as I do think it is a lot of fun. The driving is both accessible and challenging. The racing is fun. The customization is good. It's not absolutely horrid in terms of monetization. It's nothing groundbreaking, but is a solidly just above average racing game that is great to play while watching something else.   But I kind of don't understand the point of it being open world.... A lot of this game is just driving from one part of the map to the start of a race. Which is fine, I guess, but not very interesting. I get why a game like Need For Speed is open world, because you need a playground to run away from the cops in. You are encouraged to learn the map so you can get away more effectively. Not so in Forza. The open world here functions more as an overly elaborate race select screen. There is no reason to do anything other than follow the GPS to the next race. There isn't really anything interesting to see or find, nor are there any particularly interesting challenges.   Does this ruin the game? No. But honestly I think it would be a better game without the open world. Or at least with the ability to just start any race from anywhere. Would reduce the amount of down time greatly.

The game continues the legacy of the Forza Horizon series by focusing on freedom, exploration, and a vibrant festival atmosphere. With a mix of arcade fun and authentic driving mechanics, the experience targets a broad range of racing fans. While the title stays consistent with past entries, it manages to keep its charm intact. There isn't really a story with these Horizon games, other than its a festival where competing in and winning races gains you infamy and money which allows you to participate in more races and buy cooler stuff. With The Festival going to the USA, Italy/France, Australia and the UK, its time the festival visited Mexico! The map, while not to scale, includes some of the iconic Mexican landscapes, such as the City Of Guanajuato, the Uxmal Ruins and the Gran Puente Bridge! Gameplay is where Forza Horizon 5 truly shines, offering a massive variety of races, challenges, and stunts. The open-world design encourages exploration, and the game includes seasonal events and multiplayer modes to keep things engaging. Some repetition can set in over time, but the core mechanics remain enjoyable. Visually, Forza Horizon 5 is a standout in the racing genre. The game’s rendition of Mexico is rich with diverse biomes, including deserts, jungles, cities, and beaches. Weather systems and lighting effects enhance the immersion, particularly during dynamic events like storms or sunsets. Vehicle models are highly detailed, contributing to a visually polished experience throughout. Overall, Forza Horizon 5 delivers a solid open-world racing experience with stunning visuals and strong gameplay mechanics. Although the narrative lacks depth and certain activities may become repetitive, the sheer scale and quality of the game's environment and driving feel make it a rewarding title. It doesnt really build on the strengths of its predecessors, but offers enough content to keep players invested. The game succeeds in being accessible yet satisfying for car enthusiasts and casual racers alike. Forza Horizon 5 gets a 6/10. Its pretty good, to get right on down to the brass tax of it, lets start out with the bad: - Servers can be jank and register achievements late, early, or not at all.  - There is a rampant bot/hacker problem with the leader boards that is well known but ignored. - You have to use Xbox services to play multiplayer, using Windows Game Bar (though this does work with Proton from what I've heard. - The music in the game is laughably censored and retains copyright though there is a "streamer mode" which can circumvent the copyright. - Microtransactions, though not too in your face are there. - Fomo-centric "Forza Playlist" which lets you get some fun new cars, extra "spins" for the lootbox systems, and some cosmetics. (Although, with "Realms" now, you are no longer season locked out of some accolades) - Some accolades or events can be just a little silly or confusing - Absolutely massive file size (150GB)  NOW with the bad out of the way lets get to the good: - Beautiful scenery with a carefully thought out map that has loads of interesting events, areas, courses, and environments in general. - Lots of lovely things you can unlock to customize your characters. - Shockingly good AI implementation. Forza Horizon 5 – A Breathtaking, Fun, and Enormous Racing Sandbox  I've spent some time playing Forza Horizon 5 now, and it's been fun in general. If you like racing or just like roaming open worlds in pleasant cars, there's much to appreciate here.  What I Enjoyed  First of all, the game is beautiful to look at. The Mexico-themed map is huge and highly diverse — everything from beaches and jungles to deserts and cities. Lighting, weather, and seasonal changes all contribute to making it feel very much alive. Drifting through a thunderstorm or watching the sun set over the mountains is never a repeat experience.  The car selection is also fantastic. There is a massive list of cars, from supercars to off-road pick-ups, and they all drive differently. The driving is smooth and rewarding, both on controller or steering wheel.  I also appreciate how flexible the game is. You can be a specialist for serious races, drift competitions, off-road competitions, or even just cruise and complete stunts. There's no compulsion to follow a strict path, which makes it very accessible for casual players as well.  What I Didn't Like:  All that notwithstanding, the game is not perfect. The online features are a hit or miss — sometimes matchmaking is too slow, or connectivity drops. Not game-breaking, but annoying when playing with friends.  Also, even with tons to do, some events and progression systems become repetitive after a while. The game just showers you with rewards all the time, which is great initially but eventually seems like it starts to feel like a bit out of challenge sense.  Do I Recommend It  Indeed. Forza Horizon 5 is as much fun to play as there is for racing games, specifically if you love open-world exploration and a gentler approach to driving. Even if you are not a committed racing fan, it's certainly worth checking out for just how well and cleanly made it is. Just beware of a tad online goofiness and some repetitiveness on occasion.

First of all, I have to say for all its flaws, Forza Horizon 5 is still one of the best racing games out there. The driving physics and graphics are amazing, and I genuinely enjoy just cruising around and testing different cars. It’s really fun. I still have to say, the grip in Forza Horizon 5 is worse than in Forza Horizon 4.  BUT I also hate this game sometimes, mostly because of Microsoft’s laziness and weird design choices.  Compared to Forza Horizon 4, FH5 definitely has better graphics, and the physics are still top-tier. But the story and missions? Boring and repetitive. In FH4, I never felt this way I didn’t have to repeat the same race five times because there was actually more variety and purpose. In FH5, the missions feel out of context and way overhyped for how dull they actually are. It’s kind of cringe.  The in-game economy is a mess. You barely earn anything from races. Wheelspins are awful I maybe got two legendary items the entire game. The only real way to make money is by grinding seasonal challenges to unlock exclusive cars, then selling them for 15 million credits. That’s how you buy anything. In FH4, you could earn more through missions, better wheelspins, and even from businesses. FH5 technically has a “business” section too, but it’s just copied from FH4 and completely useless now.  And the map? Not great. Seasons barely change anything winter and summer look almost identical. The only thing keeping the game “alive” are those repetitive seasonal events and occasional new locations they eventually remove anyway.  TL;DR: They basically recycled a lot from Forza Horizon 4, updated the graphics, create new map (without seasons), add few boring races, and called it a new game. It’s still good but the laziness behind it really shows.

Then, within the first hour of playing, it crashed on me.  In terms of the gameplay itself, driving feels nice, in my opinion it's a good balance of arcade-y and realistic. Sometimes I feel that games will try fully to be one or the other, but Forza feels like more of an in-between. One glaring issue I had however, is that you can't turn the camera without holding right mouse, and even then it's very stiff and constrained. I know that it's a racing game and having a more restricted camera makes sense for most players, but not even having an option for a proper 360 camera is odd to me.  My biggest letdown though was the world. I don't think I've ever felt more bored driving through an open world. It looks nice enough, but to me it was incredibly bland and empty. Mexico is a fantastic setting but I'm not a fan of how this game executes it.  Finally, and this is especially based on person preference, but the whole experience feels a little... artificial. Characters try too hard with their dialogue, there's fake drivers everywhere with name bubbles above their heads, the game literally gave me an ad for the new realms update after a mission, the list goes on.  Overall, I can see why people like this game simply for the races and driving mechanics. Otherwise, though, I found it to be pretty dry.

This is a fun racing game with decent driving mechanics, but it's held back by comically unrealistic collision physics, and a map that gets boring really, really quickly.  It's a better game than its predecessor in many ways: the graphics are sharper, there are more activities, the driving feels more lifelike, and the map's regions are more distinctive. But there are weak points, some more severe than others:  1) The game focuses heavily on off-road and rally racing, which would be fine, except the off-road collision mechanics are laughable, with very little vehicle damage. There are wonderful desert, mountain, and jungle settings, but players can blast through them in a McLaren or Ferrari, consequence free. There's zero environmental challenge or peril. What's the point?  2) Due to its locale FH5's seasons are much subtler, which kind of sucks the life out of the roads. It's pretty for a while, but becomes empty and lifeless far too quickly. FH4's greatest strength was its dramatic seasonal changes, which completely transformed the map every week (except maybe the spring to summer transition).   3) The menus are an omnishambles. The goal was to make the boring administrative side of the game more fun and dynamic, but the result was a confusing and frustrating series of screens and tiles. There's a Microsoft burn in there somewhere.  4) Too many festivals. The game tries to silo its different modes into separate outpost festivals spread around the map, and each one has a set of story objectives to unlock. The idea is fine, I guess, but the implementation feels tacked-on, tedious, and unrealistic (yes, I'm aware this is a game whose opening scene involves parachuting out of an airplane in an offroad vehicle and racing down the face of a mountain, but still.)  5) The city, Guanajuato, is too small. I know the Forza Horizon games want to have a little bit of everything for all kinds of drivers, but as someone who loves urban driving setting, this was a letdown. FH5's Guanajuato probably has more kilometres of road than FH4's Edinburgh, but it sure doesn't feel that way.  Anyway, I do like this game, and recommend it - if only because it's the most comprehensive driving game currently available on PC. It just feels a little hollow compared to previous entries in the series.

Lots of flash; very little substance.  Very poor integration with Logitech G29 Wheel/Pedals setup.  Not possible to dial out the absurd amounts of steering oscillation. Checked the (mostly useless) online setup guides and tested their settings however the underlying controller interface is not sufficiently flexible to tune out the yaw without deadening (and substantially degrading) the overall steering performance.  Might work with a controller, however I purchased it in the hope of being able to drive cars in a semi-arcade / semi-simulation mode using a wheel and pedals. During the "refund window" most of the game time was spent yawing from one side of the track to the other and ending up backwards.  Despite lots of bump vibration through the FFB wheel the actual engagement between the vehicle and the track is remote and lacking in any real road feel. If the car behaved more in an arcade mode (i.e. did not enter excessive yaw oscillation at the slightest provocation) this lack of track engagement would not be so much of an issue. However in the current case the lack of track engagement, and the tendency to oscillate wildly at the slightest provocation, the overwhelming sensation is one of lack of control.  This means the game sits uncomfortably between "arcade" and "simulation" modes. It is neither accurate enough to even approach a "simulation" nor unrealistic enough to perform well as an "arcade" style driving game.  Requested a refund.  Looks like it is back to Assetto Corsa (surprisingly good car simulation) or iRacing...

Whether you're tearing through off-road terrain in a rugged 4x4 or hugging tight corners in a sleek supercar, each vehicle feels unique and responsive.
