The Horizon Festival is a celebration of speed, style, and freedom, and it's reflected in every aspect of the gameplay. The open-world design encourages exploration, with hidden routes, stunt jumps, and collectibles scattered throughout the map. The Horizon Story missions provide a captivating narrative to accompany your racing exploits, adding depth to the overall experience.  The social aspect of Forza Horizon 5 is a highlight, with the ability to seamlessly connect with other players in the shared open world. Whether you're engaging in impromptu races, joining a convoy for a cross-country trek, or competing in the intense Horizon Arcade challenges, the multiplayer component adds a dynamic layer to the game that keeps the excitement alive long after the single-player campaign is completed.  The soundtrack deserves special mention, featuring a diverse and energetic mix of music that perfectly complements the game's exhilarating pace. From pulse-pounding tracks during races to laid-back tunes as you cruise through picturesque landscapes, the soundtrack enhances the overall atmosphere and keeps you immersed in the world of Forza Horizon 5.  In conclusion, Forza Horizon 5 is a triumph of game design, offering a stunning open-world playground for racing enthusiasts. With its unparalleled visuals, extensive car lineup, engaging gameplay, and vibrant social features, it's not just a game – it's an unforgettable journey that redefines the standard for open-world racing games. I'm not sure which of those things fixed the issue, but in case anyone else has the issue, try the above.  As far as the game itself goes, now that the stuttering is gone, I am really enjoying it. There isn't really a strict progression from low end cars to high end cars as I was expecting, rather there are a butt ton of cars to try out and customize and it let's you get right into it right away. I've actually grown fond of it.  The graphics are great, the variety of cars and race types keeps things fresh. I haven't played multiplayer yet but I hear good things.  As for the Dev who reached out to try to help, I really appreciate you taking the time to do so. Its no longer needed now, I was just to hasty to leave a review, and I apologize for that.

This game tested my skills as, from what I see, it requires you to watch tutorials for the best settings, driving patterns and tips on obtaining the most from missions, events, etc.  It could be pretty daunting at first, and the mechanics were really complex for a player like me who hadn't driven online before. I recommend it for its highly detailed cars, the vibes you get from the game, and the functionalities implemented in the it. As far as casual play goes, FH5 is a perfectly fine game, but for me there is one major glaring issue. The progression system sucks. Instead of starting the game with the lowest class of car and working your way up higher and higher on the performance ladder, the game starts you out with 3 cars that sit in the upper middle section of performance classes. Having cars that start at A and B class ratings invalidates classes C and D outside of experimenting for fun several dozen hours into the game. There's also the wheel spin system of level-up rewards that makes leveling up feel less rewarding. Instead of starting at 5-20k dollar rewards and, as you play, increasing this to higher value cars and greater cash rewards, there is a chance that the level up reward for reaching 20 is a Ferrari FXX and the level reward for reaching level 80 is 20k dollars. It doesn't make me get excited for leveling up as it kinda kills the idea of progressing rewards for progressing levels. All of this led me to feeling like I have "completed" the game 5-10 hours into the game after I got a S2 class supercar through the wheel spin relatively early on. A car that would usually be rewarded in the last few "levels" of other racing games, found its way into my hands as I was still beginning. I felt great that I had gotten so lucky, but after a while it kinda killed my drive to keep playing as much as I had. The game is still fun on a purely driving basis, and I can imagine it is even more fun with friends; but the idea of random progression rewards turns you off, there are probably other options available.

A car, or an automobile, is a motor vehicle with wheels. Most definitions of cars state that they run primarily on roads, seat one to eight people, have four wheels, and mainly transport people rather than cargo.[1][2] There are around one billion cars in use worldwide.  The French inventor Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot built the first steam-powered road vehicle in 1769, while the Swiss inventor François Isaac de Rivaz designed and constructed the first internal combustion-powered automobile in 1808. The modern car—a practical, marketable automobile for everyday use—was invented in 1886, when the German inventor Carl Benz patented his Benz Patent-Motorwagen. Commercial cars became widely available during the 20th century. The 1901 Oldsmobile Curved Dash and the 1908 Ford Model T, both American cars, are widely considered the first mass-produced[3][4] and mass-affordable[5][6][7] cars, respectively. Cars were rapidly adopted in the US, where they replaced horse-drawn carriages.[8] In Europe and other parts of the world, demand for automobiles did not increase until after World War II.[9] In the 21st century, car usage is still increasing rapidly, especially in China, India, and other newly industrialised countries.[10][11]  Cars have controls for driving, parking, passenger comfort, and a variety of lamps. Over the decades, additional features and controls have been added to vehicles, making them progressively more complex. These include rear-reversing cameras, air conditioning, navigation systems, and in-car entertainment. Most cars in use in the early 2020s are propelled by an internal combustion engine, fueled by the combustion of fossil fuels. Electric cars, which were invented early in the history of the car, became commercially available in the 2000s and are predicted to cost less to buy than petrol-driven cars before 2025.[12][13] The transition from fossil fuel-powered cars to electric cars features prominently in most climate change mitigation scenarios,[14] such as Project Drawdown's 100 actionable solutions for climate change.[15]  There are costs and benefits to car use. The costs to the individual include acquiring the vehicle, interest payments (if the car is financed), repairs and maintenance, fuel, depreciation, driving time, parking fees, taxes, and insurance.[16] The costs to society include maintaining roads, land-use, road congestion, air pollution, noise pollution, public health, and disposing of the vehicle at the end of its life. Traffic collisions are the largest cause of injury-related deaths worldwide.[17] Personal benefits include on-demand transportation, mobility, independence, and convenience.[18] Societal benefits include economic benefits, such as job and wealth creation from the automotive industry, transportation provision, societal well-being from leisure and travel opportunities. People's ability to move flexibly from place to place has far-reaching implications for the nature of societies.[19]

Forza Horizon 5, A fun grind fest. Rare in this world. over 800 cars to collect. Difficulty settings can be manipulated heavily. With the rewind feature that allows you to rewind to a previous location in your race (if you decide it) you will never lose a race.  The complicated engine and cosmetic tuning for each vehicle adds to your experience. But do not fear. if you arent good at it you can choose a player rated premade tune from other players.  Pro's:- - Graphics. - Sound design. - Game-play. - Story-based content. - DLC (its simple, adds new cars or playable locations. i enjoyed the DLC). - As of April 2025 the game is still recieving regular updates and support. - Next to no micro-transactions. Nothing vital.  - Con's:- - DLC... alot of it if you are a completionist. - Will take forever to collect all the vehicles. - Micro-transactions. Only one way to give real money for in-game currency. Car vouchers that allow you to buy stuff cars from the car shop (autoshop). During my playtime i have purchased the 24 car vouchers for £15.99. I dont regret it. Note: you can buy the autoshow cars without the vouchers, with your race winnings.  Conclusion:- I enjoy this game and will continue to play it for as long as it is supported and perhaps even after that.

Frame drops and texture pop-ins are VERY apparent, and will make sure you get good use of that re-wind feature. I have troubleshot this issue personally from downgrading the game to Minecraft esc graphics, to boosting absolutely everything I could and still had frame drops and texture pop in mid race. And since Turn 10 absolutely hates single player gamers when it comes to Forza Horizon, you can't use mods to get around this and HAVE to play online for some of them, not to mention all of the challenge event cars, which aren't even worth it half the time since some of the cars handling was handled TERRIBLY. All in all, your average corporate triple A "Car Enthusiasts Racing Game" with no effort put into the actual quality, performance, or game-play, but rather the ways to increase artificial playtime, and rake in money. After 30 hours in Forza Horizon 5, I can confidently say it’s one of the most entertaining open-world racing games out there—but it’s not without its flaws. Here’s my breakdown of what stands out after extended playtime.  What Keeps Me Hooked  The Map is a Joy to Explore Mexico’s diverse landscapes still feel fresh, even after hours of driving. I’ve raced through jungles, climbed the volcano, drifted through city streets, and blasted down highways at ridiculous speeds. The seasonal changes keep things interesting, especially in the rainy season when the roads get slick.   Driving Feels Fantastic The balance between arcade fun and realism is spot-on. Whether I’m throwing a rally car through dirt roads or maxing out a hypercar on the highway, each vehicle has a unique feel. The tuning and upgrade options add even more depth—I’ve spent a lot of time tweaking my favorite cars for optimal performance.   There’s So Much to Do Every time I log in, there’s something new: speed traps, danger signs, barn finds, showcase events, and Horizon Stories. The seasonal challenges and festival playlists add weekly incentives to keep coming back. I still have tons of cars to unlock and haven’t even completed all the event types.  Online Play Can Be a Blast Convoys with friends, custom races, and The Eliminator (Battle Royale mode) add variety. When it works smoothly, online play is some of the best fun I’ve had in a racing game.  What’s Wearing Thin After 30 Hours  Repetitive Gameplay Loop After a while, races start to feel a bit samey. Many events follow the same formula, and while the variety of cars helps, there’s a sense of déjà vu when tackling yet another dirt race or street sprint.  Progression Feels Too Generous At first, unlocking cars felt exciting, but after a while, the game just throws rewards at you. I have more cars than I know what to do with, and credits are so easy to come by that buying new vehicles doesn’t feel like an achievement.   AI and Difficulty Balance Issues Drivatars are hit or miss—sometimes too easy, sometimes overly aggressive. Rubber-banding can make races feel artificial, and AI traffic can be infuriating during street races.  Online Connectivity Can Be Frustrating Horizon Open and co-op events are fun when they work, but connection issues and lag can ruin the experience. Sometimes convoys randomly disconnect, making it frustrating to play with friends.  Final Verdict After 30 Hours Forza Horizon 5 is still a must-play for racing fans. The open world is gorgeous, the driving is addictive, and there’s an overwhelming amount of content. However, the repetitive structure and online issues become more noticeable over time. If you love open-world driving and casual racing, it’s 100% worth it. If you’re looking for deep progression or a serious challenge, the game might not hold your interest for as long.  Would I still recommend it? Yes, but with some caveats. It’s a fantastic game, but after 30 hours, I’m starting to feel bored. Still, I’ll probably keep coming back for more seasonal events and casual driving sessions.

Technical and performance issues:  The game crashes pretty often, just as FH4 did. At this point, im pretty sure its a memory leak thing in both FH4 and FH5 games. The system of gifting the cars is glitchy. At least the receiving the gift part is - the game crashes (at this point, for million times already), and after turning the game back on, only then the gift shows up in the barn. Tour CO-OP races causes crashing every time i start the first race or finish the third (last) one. Its impossible to complete the whole CO-OP tour championship event, without lowering down the graphical settings to the lowest... Damn those memory leaks.......  EDIT: FOUND A FIX FOR THE ISSUES MENTIONED ABOVE (OR AT LEAST SOME OF THEM - I HAVE TO PLAY AROUND MORE TO BE SURE MYSELF). I DONT KNOW IF THIS WOULD WORK WITH FH4, BUT IT WORKS FINE WITH FH5. WHAT I DID: FOUND THE STEAM LOCATION OF THE GAME'S FOLDER, AND THERE ON THE "forza.exe" FILE I CLICKED RIGHT MOUSE BUTTON, THEN PRESSED ON "Properties", AND THERE CHANGED THE "Compatibility" SETTING TO "Windows 8". THAT ACTUALLY HELPED ME, AND SOME OTHER PEOPLE ON FORZA FORUMS APPROVED THIS TOO. I WAS WARNED, THAT CRASHING STILL CAN OCCUR, BUT NOT THAT OFTEN ANYMORE.   Arcade (Forzathon) events are glitchy sometimes as well, and not too many people playing them, especially if compared to FH4. That's sad, because these arcade events have more interesting and diverse games to play.  And another issue, that gave me some trouble too - rival racing is very frustrating, because the servers are not working properly, and the game giving server timeout errors pretty often. My internet is fine by the way.  Same goes with the auction servers - its scary to bid bigger amounts, because the servers arent stable, and money used to bid sometimes gets stuck for a long time without a possibility to take them back - this is definitely a new one, and wasnt in FH4.  With such issues, sometimes the game feels like a downgrade from FH4, which otherwise would not be the case.    Atmosphere, visuals, sound and story:  Atmosphere wise, i prefer FH5 more than FH4. I like the dunes, beaches, jungle with the temples, and of course the mountains. Love the dust and tropical storms. Some say, that they miss snow in this game. Well, i dont. Definitely was enough of snow in FH4 for me. And i get enough of it in real life too. So yeah, not a problem to me. I actually like the tropical climate and weather in the game, that i dont get to feel often in real life. At the same time i do understand other players who actually dont experience snow too often - in that case i completely understand why they would miss it so much in a video game.   Gameplay and world roads wise, both FH5 and FH4 are kind of equally amazing. Both have their own type of fun, challenges and terrain. In FH5, i like the little bit broader diversity of roads - there are plenty of them to unlock by a player. Same goes with the cars and activities too.  I like the music and graphics too - both are better than in FH4.   The story line of a Festival is better in this one - its more interesting and haves better continuity. So i just hope it will have a better ending too (still far from finishing this game, there is a lot to do in it), because FH4 felt like it didnt have an ending at all. Not gonna lie, even in an online racing game, i care about the story line enough, that having no closure like that pisses me off a little.    Rating:  So far im giving this one 8.5/10, a 0.5 points better score than i gave FH4.  Both games are worthy of the attention to at least try.

I started playing at Horizon 2 on XBox, and honestly you'll probably be just fine playing Horizon 3 or 4.   Problem 1: Pacing This game seems to be built with the assumption that the player has ADD as it is constantly interrupting you to try and advance things. I never really finished everything in the other Horizon games but those titles were far better at their pacing. I was allowed to move and do things as I wanted, and was really only pushed to expand after a few days of game play at the pace I played. Horizon 5 probably interrupted me, stopping my play in its tracks something like 20 times in less than 2 hrs.  Issue 2: Voice customization The Devs put a lot of effort into the physical customization of your character. Its nice and all that they've added the option for prostetic limbs, and hearing devices for players who need those IRL but it seems silly to put all that effort into these choices but then saddle players with only 2 voice options, and they both are annoying English, bro-ey kind of accents. Seriously how much effort would it have been to find a couple extra VAs who didn't sound cockney, or better yet, just have the two you hired just try and talk without the English accent.  Issue 3: The constant, unnatural sounding, talking Not only is it just annoying how much these characters are talking (in previous titles they talked less at least) but they also don't sound natural, like this is not how people actually talk. Forza Horizon 5 - 8/10: A Beautiful Drive with Room to Evolve  Forza Horizon 5 delivers an experience that is nothing short of breathtaking. Set in the vibrant, open-world playground of Mexico, this game showcases the series' signature blend of speed, freedom, and spectacular visuals. The vast landscapes—from sun-kissed deserts to lush jungles—are a visual treat, and the game truly captures the essence of Mexico’s diverse beauty, making it a joy to explore.  The driving mechanics are fluid and accessible, allowing both casual players and hardcore enthusiasts to have fun. Whether you're flying through the streets of Mexico City or drifting through a mountain pass, the game feels responsive and exciting. The addition of the wide variety of cars, customization options, and dynamic seasons further enhances the sense of freedom and immersion, giving players endless opportunities to craft their perfect ride and experience the open world in new ways.  On the flip side, while Forza Horizon 5 excels in visuals and gameplay, it does feel a bit safe at times, sticking closely to the formula that made its predecessors so beloved. Some may find that the core experience doesn’t evolve as much as they’d hoped, especially after the high expectations set by Forza Horizon 4. Also, the progression system can feel a tad grindy at times, and while the game offers an abundance of content, there are moments where the variety can feel a little repetitive.  That said, Forza Horizon 5 is a massive, incredibly polished racing game that offers hours of enjoyment. It's a perfect fit for players looking for a fun, visually stunning racing experience. If you’re a fan of the genre or just want a game to get lost in, you can’t go wrong here. With a little more innovation and tweaks to the progression, this could have been a true 10/10. But for now, it remains a must-play for fans of the series and racing games in general.  Verdict: 8/10 – A masterpiece in many ways, but still with some room to grow.

Forza Horizon 5 Review – A Stunning but Flawed Experience Forza Horizon 5 is undeniably a beautiful game. The vibrant open world, stunning lighting, and detailed car models make it a visual treat. However, beneath the polished exterior, there are some frustrating flaws that hold it back from being a truly great racing experience.  One of the biggest issues I’ve encountered is the game crashing completely at random. There’s no warning, no error message—just an abrupt crash to desktop. For a game of this scale, stability should be a top priority, yet it still suffers from these unpredictable failures.  Another puzzling choice is the inclusion of Frame Generation. With an RTX 5080, the game runs effortlessly at 4K max settings, holding a steady 120 FPS without breaking a sweat. Frame Generation feels unnecessary here, which makes me question why it was implemented at all.  While the open-world environment is undeniably impressive, I personally wish the game was more focused on actual racing rather than free roaming. Forza Horizon 5 leans heavily into exploration, and while that appeals to some players, it takes away from the structured racing experience that I enjoyed more in previous entries.  Another major frustration is the unskippable cutscenes and forced dialogue sequences. If you're here to race, being constantly interrupted by unnecessary cinematics and chatter can be a serious annoyance. These interruptions slow down the pacing and make the experience feel bloated, especially for those who just want to jump into events.  Is Forza Horizon 5 worth buying? Yes, but only on sale. If Forza Horizon 4 was still fully supported and had an active player base, I’d honestly stick with that instead. It had a better soundtrack, a more straightforward experience, and fewer unnecessary distractions.  Final Verdict: A visually stunning open-world racer with frustrating technical issues and an overemphasis on free roaming. Worth playing, but not at full price.

Forza Horizon 5 was actually my introduction to the Forza franchise, when I played it on Game Pass a number of years ago. With over 200 hours logged, it is needless to say that I fell in love. However, after playing Forza Horizon 4, I will say there are some things that 5 didn't live up to.  The UI feels worse. It looks much more cartoony and feels less intuitive that the UI from 4. The bonus credits you get from turning up the difficulty seem to only apply for Drivatar difficulty, and not things like racing line, rewind, shifting, and traction control, all things that massively affect how difficult the game is to do well in, especially for inexperienced players. Not only does this give an incentive to play with more driving assists, it also makes it more difficult to earn more money by challenging yourself. In Forza Horizon 4, I was consistently earning credits at an 85% bonus playing against Unbeatable drivatars with no traction control, no rewind, and a braking-only racing line. Now it seems that it would be financially advisable to keep those assists on, because it makes no difference in your bonus. Wheelspins seems fewer and farther between, and seem to give good rewards at a much lower rate than 4. And, of course, even purchasing the Ultimate edition (or whatever they call it) of this games still doesn't give you all the DLCs, leaving a $50 bundle for you to purchase after you already bought the game.  Now for the pros. Forza Horizon 5 has, in my humble opinion, a VASTLY superior map to Forza Horizon 4. Yes, the map for 4 is pretty, and as someone who has been to the UK I can say that it definitely captures the vibe. However, deciduous forests and farms for 20 kilometers does eventually get boring. It even lacks meaningful terrain height variation, with there only being 2 or so roads that even begin to venture into the mountainous area of the map, and even then it doesn't feel all that great. 5, however, has not just one prettier biome, but it seems like almost all of the much more varied map biomes are more enjoyable to drive through than a majority of the map from 4. There's the tropical seaside in the east, which is my personal favorite, the pine forests in the north, which are a close runner up, the jungle in the south, and the sand dunes in the west, with a city in the middle of the map that is notably larger and more detailed than Edinburgh from the map of Forza Horizon 4. With the variation, you can spend more time driving without feeling like you've seen it all before, and the beauty makes what you DO see more pleasant. Forza Horizon 5 has, partially due to it just being a newer game and partially due to a simply larger scale, a much wider and honestly much better selection of vehicles to drive. Very few cars from Forza Horizon 4 are absent from the 5th game, and while a select handful of these are missed (Aston Martin Vulcan, why...) it is pretty much instantly made up for by the cars that are new to the franchise in 5. For McLaren alone (my favorite manufacturer) we have the 620r, the 765lt, and the Sabre, among others, all cars that I am absolutely thrilled to have added. As for vehicles I can't name, I believe the total cars in Forza Horizon 5 is almost 200 more than Forza Horizon 4, which is just awesome. Additionally, while this isn't quite a pro based on the game's content, it *is* currently the only Forza Horizon game that is actively being sold in online stores, and the only one with a running festival playlist. Not really something the game worked for, but a pro nonetheless.  All in all, I think this game is an absolute win overall, despite a number of its shortcomings. If you're new to the Forza Horizon franchise, you likely won't have any issue with many of my criticisms that stemmed from comparison to the previous game, and if you're someone who likes cars and isn't looking for an automobile sim, then this is going to be a GREAT game for you. Within any given period of 6 weeks, the game should go on 50% sale and you can get the Ultimate edition for $50, less than you would spend on many AAA games that give you content, less quality, and less replayability. Enjoy.

[h1]Forza Horizon 5 Review – The Ultimate Open-World Racing Experience[/h1]   [h2]Introduction [/h2] Forza Horizon 5 takes everything we loved about its predecessor and cranks it up to eleven. Set in the vibrant and diverse landscapes of Mexico, this game delivers a stunning open-world racing experience with refined gameplay, breathtaking visuals, and an endless variety of activities. Whether you're a hardcore racing enthusiast or a casual driver looking for some arcade fun, FH5 has something for everyone.   [h2]Graphics & World Design – A Visual Masterpiece [/h2] One of the biggest highlights of Forza Horizon 5 is its insane level of detail. From sun-soaked deserts to dense jungles, active volcanoes, and lively cities, every environment feels alive. The dynamic weather system adds another layer of realism, with tropical storms, dust clouds, and seasonal changes affecting both visuals and driving conditions. The lighting, reflections, and ray tracing (in select modes) push the limits of what an open-world racing game can achieve.   [h2]Driving & Physics – A Perfect Balance [/h2] Forza Horizon 5 nails the balance between realism and arcade fun. Cars feel weighty and responsive, but the handling remains forgiving enough to keep the action flowing. Whether you're drifting around mountain roads, smashing through jungle trails, or hitting top speeds on highways, the driving experience is exhilarating. The physics engine accurately simulates different terrains, making off-road racing just as thrilling as street racing.  The car roster is massive, with over 500 vehicles at launch, covering everything from hypercars and off-road beasts to JDM classics and muscle cars. Each car is finely tuned with realistic engine sounds, custom mods, and deep tuning options for those who love to tweak performance.   [h2]Game Modes & Customization – Play Your Way [/h2] Forza Horizon 5 is packed with content. The Horizon Adventure mode introduces a loose story structure, guiding you through key racing events across Mexico. The Expedition missions add a sense of discovery, where you explore new areas and unlock new festival sites.  Online multiplayer is seamless and engaging, with events like The Eliminator (a battle royale mode for cars), Horizon Arcade (co-op challenges), and custom racing lobbies keeping things fresh. The new EventLab tool allows players to create custom races, challenges, and even full-blown game modes, making the replayability factor nearly endless.  Customization is also top-tier. Forza Horizon 5 is nothing short of a masterpiece, delivering an unparalleled open-world racing experience that sets a new standard for the genre. From the moment you hit the vibrant streets of Mexico, you're greeted with stunning visuals, a dynamic weather system, and an incredibly diverse landscape that keeps every drive fresh and exciting. The attention to detail is breathtaking, and the sheer scale of the world is awe-inspiring.  The gameplay is as smooth as it gets, with responsive controls and a wide variety of cars that cater to every driving style. Whether you're tearing through the jungle, drifting across sandy dunes, or cruising through picturesque towns, Forza Horizon 5 offers an adrenaline-pumping adventure at every turn. The soundtrack is equally impressive, featuring a perfect mix of genres that keeps the energy high and the vibes immaculate.  One of the standout features is the sheer amount of content. With countless events, challenges, and collectibles, there's always something to do. The game strikes a perfect balance between casual fun and competitive racing, making it accessible to players of all skill levels. The addition of the EventLab allows for endless creativity, letting players design their own races and challenges, which adds a whole new layer of replayability.  That said, if there's one area where I wish the game could expand, it's in the customization of engine upgrades. While the game offers a decent range of tuning options, I found myself craving more depth when it comes to tweaking and personalizing the performance of my cars. More granular control over engine components, exhaust notes, or even unique visual modifications under the hood would take the customization to the next level and make each car feel even more uniquely mine.  Despite this minor wish, Forza Horizon 5 is an absolute triumph. It's a game that celebrates the joy of driving in every possible way, and it's clear that the developers poured their hearts into creating this vibrant, living world. Whether you're a car enthusiast or just someone looking for an incredible gaming experience, Forza Horizon 5 is a must-play. It's not just a game—it's a celebration of speed, freedom, and the open road. Bravo, Playground Games!

[h1]🏎️ Forza Horizon 5 🏎️[/h1]  [b]Score: 9/10[/b] 128 hours in and I still just drive around Mexico sometimes doing nothing in particular. No race, no objective. Just the road and whatever car I felt like taking out that day. [hr][/hr] [h2]The basics[/h2]  Open world racing in a massive map of Mexico. Every terrain type, every weather condition, hundreds of cars ranging from daily drivers to things that have no business existing on a public road. The world is genuinely beautiful and the variety of events means you rarely feel like you're doing the same thing twice. [hr][/hr] [h2]How it plays[/h2]  Smooth, accessible and endlessly rewarding. The driving feels great whether you're on tarmac, dirt or cutting through a jungle. Seasonal events keep things fresh and the car customisation goes deep enough to keep gearheads busy for a long time. Online is mostly seamless, dips in and out without interrupting the experience. [hr][/hr] [h2]Is it worth it[/h2]  Content is overwhelming in the best way. The one thing worth knowing before you get attached to a specific car is that the in-game market is a mess. Some vehicles are locked behind DLC, others only appear in the auction house at prices that require either serious grinding or serious luck. You will find a car you want and discover you basically can't have it without paying extra or waiting indefinitely. [hr][/hr] [h2]Overall[/h2]  Still one of the best driving playgrounds out there even with FH6 out now. Just accept early on that you won't own everything, and you'll have a great time with what you do have.

FH5 is one of the most enjoyable open-world racing games I’ve played. The driving feels amazing, the car selection is massive, and the map is absolutely stunning. Mexico looks incredible, with a ton of lush jungles, sandy deserts, and long highways. The lighting and weather effects make everything feel more alive, especially during blue or golden hour. That being said, while the graphics are top-tier, I still prefer the map of FH4. Something about the UK’s roads, scenery, and overall layout just felt more connected and fun to drive around. Mexico is great, but I found myself missing FH4’s vibe at times.  It hits a sweet spot between arcade and realism. Off-road racing is especially fun, and the terrain feels rough in all the right ways. Customization is deep, from performance tuning to cosmetic changes. Whether you’re a casual player or someone who loves fine-tuning every setting, FH5 just gives you the tools to play your way.  The events are fun and diverse. There are plenty of races, from street circuits to off-road challenges. I like how the game keeps things fresh with different types of challenges, but to be honest—the story-driven missions didn’t do much for me. They’re not bad, but they feel like filler at times. Multiplayer can also be hit or miss. When it works, it’s great, but connection issues can make online events frustrating.  Overall, FH5 is a fantastic game. It improves on a lot of things, but I personally still like FH4’s map better. That doesn’t take away from how fun and enjoyable this game is, though—there’s always something to do, and the driving never gets old.

Its been officially 4 years since this game came out and it is STILL riddled with problems.  I have never encountered a game that crashes so bloody much or a game that has so many technical issues that compound the gaming experience.  Let's go over it:  1 - Mandated Tutorials that you can't shut off: The game FORCES you to play at its pace, not yours, and too bad if you want to go out and explore. 2 - Consistent Crashes: The game has almost consistently and constantly crashed on me both during and after story event missions. This is unacceptable for a game that's been out for 4 years and where the developers are actively publishing DLC and other packs but aren't maintaining the health of the game. 3 - Excessively Priced: The base game is 60 dollars, and it comes in editions scaling up to 100 dollars. This "Premium Pack" does NOT include the Car DLC Pack which is an additional 75 dollars. And honestly, the Premium pack doesn't give anything that's honestly worth it--the cars it gives are kind of garbage and the cosmetic items are 'meh' at best. 4 - Not Optimized for Streaming: Unless you're a live camera streamer, this game is going to cause your VRM software to excessively lag. This is a minor gripe for everyone else and will not apply to most people. 5 - Unskippable Lengthy Cutscenes: NONE, absolutely NONE of the cutscenes in this game allow you to skip them. And some of them are rather lengthy. If you want to repeat and try to get a higher score on a story mission? You are -forced- to have to sit through their boring storytelling for 30 seconds upwards to almost 2 minutes.  I have one final gripe for the game, and this one is THE most serious of them all...  6 - DOXes your first real-life name: Exactly as it is stated. The game will DEFAULT to forcibly using your real-life first name as your character name and requires you to have to go into settings in order to change only AFTER the game lets you actually EXPLORE after about 20-30 minutes of mandated cutscenes that you can't skip through--and if you're an extremely private person like me? This invasion of my privacy without my authorization or permission is THE primary reason why I will NOT recommend this game.   The positives of this game is the races are fun, the cars are beautiful, the scenery is gorgeous, but none of that can just override the bad for me. I expected better from this studio and, as usual, another Triple A developer has disappointed me on almost every level.

In general this is a great car and racing game which I have greatly enjoyed for at least 250 hours. Graphics, soundtrack, and gamemodes are great. Altough I don't really like the sometimes somewhat childish approach of the campaign and voice acting I do like that it's a game with a lot of depth in which one can spend hours driving around the different maps (of which the main map is not big enough to be honest) and the various race challenges. one can spend hours in the garage painting each car and there's a lot of cars to buy or unlock.  HOWEVER The game has been crashing randomly ALL THE TIME since a while now and most of the time it happens only after 10 or 20 minutes. This didn't happen before. But it started happening after about 250 hours of play. So I played this game without any trouble for a year or two and now after having invested so much time the ironic reward is that the game has become unplayable. Even on my new recently acquired next gen Windows 11 system with a clean install this game crashes and is still unplayable. Often I can't even finish the first race I start, let alone play online.  Even though the dev's keep releasing new cars and DLC which I applaud I'd rather they focus on game stability and finally addressing this issue of which a quick search online will reveal thousands of other players worldwide experience exactly the same thing. It's an embarrassement to be honest. This needs to be fixed! And until it is not I will NOT recommend this game.  Other issues: - Playing online mostly means short races and long loading times in between due to players with low end systems which is not a great balance. - Another issue with the gameplay is that missing a checkpoint in a race, most of the times means you can abandon it when playing online. This is definately not the best design choice to create dynamic competitive races with chances of comebacks.  - Collision prevention system also seems to be working randomly and never in my favor it seems - Lastly I don't think the car upgrade system is very polished or very well thought through. Maxing out a car usually means it ends up getting off road tires and a 4wd setup which destroys the uniqueness of the individual cars.  The car library needs some big improvements There's a way too heavy BIAS towards some brands while other brands are left bare handed. In my opinion I really don't care for 60 different Audi's, Porsches and VW's that all look alike. There are so many great ánd sporty cars in the world that are not included in this game which is a shame. French cars of which there are a lot, even sporty ones (Remember Peugeot dominated Dakar and Pikes Peak and built so  many GTI cars and Citroën dominated WRC for years) are completely left out! The game only offers some Renaults and even the Clio V6 is missing.  They don't even get the brands right as a DS is definately a Citroën and not a DS Automobiles car.  Italian cars the same. Alfa Romeo, Lancia and Fiat have a long pedigree of great cars. It's bare mininum in this game. Same goes for British cars like Jaguar, and even Opel seems next to non existant in this game.  Japanese cars are better represented as well as American brands but really the emphasis is waaay too much on the same boring all the same looking German cars.  In a game like this I absolutely like being able to drive not only the supercars of fame but also the mainstream cars that we all see on our roads. And from each era. The developers are taking way too long to complete the car library and clearly they haven't got their history of great cars in order.  So a great game , but in potential a much better game, however it keeps crashing which destroys the entire experience  I'd love to see a Forza Horizon Europe or Asia edition in the future. This is a really good entry in the FH series, with a few caveats.  The driving feels just as good as FH4, though the seasons (in my opinion) do not offer as much variety on the terrain in Mexico as they do in the UK.  I miss how the roads would feel totally different in winter, covered in snow, and some of the lakes would freeze giving to access to some different locations in the UK.  Mexico has some great areas to explore though, and if you like hillclimb-type driving with lots of switchbacks, the volcano offers a great time with both paved roads and dirt roads.  Car upgrades have been changed slightly but remain similar enough to FH4.  You still have a lot of customization with adjusting how your car handles, although my experience with that has been limited.  I have changed parts and customized that way but I have not delved into the actual settings of changing the details of things like ride height, etc.  The "story" mode or campaign I found fun.  The way the voice actors approach their roles made me feel like I was in a Saturday morning cartoon version of FH, and I mean that as a compliment.  It's all delivered with a very positive vibe.  Now for the bad: the online system.  The game will remind you immediately when trying to play with friends that this is a MIcrosoft game...any invites are handled through the Xbox app on your computer, or whatever they are calling the app these days, instead of Steam.  That means if you're not playing this on a PC (Mac/Linux or Steam Deck) you are going to have a ROUGH time trying to play with friends.  It's easy enough to just jump into a multiplayer race with the random people who are already present in your game instance.  But for Steam deck players you have to jump through some hoops to actually play with your friends.  Since there is no Xbox app on the deck, you can TRY running the mobile app on your phone.  Once you are in the game, you can send invites to people on your Xbox friends list from the mobile app, and they can join your game.  This only works if you're the host though.  If someone sends you an invite, you'll never see it; the mobile app only seems to allow you to SEND invites, but not receive or accept invites sent from your friends.  Just something to keep in mind.  In summary, aside from the extra hassle of the online system, the game runs great on the deck and has been a lot of fun racing and exploring Mexico.

It didn’t take much to get me interested in [I]Forza Horizon 5[/I]. Although I prefer [I]Forza Horizon 4[/I]’s British setting over this game’s Mexican locale, I still find it to be very fun and enjoyable. Enough changes and updates were made to [I]FH5[/I] to distinguish it from its predecessor, but it’s also similar enough that fans of the franchise will feel right at home upon the game starting.  [I]FH5[/I] is a very good game in and of itself. It features plenty of road, dirt, cross country, and street racing, plus a good handful of speed traps, speed zones, drift zones, and jump challenges. At the same time, it leans into the vehicular adventure and story offerings, giving this open-world arcade driving game a bit more structure for (new) players who need some guidance on where to begin.  In Horizon Adventure, you are tasked with establishing outposts for the main event, road racing, dirt racing, cross country racing, PR stunts, and street racing. You then earn Accolades to unlock and take on the outposts’ lineups of expeditions and stories, as well as win the finale races. Of these, I especially enjoyed the few stories that flesh out the supporting characters, specifically Alejandra and Ramiro.  “Vocho” tells the importance of the VW Beetle to Alejandra’s family, and to Mexico by extension. It plays like [I]FH4[/I]’s “British Racing Green”, but with a touch of personal history. Ramiro’s fun nature shines in “Lucha de Carreteras”, which features street racing infused with lucha libre styling. “V10”, the sequel to [I]FH4[/I]’s “The Stunt Driver” that marks the return of stunt coordinator Mike Steele and actor Frankie Beaumont, is also a standout.  [I]FH5[/I]’s map is the largest one in the series to date, with varied geographical and topographical features: desert, volcano, mountain range, wetland, jungles, beaches, and plains. This map is also meteorologically diverse, with adjacent areas possibly having different weather conditions. To see a dust storm brew up during spring season is breathtaking, and to race into it is thrilling.  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3412788084 What I enjoy about [I]FH5[/I]’s Accolades system is its clarity. The game openly states what Accolades can be earned, how to earn it, and how far along you are in doing so. Browsing the lists of over 2000 Accolades inspired me to try things I previously didn’t care much for, including making an earnest effort in drifting and tuning cars. Essentially, [I]FH5[/I] fine-tunes the tried-and-true gameplay that [I]FH4[/I] offered, and provides a more well-rounded and approachable gaming experience as a result.  That being said, Accolades being one of the measures of success makes Horizon Adventure a bit too easy. Despite my benefitting from it, I feel like I didn’t earn the privilege to participate in the finale races. Does it make sense that I get to race in The Marathon, the Horizon Street Scene finale race, without having competed in a street race event? Frankly, once you’ve completed the finale race, going back to the individual race events is rather anticlimactic.  The game’s large map, while a selling point, is also a weakness. With points of interest far apart and the scenery in between being generally unremarkable, long drives get tiresome quickly. In fact, it’s more fun, efficient and productive to drive from point A to B as crow flies, so you can earn some Skill Points while you blaze across the terrain. While I’m partial to road races in [I]Forza Horizon[/I] games, I found this Mexico game map to be remarkably conducive to cross country racing and trailblazer challenges. They’re easily the best racing parts of [I]FH5[/I].  On the other hand, I found dirt racing to be spectacular, and road racing exhilarating in the [I]Rally Adventure[/I] and [I]Hot Wheels[/I] expansion packs respectively. The Badlands map in [I]Rally Adventure[/I] is more compact, but topographically interesting and fun to explore. Rally racing, a new addition to the [I]Forza Horizon[/I] franchise, introduces a layer of complexity to dirt racing that I welcome wholeheartedly. I’ve started playing rally racing in first-person mode for the extra sense of realism and excitement.  [I]Hot Wheels[/I] feels wholly unique with the setting being three aerial islands connected by the toys’ signature orange tracks, as well as ice tracks, water flumes, and magnet tracks. Although you’re confined to the tracks most of the time, thus losing some open-world exploration, speeding through loop-the-loops, diving straight into a volcano, and winding through giant trees and mountains mid-air, exploring this fantastical racing wonderland at top speed make up for the constraints.  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3412788046 And once you’ve played these expansion packs, the flaws of the main game’s map become more apparent. With it being so big, it regularly feels empty during the past two months of playing. I rarely run into other online players on the road since they’d often be hanging out at the Horizon Festival outpost or seasonal challenge locations. Other outposts are usually empty. With few traffic vehicles on the roads as well, the game world feels very dull.  Only Guanajuato, one of two featured cities, makes for interesting setting for races. Its winding narrow roads make street racing exciting, and its underground tunnels make the Hide and Seek game mode rather challenging. And of the four featured archeological sites, only Ek’Balam and Teotihuacan get the most exposure and use. It’s a shame not all landmarks get the same love and attention.  Back in February 2025 when I posted the original review, I had clocked in close to 250 hours of playtime. Back then, [I]FH5[/I] was on its 43rd monthly Festival Playlist series that features daily and weekly challenges. 400 more hours of playing later over the past 9 months, it’s without a doubt that these challenges keep me coming back more, even if it’s just for several minutes each day. These live service content manage to keep this 4-year-old game interesting for just a bit longer.  Regardless of [I]FH5[/I]’s longevity at the time of this review, I think this game is absolutely worth playing even without the live service content. While I admit the game is less fun without them, there is plenty of offline content in [I]FH5[/I] to satisfy fans of arcade driving and open-world adventure games. Because the gameplay is fine-tuned and accessible, and made even more fun with the two expansion packs, I recommend not just the Standard Edition game, but also the Premium Edition.  In my original review, I predicted that the next [I]Forza Horizon[/I] game will be set in either Germany or Japan given their rich automotive and racing histories, as well as their iconic geography and monuments. I was right! With Japan being the setting for [I]FH6[/I], I can’t wait to see how the country will be featured! Here’s to hoping [I]FH6[/I] will smooth out the few rough edges of this game and give us an even more polished racing adventure experience.  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3410009103

A must buy if you like racing games, beautiful graphics, a much more diverse map design than FH4, thousands of cars to try out and a few interesting game modes that'll keep you entertained for hours on end. I got Horizon 5 on a bundle with 4, I wasn't exactly won over except for the fact that back then it was a "new" game. Didn't even try it until after beating 4 to 100%, a game that was a bit difficult to get used to, coming from arcade racing games like NFS and Burnout, but I did find the fun on the "simulation" aspect of Forza and the pretty graphics helped a lot.  FH5 isn't that big of an upgrade on graphics but it definitely looks stunning, one thing I would like to see more on Forza games are cities, I mean, 80% of this game and the previous is in the countryside, and like I said before, coming from NFS it leaves a desire for more. FH5's map in general was an upgrade to 4 though, I like the variety of environments: jungle, desert, beaches, etc. and while FH4's main feature is missing here (more distinct seasons) I don't really miss it, I truly hated driving in the snow.   Regarding alternative game modes to common racing, it has the same as FH4 and Hide and Seek, which I did enjoy more than the others, lots of fun to be had, on the other hand is the bane of my existence, Eliminator, it wasn't that much of a headache on the previous entry, but damn this game, I read somewhere that it became so important for the developers that, supposedly, they built Mexico's map around it, like a big cauldron. I hate it, this time around there's only one achievement for it (look out achievement hunters) but boy, is it such a pain, took me 40 hours of nonstop grinding to win the game mode ONCE. I sure hope they don't make it such a big part of the next Horizon.  In conclusion, pretty fun game, breathtaking graphics, diverse map and gameplay, with the only downside being Eliminator.
